speechtext: Mr. Speaker, the hon. member for Pictou (Mr. Macdonald), in view of your ruling of yesterday in regard to the report of the Old Age Pensions Committee, has suggested that this report be referred back to the committee. Therefore it is moved by Mr. Macdonald, seconded by myself, that the report of the Old Age Pensions Committee be referred back to the committee.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: I have been looking into this matter, and I find that the report which was presented to the House has already been dealt with. The only recommendation in the report for which, I think, concurrence was desired, was with regard to printing, which would necessarily require to go to the Printing Committee. After the report was presented to this House, it was submitted to and was dealt with by the Printing Committee; therefore it could not be referred back.

The circumstances
with regard to the report were these:	A
sub-committee of the regular committee was appointed for the purpose of drafting a report. That committee did not meet, and the report as presented to the House, though assented to hurriedly by the different members, was not a full expression of the desires of the Committee. I submit that the opportunity to place properly before the House the findings and recommendations of the committee ought not to be barred by the assumption of authority on the part of any other committee of the House. In order that the matter might come before the House in proper shape, and that the views and opinions of the members of the committee might find proper expression, I suggested that the motion which has been stated by the hon. member for West Peterborough, should be made. In order that everything may be regular, and that the report of the committee may be made in proper shape, I would suggest that the consent of the House be given that the report be referred back to the committee.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext:
I think the House had a right to assume that the report as presented by the chairman of the committee was a correct and regular report. As a portion of the report refers to printing, it
was, by what authority I do not know, referred to the Printing Committee. The Printing Committee having dealt with it, the House assumes that it was a proper report, and, in my judgment, it could not now be referred back.

Except by consent of the House. Perhaps I may be permitted again to point out, with all due deference, that the control of the House over the report of any one of its committees is an absolute control, which cannot be abridged at any time by the assumption of authority on the part of any other committee. There is no great principle involved in the matter, except that the record may be proper; there is no political issue involved in it, and I would like to ask the right hon. Prime Minister, with a view to straightening the matter out, that he would consent to the passing of the motion.

I am not thoroughly familiar with the various phases of the situation, and, if the hon. gentleman will let the matter remain until Monday, I will confer with His Honour the Speaker, and members of the committee, and see what can be done.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext:
From my knowledge of the situation, as the committee has not yet dissolved, I think that if they desire to give any further consideration to the subject matter which was referred to them, it would be quite in order for them to do so.
Motion stands.

On motion of Hon. T. W. Crothers (Minister of Labour), the House went into Committee to consider the following proposed resolution:
That it is expedient to authorize the Minister of the Interior to issue a Military Bounty Land Certificate to Miss Lois B. Hutchinson, as the sole heir and personal

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext: representative of her deceased father, James Hutchinson, entitling her, or her substitute, to obtain, free of charge, an entry for a homestead of two adjoining quarter-sections of Dominion, lands, and to receive letters patent therefor, provided that such entry is made and obtained on or before December 31, 1913.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: Explain.

speakerposition: Minister of Labour
speechtext: The facts in connection *with this matter have been pretty fully , set forth in the recital. They are as follows: The father of this young lady, the late James Hutchinson, was killed at Fish Creek in the year 1885. The same year a statute was passed providing for the issue of the military bounty certificate from the Militia Department for the conferring on men who were engaged in that outbreak two quarter-sections; the party in whose favour such warrant issued was entitled to locate two quarter-sections. The original Act provided that these locations should be made not later, I think, than some day in the month of August, 1886. The time for locating was from time to time extended, the last extension being made, I think, in 1906, until the 31st of December of that year. A warrant was issued in favour of the late James Hutchinson, but his daughter never located the scrip. At the time of her father's death she was a child in arms, her mother has since died, and she is the sole representative and heiress of her late father. It is thought well to grant her now what she would have *been entitled to prior to 1908 if she had not overlooked the locating of it. Of course it may be regarded as un undesirable precedent to pass such a Bill, but I am told by one of the officers of my department, Mr. Cote, that there is no other similar case before the department. I understand that when my hon. friend from Edmonton (Mr. Oliver) was Minister of the Interior, he considered the circumstances of this case and was in favour of introducing a Bill such as I am proposing to found on this resolution. I think this is a case where we should render this young woman the special privilege that is proposed under this resolution and the accompanying Bill.

As my hon. friend has said, this matter was brought to my attention when I was Minister of the Interior, and I was entirely favourably impressed with the righteousness of the claim made by the young woman. I think a Bill was prepared for introduction to Parliament, but the Government changed, and of course the Bill dropped. I know it is objectionable to revive old claims, but, whatever might be said of the general principle, this is such a very exceptional case, that I think Parliament will do itself credit to pass the legislation which is proposed by the minister. As my hon. friend has said, the father of the applicant was killed in battle. He was entitled, or his heirs were entitled, to this consideration. A scrip was issued, but there Mr. CROTHERS.
was no person to take it up at the time. The father was dead, the mother died, the child had not come to years of knowledge, and consequently the right lapsed. Now the young woman, having become of age, desires to assert her claim, which I would consider her right, to the property earned by the sacrifice of her father's life."
Resolution reported, read the first and the second time, and concurred in.
Mr. CROTHERS thereupon moved for leave to introduce Bill No. 232, to make further provision respecting grants of land to members of the Militia Force on active service in the Northwest.

speechtext: The House proceeded to consider the Senate amendment to Bill No. 180, to amend the Supreme Court Act. - Mr, Doherty.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
The amendment made by the Senate is to the last clause of the Bill as it passed this House, amending sec. 49 of the Supreme Court Act. That is the sec. dealing with appeals from Ontario. The amendment of the Senate provides that:	,
Where the right to appeal depends upon the amount or value of the matter in controversy, and no specific sum is claimed, the amount or value of the matter in controversy may be proved by affidavit or affidavits.
That amendment was made by the bill as it passed this House to section 49 of the Act which deals with appeals from Ontario. The preceding section, which deals with Quebec, also makes appeals in certain cases dependent upon the amount yi issue and contained precisely the same provision that the amount demanded or the value should be a certain sum to entitle a party to appeal. Amending section 49 made the amending provision applicable only to appeals from Ontario, whereas, the provision, if desirable, should be equally applicable in both cases. The amendment consists in making provision generally that where the right to appeal depends upon the value in controversy and no specific sum is claimed the value may be proved by affidavit or affidavits.

Does that apply to
every appeal in any part of Canada?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Wherever there would be a section providing that the right to appeal depended on the amount in issue and no demand was made of a specific sum so that on the face of the record the value of the matter in issue did not appear, it would apply.
It applies to any of the other provinces?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
To any provinces where the Tight of appeal depends on the value in issue and the amount does not appear on the record.
Amendment read the second time and agreed to.

speechtext: With regard to this motion to go into Committee of Supply, I am not sure how it stands under the new rules, under which on Thursdays and Fridays the Speaker leaves the Chair without any motion being put; but only those estimates which have been taken up on some other day than Thursday or Friday can be considered, except with the consent of the House. I take it that with the consent of the House we follow the rule, and the Speaker leaves the Chair without motion.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: I do not know whether I understand the rules rightly or not. Mv interpretation of the motion is that on Thursday and Friday the Speaker leaves the Chair without motion, automatically; but on that day no estimates can be taken up except those which have previously been considered.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: I do not know if I understand correctly. Mr. Speaker seems to be under the impression that he must know what estimates are to be taken up. Automatically the Speaker leaves the Chair, but then the Government are required to take up estimates which have been previously considered.

It seems to me that this question does not arise at the present time, because the estimates of every department have already been considered during this session. That was before the
new rules.

Rules are technical things.

Department of Marine and Fisheries-civil-government, $246,200.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: My civil government estimates are practically the same as those of last year, with certain statutory increases.
Would the hon. minister indicate the promotions that have taken place in his department in the last year and the additions to salaries?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
There are practically no additions to salaries beyond the statutory increases. The salary of the Deputy Minister is the same. In the first division, subdivision A, the salary of the assistant Deputy Minister is the same; of the Chief Engineer, the same; of Professor Prince, Inspector of Fisheries, the same; Mr. Dou-tre, Purchasing Agent, statutory increase: Mr. Fraser, Assistant Chief Engineer, statutory increase; Mr. Boyle, Accountant, statutory increase; Mr. MePhail, statutory increase; Mr. Boyle, Accountant, statutory increase; Mr. Found, statutory increase; Mr. Lindsay, statutory increase. There was a vacancy in the position of Chairman of the Board of 'Steamboat Inspection. The salary of the Chairman is $2,800. That vacancy was caused by the retirement of Mr. Adams and has been filled by the promotion of Mr. Ferguson, who has been stationed at Quebec. Then there is the salary of Mr. Halkett, $2,800.
In the first division, subdivision B, the salaries last year were $41,650; this year they are $45,100, being the same as last year with the statutory additions.
In the second division, subdivision A, the salaries last year were $49,600; this year they are $55,850. There are thirty-two positions provided for, an increase of three over last year. It is proposed to appoint a fog alarm inspector, a mechanical engineer and an inspecting engineer, whose services are found necessary in the work of the department. As regards the salaries paid to the different officials, there is a full list here if any hon. gentleman desires to see it. In reference to the appointment of a mechanical engineer, the department has been without the services of such an engineer since Mr. Macdonnell was transferred some years ago to the Steamboat Inspection branch, which takes up the whole of his time. He used to be able to give us his assistance when the services of a mechanical engineer were required. The mechanical engineering branch is constantly engaged in the design, manufacture and repair of fog alarm and other apparatus of all kinds, including numerous kinds of buoys. The opinion of the head of the branch is that the services of a fully qualified mechanical engineer are absolutely essential. With regard to the Fog Alarm Inspector, Mr. Macdonnell has performed this work for a number of years. Since his transfer, the Commissioner of Lights, Mr. MePhail, has carried on the work as best as he could. He has not found it possible, along with the general work of his office, to give this inspection the attention Mr. HAZEN.
it requires. It is therefore necessary to_ provide for a third position in subdivision A at $1,600.
In the second division, subdivision B, there are thirty-four positions provided for, an increase of seven over last year. The salaries last year were $32,550; this year they are $38,050. These seven new places will be filled by appointing clerks in the various branches, some at $800 and some at $850 a year.
With regard to naval architects at $1,200 a year, the work of designing and preparing plans for all steamers that are constructed by the Government is done by the Department of Marine and Fisheries. The head of the branch, the chief architect, is Mr. Duguid. It is found that we cannot keep up with the work, as Mr. Duguid has to be away from the office so much of his timfr inspecting vessels that are in course of construction. It is nteoessary therefore, to give him assistance in his work.
Does the minister think that we can secure the services of a good naval architect for $1,200 a year?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: These are only draughtsmen and assistants. We have I believe,_ a first-class naval architect in Mr. Duguid, a gentleman who, some years ago, I understand, was recommended by Lord Strath-cona who had been applied to to assist in securing the services of such a man. The assistants will be young men of experience as draughtsmen and who will no doubt develop. They will be in the class whose salaries begin at $1,200, and go on by annual increments to $1,600.
Will they be subject to examination?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
These men will be chosen through the Civil Service Commission, who no doubt, will advertise for applicants and make the choice in the ordinary way.
M.r. SINCLAIR : This is a matter of very great importance. I have heard it stated by those engaged in ship-building that the Department of Marine and Fisheries has not been able to supply the information on which a tender should be made. I am informed that in many cases the Department ask the builder who is tendering to submit his own plans.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: That has been done.

That is a very awkward and unbusiness like way to deal with the matter. The department should know what kind of ship they require and should be able to give the builders, especially the builders in Canada who have not yet had great experience, full details to form the basis of a tender.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: That is exactly the reason we are trying to increase this organization. Formerly description was given in a general way of the kind of ship wanted, and the builders were asked to tender submitting their own designs and plans. I do not see how it was possible to come to a fair conclusion as to whom the contract should be given to. I found that state of affairs when I entered the department and discussed the subject with the officials. Hereafter, when we ask for tenders we expect to give plans and full details. When all tenderers base their offers on the same plans, we can then judge whose tender is the lowest and most advantageous. But, until we complete the organization, we cannot follow that method.

How many officers has
the minister appointed in the inside, and how many in the outside service, since the present Administration came into office?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: Very few in the inside service, in the higher positions; nearly all minor clerkships. There have been some in the outside service in connection with the lighthouse service and that sort of thing. I cannot give figures at the moment, but will be able to give them later on. Passing from that, we come to the third division subdivision (A). Last year the amount was $35,050, and this year $40,800. There is no change in the number of clerks-there are thirty-eight-and the increase is made up of the statutory increases alone.
Do statutory increases depend upon the recommendation of any officials in the department?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
Upon that of the deputy
Minister. If the Deputy recommends the official as worthy of the increase he gets it, but if the official's work has not been satisfactory and the Deputy-Minister so reports, he does not get it. Coming down to the third division subdivision (B), last year the amount was $20,900, this year it is $17,850. We are providing for twenty-nine positions as against twenty-four. The clerks to be appointed numbered five, at $500 a year each, the very lowest class-they are stenographers. There are but two permanent stenographers for the fisheries correspondence proper. They have been unable to cope with the work and it has been necessary to employ temporary clerks almost continuously throughout the year. There will be an additional one also in the Commissioner of Lights' branch. This was made necessary by the fact that Miss Percival was transferred to the Accountants' branch and to fill the position Miss Hill was employed temporarily. That position must be filled permanently. These are all positions which it is absolutely necessary to fill that the work in the department may be carried on. I am told by men in the department
who have been there for years, that the work in the department increases every year and has increased very rapidly in the last few years. This is due in part to the greater volume of business in connection with the fisheries of British Columbia, where there has been a tremendous development. Then, for messengers, the amount provide^ last year was $5,500, and this year $6,700. This increase provides for the statutory increases and also for two additional messengers. The Department of Marine and Fisheries is scattered almost all over town. There is not only the main office in the western block, but there we have an office on Sparks street, one on Wellington street, and the branch in the Corry building and others. An increase in the staff of messengers is absolutely necessary, as papers have to be constantly carried by messengers from one branch of the department to another. That covers the different items which make up the civil government estimates

How many dismissals
have been made for political partisanship in the department of the minister since he took charge?
Mr. HAZEN. So far as the inside service is concerned, I do not think there have been any dismissals for political partisanship. In the outside service there have been quite a number of dismissals. I have not a statement before me, but I will have it made out for my hon. friend if he so desires.

The feeling in my constituency and along the coast of Nova Scotia in regard to the Marine and Fishery Department is that the minister has been very reckless indeed so far as dismissals are concerned. He has resorted to the spoils system, pure and simple, showing very little regard for the rights of the officers and not extending to them an opportunity for a fair and proper investigation of their cases. I would have expected that the minister, coming from the maritime provinces, knowing the hardships endured and the small salaries received by the lighthouse keepers on the coast, would have had some consideration for them, and, at ail events, would have given them a fair trial, but so far as the action of his department in this regard has come under my own observation, I cannot say that he has done so. There have been a very large number of dismissals in my constituency, and in many cases trials have been conducted, in a star-chamber way, in the bedrooms of hotels, garrets and places of that kind. Witnesses have been examined. in some cases in the absence of the person accused. Most of the marine officers on the coast of my constituency have been dismissed, with
106S7

the exception of a few lighthouse keepers. The greatest sinners in this regard are the Postmaster -Genera] (Mr. Pelletier), the Minister of Customs (Mr. Reid) and the Minister of Marine and Fisheries (Mr. Hazen). There is a very striking passage in one of the minor prophets of the Old Testa-.ment in which a scourge of insects or grub3 is described in this way: What the locust left, the canker-worm ate; what the canker-worm left, the caterpiller ate, and when the caterpiller got through there was not anything left. That very fairly indicates the conditions connected with the dismissal of Liberal officials employed on the coast of my constituency. What the Minister of Customs left, the Postmaster General devoured, what the Postmaster General left, the Minister of Marine and Fisheries devoured, and when the Minister of Marine and Fisheries got through there was scarcely a single Liberal officer left in the fish hatcheries and lifeboat stations on the one hundred and fifty miles of the coast of my constituency.
The case to which I wish to refer specially is that of W. L. Munro, who was light-keeper on an island known as Three Top Island in the harbour of Whitehead. He was appointed to the position in 1879 by the Conservative administration, and served in the capacity of lightkeeper for 32 years. The island is an unsheltered rock off Whitehead, exposed to all the storms of the Atlantic; in winter time it is very difficult to reach the shore at all, and the keeper is often imprisoned for weeks at a time. Mr. Munro tvas appointed under the old system under which light keepers, after serving a certain number of years reaching a certain age, were entitled to be retired under pension. Mr. Munro claims that he was entitled to receive a pension after being thirty-two years in the service, but his dismissal has been used as a reason why he should not receive a pension. This man is a sailor, and somewhat excitable, and while a Conservative in his early days, he later acquired an admiration for Sir Wilfrid Laurier. At the close of a meeting in the . schoolhouse in his district he is said to have proposed three cheers for Sir Wilfrid, and I understand that that is one of the . chief reasons why this man, who served for thirty-two years in the capacity of lighthouse keeper, and who was entitled to a pension, was discharged from the service and refused a pension.
The charges against this lighthouse keeper were first made in February, 1912, and there was a lengthy correspondence between him and the Department of Marine and Fisheries, part of which I wish to put on record. The minister delayed action for a long time and finally threw Munro to the wolves and denied him his, position and the pension to which he claimed to be entitled.
Mr. SINCLAIR.
His case is a hard one. He has a family, and is now well up in years. He opened his heart to the minister, approaching him personally by writing a letter of which he sent me a copy. In February, 1912, Mr. Munro wrote the following letter to the minister:
Whitehead, N.-S., February 8, 1912. To the Honourable,
Minister Hazen,
Minister of Marine and Fisheries, House of Commons, Ottawa.
My Honourable Sir,^I presume among others, you have me slated for my dismissal. And whether I am right in doing so, I thought I would drop you a line regarding it. I trust, honourable Sir, as I have been keeper of this station for thirty-two years and some months, that if I am dismissed, that you will see that I get a superannuation, as of course, after twenty years of any man's life there is not much strength left in him for hard toil and dragging. I am now sixty years of age past, and sti'l burdened with the care of three grandchildren after raising a family of my own, ten children, and among them only one hoy and what help I had it was always hired help; and the small salary I always got which of course was a help, I always had to work hard in order to make ends meet.
I am not ashamed to say I was appointed in 1879, and up to 1896 I always voted Conservative, hut as the latter Government was good enough to let me hold my job, I thought it my duty to vote for them, and as far as votes goes we are square; however, you will, I trust, honourable Sir, allow me your sincere consideration, and have me granted a superannuation if I am dismissed. I trust you won't have it done this winter while so rough and boisterous.
I am dear honourable Sir,
Your very obedient servant,
(Sgd.) W. L. Munro.
Mr. Munro also wrote a little sketch of his life, setting forth some feats of bravery he had performed while residing on this island. This he handed to the press for publication, sending me a copy as well. It is a very interesting story; it discloses the hardships suffered by and the heroic conduct of this man while he was in the service of the department. I submitted this statement of Munro to the minister prior to his dismissal, so that the minister would not have the excuse that he was not familiar with all the details with regard to this man's service and his merits. In sending this sketch to the minister, I wrote him as follows:
February 13, 1912.
Hon. J. D. Hazen,
Minister of Marine and Fisheries, Ottawa. Re proposed dismissal of IV. L. Munro.
Dear Mr. Hazen-Referring to this case* I am enclosing a letter written by Mr. Munro himself to the press, some time ago, relating some of the feats that he performed in saving life, during his long service as light keeper at White Head.
I submit that these matters ought to he considered in connection with the action of
1C689

the department at present. It would be quite satisfactory to Mr. Munro and his many friends there on both sides of politics, if lie received his pension under the original arrangement in _ force at the time that he entered the service.
You will notice by his answer which you have on your file, when asked to select between his pension and the payment of his *money back, that instead, that he gave a sort of indefinite reply by saying that he would ' vote for this.'
There is not the slightest doubt that Mr. Munro intended to retain his pension. At all events, even if the other view is taken, it is very clear that if the matter was fully explained to him, he would never have selected to take back the money paid in instead of his retiring allowance. I understand that his retiring allowance for two years would amount to more than the cash to ' which he would be entitled.
I trust, therefore, that you can see your way clear either to leave this light in his possession or grant him his pension.
I remain;
Yours truly,
J. H. Sinclair.
I want to read to the Committee the statement given by Mr. Munro to the public and to the minister with regard to the services that he performed. Told in his own simple, sailor fashion, it contains some real touches of nature, and ought to have reached the heart of the minister:
Allow me space please in your valuable
paper to insert a sketch of my past thirty-two years as lighthouse keeper on what is known as or called by mariners, Three Top Island, which lies at west entrance of White Head harbour, one mile from the mainland being W.N.W. from White Head light, distance one mile. The light is called a harbour light by many, but not like many harbour lights on the coast, whereas most such lights are situated on the mainland.
Thi9 island takes its name by having three hills as nature formed it, each hill or peak, as we wish to call it, running eighty to a hundred feet, horizontally, with no real landing place, such as a beach but is iron bound, so to speak, all around, with a boat slip running down a steep embankment where with block and tackle *attached to a capstan that is fixed in a boathouse on the side of the cliff, we haul our boat to safety, which by times, when there is a heavy sea on, is a pretty risky piece of business. Many times I have had my boat filled in effecting a landing.
Well, Mr. Editor, the life of a light keeper is a dreary one, watching the storm tossed seas that I have witnessed time and again caused by heavy winter gales on the southern coast of our province, facing the Atlantic ocean.
I remember one storm in particular about eighteen years ago in February. The sea in one of its fierce rushes burst in our door at ten o'clock at night and flooded our floors to a depth of six inches of water. My wife and the children screamed, thinking they were doomed. I got them gathered to a window, there to make our exit and flee to one of the highest peaks, but in this case Providence favoured us by the gale moderating, and, the
sea falling some, did not cause us to face such an ordeal in a wintr's hurricane on a naked cliff.
Also, Mr. Editor, I could relate several eases in sheltering shipwrecked crews since my abode as lightkeeper, if space could afford. One case in particular I must relate. It was on a Christmas eve about 16 years ago, if I remember right. There was a heavy gale raging from the northeast with enow and the temperature was at zero. My three eldest daughters were on the mainland at the time attending a concert at the Methodist church that they were taking part in. The small children had retired early in the evening as usual. My wife and I went to bed about half past ten o'clock, after seeing that .Santa Claus was to visit the island, and I suppose we had been retired about 20 minutes, I had about fallen to sleep, when my wife aroused me by telling me that she heard a horn blowing. X told her she was dreaming, to go to sleep; but to please her I got up and went to the door to investigate. I found to my horror, that she was right, for there on the reef that extends southeast away from the mainland about two hundred yards, lay a stranded vessel, and they were blowing horns and shouting for their lives for the keeper to save them, as they thought from the way their ship was pounding, she would break up, and certainly they would be doomed under such circumstances. Well, my man being ashore to spend his holidays of course left me alone. I dressed and went to the cliff, as near as I could venture, and shouted as loud as I could not to attempt it until daylight. Well, I do not suppose they could hear me, but their wailings were terrible to hear on such a night. And again I went and shouted to them to take their own boat and I would guide them by a torch. Well, again they could not hear me, as they kept u.p their wailings. I could hear the wind whistling in the wreck, .but I leave that to one's imagination, what it sounded like together with their shouting to save them. Well, I went to the house and told my wife that in God's name I would try and launch a boat and go off to the wreck, and, of course, as usual with women, my wife crying and begging me not to dare such a thing on such an awful night, and the children awakened by the tumult to make matters worse, joined their mother in begging me not to go, and I was pretty near abandoning the idea altogether until daylight. Well, I went out of doors and down to the cliff, and by the way their shouting seemed to me, I imagined there were at least, some of them in the water and perhaps drowning. And then I said to myself, I am going to try it anyway and if I get lost it will be in a good cause trying to save my fellow men. Well, I lit a pine .torch, or flare up, as some call them, ancl my wife following me, I went to the slip and let the boat down, as far a9 I dared, the sea coming up by times half way to the slip. As the gale was blowing fair on it was so much the worse to get clear. Wdll, as I went to run down and after lowering her and did unhook the boat there came a heavy sea and swept the boat clear of me just as 1 was in the act of leaping into her, she turned completely bottom up. Well that pretty near discouraged me. However, I had another boat in store that I had stowed away educe

the past summer not intending to launch her until spring lobster fishing. To tier I Tan and got her on the slip but haring only one pair of oars left it was risky, losing two pairs in the first boat. However, I let the boat down part way this time, put my oars in her, unhooked my tackle and sprung into the boat, taking chances going down the slip equal to ' loop the loop ' and landed safe in the boiling water made by the gale. Well, I grabbed my oars and as skillfully as I could managed my boat until I got out to the wreck, which I found to be the George P. Trigg, from Charlottetown, Prince Edward Island, bound to Boston, loaded with several thousand bushels of oats. She was trying to make the harbour to clear the storm when stranded. They had lowered the boat when first she struck the ledge and lost the boat in the sea. I found the men very much frightened. They all wanted to get in my small boat at once, hut I told them to do as I told them and I would try and land them. So 1 took three men at a time getting to the Island. My wife held the torch and that was a great help to me. I backed the boat stern first as near to the surf as I dared, and told the men to leap which they did and landed safe, and then I began another struggle for the wreck, which I gained after a hard fight and got the captain, mate and the remaining one of the crew. Of course I dare not allow any one to touch my oars but myself as I had only one pair and to break one we were doomed. However, I reached the Island and landed safely, thank God, where we were all housed at 3 o'clock in the morning of Christmas day. The wreck presented a gloomy looking sight in the morning. The top of the hull which was above water, was a mass of ice, where no one could go near her for a couple of days. I can vouch also, for keeping five wrecked crew6 for over a week at a time. All for which I have never received one cent. Although I billed parties, I was never recognized after.
My family consists of ten children, seven girls and three boys, of which two died young and one girl died also. After reaching womanhood four reside at Somerville, Mass., the eldest, Mary, marrying Mr. J. D. McLean, a contractor in the steamfitting business, the next, Alice, a music teacher, lives with her sister, also, Edith, lives with her sister, and their next youngest sister i9 attending high school at Somerville.
I want to say Mr. Editor, that my family were all born on this island, and the seven that are living are in good health to-day. The one living son and the baby girl are home yet with us. The fourth girl, M'aud, married at home to Mr. Alden Munro. They reside at White Head. I came here in the year of our Lord, 1879, which year the light was built, after being married two years and am here yet. My salary has been very small. After paying a man a year and feeding him at the high cost of living, three hundred dollars does not go far.
Now, Mr. Editor, I will conclude by saying, To give me justice don't you think that I am worthy of a superannuation fund when I leave this island which I suppose will be very soon
new ?
Well, I will leave that part of the pro-Mr. SINCLAIR.
gramme to be judged by my superior, as it would he a help to us in our older days.
Thanking you kindly Mr. Editor for your space allotted.
Yours truly.
W. L. Munro, Lightkeeper.
The Editor published the above, and added:
Of course Mr. Munro will be superannuated. The Dominion of Canada cannot afford to do its housekeeping by turning off old servants who havq served it 60 gallantly for so many years, without anything to live upon so far as the country is concerned.-Editor, Eastern Chronicle.
The minister promptly replied to that letter which I sent to him, enclosing that statement. He said:
I am in receipt of your favour of 12th instant inclosing a letter from Mr. Munro, of Whitehead, N.S., and wish to assure you that it will have my very careful consideration.
.	Yours very truly,
J. D. Hazen.
I had a reply also from the Deputy Minister to the same effect. You will notice that three months before he took action to dismiss Mr. Munro the minister was familiar with all the details of this case. He was aware of the fact that Mr. Munro was an old and faithful servant appointed by the Conservative government a long time ago. He was aware that he had spent 32 years on the Island, and that there was no legitimate complaint against him. He was aware of the fact that he had served for a mere pittance, receiving only about $300 a year. He was also informed that this man claimed a pension, and that under the law. as it existed at the time of his appointment, there was no doubt at all that he was entitled to a pension. The next letter I have here is an intimation from the department that this man had been dismissed. It is a letter from Mr. Staton:
I have to inform you that by Order in Council of the Ith April, 1912, your services as keeper of the light at Three Top Island, N.S., have been dispensed with owing to political partisanship, and that Mr. Howard IS. Munro has been appointed temporarily keeper of the light, to whom I have to request you to give up possession of the light and of all Government supplies pertaining thereto when required.
What was the charge of partisanship?

It appears that there
was an investigation, but it also appears that it was a very one sided and unfair investigation. The commissioner who conducted this sham investigation disregarded the law altogether, and declined to allow Mr. Munro to be represented by counsel.

The committee can understand how helpless a man of this character would be in a court of that kind without any one to assist him, or to place his case before the court.
Was Duchemin the examiner?
He was the examiner.
Did he decline to permit Mr. Munro to have counsel?

Yes. The declaration is as follows:
Dominion of Canada, county of Guysborough.
In the matter of the conduct of H. P. Ducliemin at an investigation in the case of W. L. 'Munro, held at White Head on the 13th of March, A.D. 1912.
I, W. L. Munro, of White Head, in the county of Guysborough, province of Nova Scotia, do solemnly declare:-
That I appeared before H. P. Duchemin, commissioner, on the 13th day of March, 1912, at the hour and place indicated in my notice and asked the said Duchemin if he would be kind enough to allow me to have a counsel to act for me and cross-examine witnesses at the said investigation. The said Duchemin refused to permit me to have a counsel and stated that he himself was all the counsel that I would require in that investigation.
And I make this solemn declaration conscientiously believing the same to be true and knowing that it is of the same force and effect as if made under oath and by virtue of the Canada Evidence Act.
W. L. Munro.
Declared before me at White Head, in the the county of Guysborough, province of Nova Scotia, this 30th day of December, A.D. 1912.
W. S. Harris.
A justice of the peace in and for the county of Guysborough.
I have already drawn the attention of the House and of the minister to the statute that was passed last year, in which it is distinctly stated that the commissioner may allow any person whose conduct is being investigated under the Act, and shall allow any person against whom any charge is made in the course of investigation, to be represented by counsel.

The hon. gentleman is aware that the premier, some weeks ago, stated, while discussing that law, that he was clearly of opinion that every man was entitled to counsel and that it would be an injustice if counsel were not permitted to him.

I am quite well aware
that the Premier took the ground that without a statute at all, every man accused of any irregularity of this kind was entitled to counsel, but there is not much use of statements of that kind being made by the Prime Minister from his place in this House if they are to be disregarded by his
officers throughout the country. This man, Duchemin, has been disregarding this provision for several months and has been doing so with the full knowledge of the Government. It has been drawn to the attention of the Prime Minister and various members of the Government, over and over again, and he is still travelling as a scourge around the coast carrying bn this same kind of work, holding these same sham investigations, dismissing honest men without proper evidence and there is nothing done by the Government, or any department of the Government, to prevent it. A few days ago a return was brought down showing that this man had received a very large sum of money from various departments of the Government. The figure, including his living and travelling expenses, amounts to something over $6,000 at the present time. I do not know whether that brings his salary up to date, but it strikes me that it is a very great farce that we should have a man like that employed at such work, travelling around, disregarding the law, committing acts of injustice day after day and being paid a very large sum of money for doing so.
Would it not be better to have a permanent executioner employed?

It would be much better if the Government would take the repons-ibility of saying: We are going to adopt the spoils system, we are going to dismiss every man who is a Liberal, and are going to put one of - our own men in his place. If they took that ground we could understand it, but sending a man of this character along the coast pretending to hold investigations and refusing the right to be represented by counsel to persons against whom charges are made, is an intolerable thing in a free country. After I had received the facts in reference to the dismissal of Mr. Munroe, I brought the question of his right to superannuation allowance to the attention of the minister in a letter dated the 16th of May, 1912, and which is as follows:
May 16, 1912.
Hon. J. D. Hazen,
Minister of Marine and Eisheries,
Ottawa.
Dear Mr. Hazen,-
I have been informed by W. L. Munro, lightkeeper at Three Top Island, White Head, N.S., that he has been dismissed from the service.
This man's case has been before your department for some time and if you can find time to deal with it I should be obliged. He appears to me to be entitled to a pension. He has served, I understand, over thirty-two years. At the time of the change in the law he signed some document which was indefinite in language and which he says was misunderstood by him, but which might he construed

to mean that he would accept a Teturn of his money with interest in lieu of his pension, to which he was clearly entitled.
I feel sure he never intended this result, and if you have not the proof at hand I could furnish an affidavit hy himself. The matter has been drifting along without any decision being given, but now, on account of his dismissal, it should be adjusted. I will, therefore, thank you to deal with the matter at your earliest convenience.
You will also note that Mr. Munroe is entitled to a proportional amount of his salary for one month and fourteen days up to the date of his dismissal.	'
Yours truly,
(Sgd.) J. H. Sinclair.
The minister was kind enough to reply to my letter blit the reply was very unsatisfactory to me. He says:
23rd May, 1912.
Dear Sir,-I beg to acknowledge receipt of your letter of the 16th dust., with respect to the case of Mr. Munro, and his request for superannuation.
In connection with this matter I beg to advise you that inasmuch as Mr. Munro was dismissed from the service, he would not be entitled to superannuation in any case. He will, however, be entitled to a refund of the money which stands to his credit in the retirement fund.
Yours faithfully,
(Sgd.) J. D. Hazen.
These are the facts of the case as briefly as I can give them to you. I thought it was important that I should put the documents on record for reference later on. The case is simply this, that Mr. Munro was dismissed on very slight evidence indeed as far as I can learn. The evident I have not yet received. It is also the custom of this man, Duchemin, not to return the evidence given by witnesses. He returns what he calls a report, and, as far ,as' I can learn, in many cases the report is r.ot borne out by the evidence. We have been unable to get the exact evidence given by witnesses, but from the statement made to me by Mr. Munro himself, there were various trifling charges brought against him. The principal one was the fact that he gave three cheers, or proposed three cheers, for Sir Wilfrid Laurier in the school fhouse at a political meeting. That, he gives me as precisely the reason why a man who had served the country for thirty-two years should be deprived of his position and also deprived of the pension to which he was entitled, You will note that the minister gives no other reason for depriving this man of his life pension except that he has been dismissed from the service. He was dismissed from the service for this partisan reason and dismissed by a commissioner who refused to give him a fair trial and refused to allow him to be represented by counsel. The minister had not , very much at stake in this matter, but Mr. Mr. SINCLAIR.
Munro had a great deal. He had spent his whole lifetime on that island and his future was involved in the decision that the minister gave. I submit that thirty-two years of faithful service ought to have had a better reward. The minister, before he arrived at his decision, ought to have made himself very certain that there was a clear case against Mr. Munro, and that Mr. Munro had obtained a fair trial. That is the least that the Minister ought to have done when we consider the fact that this man had so much at stake. During these 32 years he thought he was earning a retiring allowance, living on that bleak island, keeping the lamps trimmed and the lights burning over those rough waters and performing acts of bravery for which he was never rewarded. This is a case in which it will be very difficult for my hon. friend to satisfy the country, and especially the people who know Mr. Munro, that his action is justifiable.
It is an outiage to my mind that a man charged with a trifling political irregularity should be refused the right to be represented by counsel. A man charged with the vilest crime is represented by counsel, and in our courts, if he does not employ counsel himself, the judge sees that counsel is nominated and appointed so that the man is bound to have a fair trial in every British court. It is only in this court, and at this trial, held by my hon. friend and his colleagues week after week in Nova Scotia, that these common, ordinary rights of a British subject are denied. This is a very serious matter for Mr. Munro. I do not know what recompense the minister can give, but he certainly ought to give some. What he ought to do would be to restore Mr. Munro to his position, to take him back and give him his retiring allowance. That is the only thing I can suggest that would appear to me to do the case justice.

As I said a few moments ago before my hon. friend commenced to speak, I appreciate very much bis courtesy in telling me that he intended to bring this matter to the attention of the House, and his having notified me of the fact enables me to lay before the committee today all the facts as they appear in connection with this matter from the official files of the department, and, when I say as they appear from the official files of the department, I mean as they appear from the correspondence and the information which the department has, or which I, as minister, have, with regard to the matter. I shall first refer to what my hon. friend said about this gentleman being refused his superannuation.
Mr. Munro was appointed keeper of the light at Three Top Island, Whitehead, by Order in Council of the 31st October, 1879,

his appointment to date from the 1st September of that year.
From the records it does not appear that Mr. Munro's performance of the duties of his office was always satisfactory to the department. In the month of June, 1898, the then member for the constituency, the late Hon. D. C. Fraser, was advised by the then Minister of Marine and Fisheries, Sir Louis Davies, that it was found necessary to censure Mr. Munro for absenting himself without leave.
This dissatisfaction appears to have continued, for, in a letter addressed by the deputy minister to the agent at Halifax on the 27th September, 1901, the following extract appears:
With reference to the dissatisfaction of Supt. Hutchins with the manner in which this light is attended to, I have to direct you to communicate with the keeper, and intimate that you have been instructed by the department to censure him for inattention to his duties as keeper, and that in future he must see that his station is kept in good order, as in the event of any further complaint reaching the department it will be necessary to take steps to dispense with his services as lightkeeper.
About the same time, Mr. Munro's request that he be supplied with fuel for his light station was answered by the deputy minister of that day, who pointed out that, as all .the reports to the department with respect to the lightkeeper were unfavourable, his request would not be entertained.
On the 29th March, 1906, a letter was received at the department from Mr. J. H. Sinclair, M.P., intimating that Mr. Munro's health was failing and that he desired to be superannuated. Mr. Sinclair asked whether he was entitled to superannuation.
On the 4th April, 1906, Mr. Sinclair was advised that Mr. Munro had contributed to the superannuation tax from the date of his appointment up to the 1st December, 1898, when he elected to come under the Retirement Act from the 1st January, 1899. He was further advised that, if Mr. Munro retired, as he appeared to think of doing on the ground of ill-health, the amount to his credit in the Retirement Fund, with interest, would be paid to him, but that he would not be superannuated.
On the 4th April, 1906, Mr. Sinclair inquired as to the amount that Mr. Munro would be entitled to if he resigned. He was advised on the 24th April that the amount to which Mr. Munro would be entitled on retiring would be $268.84.
What is the hon. minister reading from?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: I am reading from a letter addressed to you on the 24th April from the department.
Will the hon. minister read the whole letter?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
I shall be glad to get it
and read it to my hon. friend.
On the 29th January, 1910, Mr. Sinclair again directed the attention of the department to the matter of superannuation for Mr. Munro. On the 7th February, 1910, Mr. Sinclair was advised in reply -that Mr. Munro was not entitled to superannuation. It was pointed out to Mr. Sinclair that Mr. Munro had elected to come under the new Act from the 1st January, 1899.

If the hon. minister will permit me, the whole of his argument is based on the alleged answer that Mr. Munro gave to the department at the time he was asked to elect. Mr. Munro has never admitted that he made that answer. His case was in dispute under the former minister and is still in dispute under the present minister. Unless the hon. minister can give us the paper under which it is alleged that Mr. Munro elected to come under the new Act, he has no basis on which to found his argument.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
If my hon. friend will have patience I shall come to that later. I am reading this to the House to show that, while the hon. gentleman accused me of being hard-hearted and cruel, he went time and again to his own political friends when they were in office; and the hon. minister, whom he was supporting in this House, would not agree to superannuate Mr. Munro and gave it as the ruling of the department that he was not entitled to superannuation.
On the 26th January, 1911, Mr. Sinclair again brought
I object to having extracts from letters read; I should like to have the whole letter read.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
On the 26th January, 1911, Mr. Sinclair again brought the question of Mr. Munro's superannuation to the notice of the then minister. Mr. Sinclair pointed out to the minister, Mr. Brodeur, that Mr. Munro alleged that he did not understand that the document which he had signed some years previously was one that precluded him from being eligible for superannuation.
The copy of the circular forwarded to Mr. Munro as'lightkeeper is as follows:
Circular.
Department of Marine and Fisheries,
Ottawa, July 12, 1898.
Sir,-I enclose herewith copy of the Act passed at last session of Parliament, providing for the abolition of the Civil Service Superannuation Act, and as you will observe by reference to the second section that the Act applies to every person now in the Civil Service, who before the 1st of January next, with the consent of the Governor in Council, elects to accept its provisions in lieu of those of the Civil Service Superannuation Act, I have to request you to inform me as soon as possible



as to whether you wish to come under this Act and to avail yourself of its provisions.
I am, Sir, your obedient servant,
(Sgd.) F. Gourdeau, _ Deputy Minister of Marine and Fisheries.
Mr. Munro's reply is dated 6th September, 1898, and is to the following effect:
The circular sent me concerning the Retirement Fund, I have received and considered it and have to inform you that I will give my vote for it.
Mr. Sinclair was advised, in reply to his letter of the 26th January, 1911, that the situation had not changed since the department's decision was communicated to him on the 7th February of the previous year.
I am just reading the information that was before the department when this decision was given on three or four separate occasions when the attention of the department was called to it by my hon. friend long before the prssent Government came into office, and when the department was under the administration of _ gentlemen who belong to a different political party. My hon. friend, when insinuating that I was hard-hearted, ought, in fairness, to have stated these facts to the House. I do not think it was quite candid and disingenuous of him not to do so. I came into the department and find the case decided.

It was not settled until the question was raised. This correspondence was preliminary. I admit the decision of the department was not to allow superannuation, but the question could not arise for settlement until the man retired from his position.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
I do not think that argument is creditable to the intelligence of my hon. friend. He wrote the department and asked whether, in the event of this man retiring, he could be superannuated; and the reply of the department, which must be regarded as a decision, was that he could not be superannuated, as he had elected to come under the Retirement Fund Act. When I carne into office on the 3rd of February, 1912, my hon. friend wrote me directing my attention to the manner in which Mr. Munro had signed away his right, and alleging that he had done so in ignorance of what it really meant. On the 13th of February, 1912, he addressed a letter to me enclosing a copy of the communication addressed by Mr. Munro to the press. The facts are as I have stated them. M-y hon. friend finds fault because I have not reversed a decision that was given by my predecessor, who was appealed to on the subject on three or four occasions, who, no doubt, gave it ipost careful consideration, and stated most emphatically that this lighthouse keeper was not entitled to the
benefit of the Superannuation Act, as he had elected to come under the Retirement Act. He said: ' I have received and considered it-' evidently according to my hon. friend he is a most intelligent man; he knows what he is doing-' I have to inform you that I will give my vote for it, -that is, for the retirement. However, it is unnecessary to argue that here. It was decided by the Minister of Marine and Fisheries long befoTe I came into office, and now the hon. gentleman wants me to sit as a court of review and to reverse the decision given by the minister whom he supported.
It could not be decided until it came up for decision.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
The hon. gentleman can
say that if he chooses, but I submit that there was a decision given. As to the dismissal, I submit the facts to the judgment of the committee. I followed the rule laid down in this House several years ago with regard to officials not taking part in political matters. On the 20th of January, 1912 Mr. G. A. R. Rowlings, the candidate of the Conservative party in the last election against my hon. friend, forwarded to the department a statement addressed to him by Mr. J. S. Wells of Whitehead, a man of ability and standing, a former member. I believe of the Legislative Assembly of Nova Scotia, charging Mr. Munro with political partisanship. The_ charge was referred to Mr. Duchemin for investigation. 1 will read Mr. Duchemin's report:
Sydney, N.S., March 21, 1912.
Re Win N. Munro, lighthouse keeper, Whitehead, Guysborough county.
I conducted an inquiry into the case ot William L. Munro, lighthouse keeper, at Whitehead, N.S. The hearing took place at Whitehead, and the following named witnesses gave evidences under oath:	O. iifCiwaiu
Pietzch, merchant, of Yankee Cove; Arthur L. Munro, Lower Whitehaven, fisherman; Matthew Munro, fisherman; Alfred T. Munro, fisherman; and Usaac Grover.	...
Mr. Pietzch' testified that Mr. William Munro had requested him to act as agentti for Mr J H. Sinclair, the Liberal candidate, in the booth at Whitehead on election day, September 21 last. Mr. Pietzch replied that he would not care to undertake the work of agent, and was then told by Mr. Munro, that if he took the job he would get paid for it. Mr, Munro also instructed Mr. Pietzch as to the kind of work he would be expected to do in the booth, pointing out that it was comparatively easy, consisting mainly of checking off the names of the electors as they came into the booth to vote.
Arthur M. Munro testified that Mr. William L. Munro was not in the lighthouse on elec-day or on the evening of election day.
Matthew Munro gave evidence to the effect that he attended a meeting at Lower Whitehead, held in the interests of the Liberal party and addressed by Mr. J. H. Sinclair, the Liberal candidate for Guysborough. Sir.
Sir. HAZEN.

William L. Munro was present at this meeting, and acted as spokesman in having the meeting constituted. He moved that one Lewi Munro should act as chairman for the evening. The motion was put to the meeting' and carried, and Mr. Levi Munro presided over the meeting during Mr. Sinclair's address. On the conclusion of the speech-making, Mr. William L. Munro proposed that the audience give three cheers for Mr. Sinclair, the Liberal candidate.
My hon. friend was too modest to mention the fact:
The cheers were accordingly given.
I have no doubt they were very hearty cheers indeed, and I have no doubt he deserved them.
Mr. Munro then proposed that cheers be similarly given for Sir Wilfrid Laurier. This was a Liberal meeting, and Mr. William L. Munro was apparently the most active one of the local residents in taking part in it.
Alfred T. Munro, gave testimony to the same effect. He was present at the meeting referred to. It was held in the school house at Lower Whitehead. He testified that Mr. William L. Munro moved the appointment, and on the conclusion of Mr. Sinclair's speech proposed cheers for the candidate and Sir Wilfrid Laurier.
I think Grover is employed by William L. Munro, as assistant lighthouse keeper. Grover is a man who claims to be about sixty years of age, but apears to be very much older. He has been assistant for the last six years, and testified that during these three months William L. Munro, the keeper, had not been in the lighthouse at any time at night.
This indicates why dissatisfaction arose with the way he was discharging the duties of his light.
Was Wm. L. Munro charged with inattention to duty?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
He was charged with offensive partisanship, and it was proved up to the hilt. But if we had been aware that he had been neglecting his duties as light-keeper, it would have been the duty of the department to have dismissed him for that reason, entirely apart from the matter of political partisanship. The report goes on to say:
The witness said that Wm. L. Munro had been there in the day time-perhaps about twice a month during that time. On these visits he stayed a very short time-sometimes half a day altogether, according to the weather, as witness put it. Witness concluded:	'At present i do all the work in
connection with the lighthouse.' It is evident from the statement made by this, witness that this is a case where the lighthouse keeper is practically farming out his work. Mr. Wm. L. Munro declined to go on the stand, or to make any statement in his own defence.
338J.
My hon. friend says Munro was refused counsel. Without intending to show the slightest disrespect for my hon. friend or questioning his sincerity in making that assertion, permit me to say that I do not believe it.

I read an affidavit to
that effect.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: No such affidavit or communication was received by the department after this investigation took place. If Munro had been refused counsel, the first thing he would have done would be to make a complaint in that regard. I say I do not believe it for ine further reason that Mr. Duehemin at my direction was instructed by the deputy minister to allow witnesses to be represented by counsel at any time the privilege was requested. We gave that instruction because it was reported to us that there were occasions upon which Mr. Dnchemin had refused to allow counsel to appear on behalf of the accused. My opinion is that it was before the investigation o! the Munro matter that these instructions were given to Mr. Duehemin. Here we have the statement that Munro was present, that he had an opportunity of going cn the stand and contradicting the statements made, but he absolutely declined to do so. I do not feel called upon to defend Mr. Duehemin's conduct, which has been condemned by hon. gentlemen on the other side of the House from the province of Nova Scotia. It has been just as warmly commended by hon.' gentleman from Nova Scotia on this side of the House, who speak in the highest terms-
Who do not know what they are talking about.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
That, of course, is a very cheap remark, and one which is easy to make. Hon. gentlemen on this side of the House,
1 say, speak in the highest terms of Mr. Duchemin's conduct as a professional man.
1 might refer to the fact that Mr. George W. Murray, the chairman of Maintenance and Ways of the Brotherhood of Railway Locomotive Engineers at Truro, has made the statement that he had been present at some investigations conducted by Mr. Duehemin, and that he was entirely satisfied with the fair-minded way in which Mr. Duehemin conducted them. I may say further that Rev. D. L. Macdonald, the parish priest at Ansaig, was present at an investigation held there and expressed himself as being thoroughly satisfied with the fairness and impartiality with which Mr. Duehemin conducted the investigation. In view of the fact that the government which the hon. gentleman supported, although he broached the matter on four different occasions, held to the view that Mr. Munro was not entitled to superannuation and that they regarded him as an unsatisfactory official. I think I am not open to censure because I did not superannuate him.

In view of the evidence submitted to me by Mr. Duchemin, and in view of the fact that Mr. Munro, after the evidence had been taken, declined to go on the stand and say one word in his own defence or in contradiction of the testimony given by the witnesses, I think I cannot be held as having acted improperly because I dismissed Mr. Munro from the position he held.
At one o'clock, House resumed, and then took recess.
House resumed at three o'clock and again went into Committee of Supply. (Mr. Deputy Speaker in the Chair.)

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: A large number accepted the other.

It is a most extraordinary choice for a man to make. If you look at the language used in the letter from which the minister read an extract, he is asked to choose between these two things and he says: I vote for this. It is impossible to say which of the things he voted lor and the man himself says he intended to vote for the superannuation. That is what he says and I believe it; I have no doubt that is what he intended. Is it fair with a doubtful answer like that, in a doubtful document, to decide a question that involves so much for this man? Of course it does not mean very much to the minister. It is easy for the minister to dash off a decision in his cushioned chair, in his- luxurious office, surrounded by electric lights and in the presence of his big salaried officials saying: I beg to advise in reply to the appeal of this man to have his case considered, that, inasmuch as Munro was dismissed from the service, he would not be entitled to superannuation in any case. He d'd not even look into his case or consider it at ah. That is the kind of decision the minister gives, although he , occupies a responsible position and should act as judge between man and man. I say it is not creditable to the department or to the head of the department that he should not have given his serious consideration to a matter of this kind and have had a careful investigation before depriving the man of rights which he had earned during the last thirty years.
Does the law provide that lighthouse keepers shall receive superannuation in any case?

The original law which was in force when this man was appointed provided that if he serves a certain num her of years and paid in a certain amount each year he would be entitled to a retiring allowance for life, but the law was changed fifteen years ago and at that time a letter was written to Munro in which he was asked to make choice as to whether he would take back the cash he had paid in or his pension for life. He said: I vote for this. I say that his answer was so uncertain and so doubtful that the minister should not have taken that as a decision, but should have inquired into it and found out what the man really meant by the language and given a judicial decision as to whether he was entitled to a pension or not.
Did he get the money?

He took the money because he could not help himself, he had no choice. The minister dismissed him and said: Inasmuch as Munro was dismissed he had no right to superannuation and he took back his money. What else could he do? The minister made a statement that he did not admit that his commissioner, Duchemin, had refused counsel. I read the affidavit of Munro, a respectable man who will be believed in Whitehead, where he is known, much more readily than Mr. Duchemin will, and Mr. Munro swore that he asked the commissioner if he would be entitled to have a solicitor represent him at the trial and the commissioner refused. If the minister has any doubt about that I can prove it from the mouth of Mr. Duchemin. Perhaps that will satisfy him if he will not believe the affidavit of Munro. This question has been up before. Mr. Duchemin made a report to the Post Office Department in regard to the charge made against him that he was not allowing counsel to act for those parties in the investigation. This is an extract from a report of Mr. Duchemin, the commissioner, addressed to the Postmaster General. It is dated April 16, 1912, and relates to the dismissal of one Parker Sangster. This is what he says:
In view of'his own sworn statement at the hearing, it is difficult to understand how he (Sangster) could have bettered his position, if I had changed my position and admitted counsel at this inquiry, while excluding it from every other one.
As a matter of fact, however, Mr. SangsteT is incorrect in saying that Mr. Floyd asked that counsel be allowed to represent him in this case. Mr. Floyd asked that counsel be admitted to represent J. W. Davis, whose inquiry was being conducted under the Marine Department. I declined to allow counsel to appear on either side, therein following the procedure which I had invariably adopted since the beginning of my work.
This man had been working from January to April, holding inquiries all ovct the country, and refusing the parties the right to be represented by counsel. He says so [DOT]himself, and yet the minister comes to this committee and says he does not believe Mr. Munro when he says that Mr. Duchemin denied to him the right to be represented by counsel. Mr. Duchemin goes on to say:
If you think it well to have counsel admit-' red for complainant and accused, at these hearings, and instruct me accordingly, I will be careful to observe your instructions in all cases arising in the future. Thus far but one of the departments has given me such instructions, that of the Marine and Fisheries.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: Hear, hear.

But this case is in the Marine and Fisheries Department. He goes on:
COMMON w
One department has definitely instructed me not to admit counsel,-that while I have not been specially advised on this point by any of the other ministers, and have excluded counsel to economize time.
I do not know what department that is to which he refers; perhaps my hon. friend will tell me.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
I can only speak for my
own department.

(Translation.) Mr. Chairman, since the beginning of the session our opponents have not ceased complaining about dismissals of public employees, and I see that the member for Guysborough (Mr. Sinclair) is one of the most fervid in raising those questions.
Really, our opponents should keep silent, because whenever such complaints are made, they are dealt with by the newspapers, and the question being brought into light again, our own friends find that, instead of being too severe, we have not been severe enough.
I am particularly surprised to see the hon. member cast his blame upon the bon. Minister of Marine, a man endowed with the truest spirit of justice, a man who has treated our opponents with the most complete impartiality, if not with all the lenience possible.
In my county a great number of our opponents have been active partisans. I could almost say that all the employees of the Department of Marine, in the county of Rimouski, have been avowed opponents of the Conservative party; vet. the hon. minister has dismissed but two, and they had fully deserved it. The others are yet holding the positions which they held under the Liberal regime, and I do not know that we are trying to disturb them. If I had an advice to give my opponents I would say to them: Do not raise that question too often, because it is of such a nature as to hurt you whenever you do raise it.
A discussion went on during two hours and a half, before the committee, to-day, about a charge which the hon. minister has proved to be perfectly ungrounded. He proved that an inquiry had been held, he even established-and the member for Guysborough admits it-that, during the meeting which he held, the famous Munro had acted as an active partisan: that he had gone so far as to invite the audience to cry out cheers in favour of the Liberal party. It follows that a man who takes part in a
political meeting and shows his preference in that way, should be considered as an active partisan; if not, I fail to understand what is an active partisan.
In the second place, the hon. member has [DOT]blamed the Minister of Marine for not settling this question by superannuating [DOT]tnat man Munro, and he admits, himself, that he had tried to have the matter settled by his own party, which refused to do so because it was impossible for them ,so to do. How can he reasonably hope that his opponents will do any more? I know that the Conservative party is actuated by good intentions, and that the hon. member may perhaps expect more justice from this party than from his own friends: but it is rather awkward that what he was not able to get from the Liberal party, he should ask from his opponents, when it is contrary to the present law to grant it, and especially when the man he would like to protect makes an admission to the effect that he has accepted the conditions which were made to him in 1898.
The hon. member for Guysborough has complained of the partiality of the commissioner in charge of those inquiries, and the hon. Minister of Marine has shown clearly, by written documents, that Mr. Duchemin, the commissioner, is impartial and just, and that he has given full satisfaction. The hon. member has, then, no reason to accuse that commissioner and say that he acted unjustly, when it is so easy to prove the contrary. In fact, if I had to reproach the hon. Minister of Marine with anything, I would say that he is too accommodating towards his opponents; this entails very much trouble for us in our counties, because our own friends blame us ourselves for such extreme goodness towards opponents who have never treated us with regard.
Our opponents should not raise that question of dismissals, for the more they shall raise it. the more they shall hurt themselves and their own friends. Let me quote, at this point, the case of a man in my county, who has been a Government employee for thirty-six years and who has admitted, at the minister's own office, that he had always fought against the Conservative party. Notwithstanding that fact, just one-half of his position was taken away from him, the Government being good enough to leave him the other half. Is not this instance sufficient to show with what generosity, with what spirit of justice the Government does treat the Liberal employees who are guilty, while they prove to be relentless opponents? This same man whom I have alluded to had organized almost a riot during the election of 1904, in order to beat to death the then Conservative candidate, who was Mr. Price. That fact is known to everybody, and vet.

this relentless opponent has been left at the Government's service.
The Government, far from being too rigid towards our opponents, should rather be accused of treating them with too much goodness.
There are, in my county, many'employees belonging to the Marine Department, who [DOT]have been left undisturbed. Which shows clearly how obliging the hon. Minister has been.
I hope that our opponents will not th'ink of dealing any further with that question which caused us a useless loss of time. The session has been so protracted, we have been here for such a long time that we should soon put an end to our work. Really it is ridiculous to talk uselessly as did the hon. member for Guyshorough, who has kept sifting that question before us here during two hours and a half.
Department of Militia and Defence- contingencies, $36,000.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: That is exactly the same as it was last year, and it is for printing, sundries, clerical and other assistance.

Has the minister considered
the question that I asked last year in reference to the payment of certain grocers and butchers in Yarmouth, who supplied Dominion Government boats and charged the accounts to the stewards of these boats who decamped and never paid the bills?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: If the hon. gentleman had been in the House at the time the supplementary estimates for last year were under consideration he would have known that the amount was put in the estimates for the purpose of paying these bills, or rather, acting on the advice of the permanent officers of the department, paying seventy-five per cent of the amounts that were contracted for by the stewards of these boats. There was no legal obligation on the Government, but it was thought that these people had sold to the stewards, believing that the Government was responsible. The condition attached is that these persons who supplied the goods will have to make a declaration to the effect that they believed at the time that the Government was liable for the payment of the accounts. These are all being dealt with by the purchasing agent of the department, and I fancy that the greater number of the cases in Yarmouth will have been dealt with.
No, they have not. *

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
Well, they are being dealt with by the purchasing agent, and if my hon. friend will come over to the department, I will get all the information for him with reference to the matter. The Mr. BOTJLAY.
matter was dealt with in the supplementary estimates for last year.

I did not notice it, and the
people of Yarmouth are not aware of it either, because I had correspondence a little while ago from them, and I was waiting for an opportunity to bring the matter up.

The minister thought
