it proper to launch off upon a side track, and to talk about this official of his. I would like to get a little further information. I would like to ask the minister if these investigating officers are appointed separately for each department, or are they appointed under one Order in Council?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: Each department appoints its own. The man investigating matters in connection with the Marine and Fisheries Department is appointed by the department and a special commission is issued to him.

I have the Order in Council here:
Certified copy of a Report of the Committee of the Privy Council, approved by His Royal Highness the Governor General on the 3rd June, 1912.
The Committee of the Privy Council have under consideration the question as to the rate of remuneration which would he allowed commissioners appointed or to he appointed to hold inquiries or investigations under the Inquiries Act, chapter KM of the Revised Statutes of Canada, 1908.
The committee advise that, except in cases otherwise provided for by Order in Council, the fees allowable to a commissioner appointed under the authority of the above mentioned Act shall not in any case exceed $15 for each full day's attendance or occupation in connection with the work of the commission, exclusive of the reasonable moving and living expenses of the commissioner to be allowed where he has to travel for the purpose of executing the commission; and that the said per diem allowance shall be deemed to cover letters and interviews on other days as well as on the day for which the commissioner is entitled to such per diem allowance; and that no further charge be allowed for such letters and interviews; and that a professional man shall not be entiteld to any fees or allowances as commissioned to which other commissioners are not entitled as aforesaid.
The committee advise that a copy of the minute be sent to every commissioner hereafter to be appointed, with his commission, or the notification of his appointment and that such commissioner be at the same time informed that the provisions of this Order in Council will be strictly followed in ascertaining the amount to which he may be entitled for his services as commissioner.
The committee further advise that thd Order in Council, (P.C. 2648) of the 21st September, 1897, fixing the rate of remuneration

of commissioners appointed to hold inquiries into public matters or departmental business, be cancelled.
All which is respectfully submitted for approval.
(Sgd.) F. K. Bennetts, Assistant clerk of the Privy Council.
I would like to ask the minister if that law, as made by Order in Council,: applies to all the commissioners?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: Yes.

' Then I would gather from the meaning of this Order in Council that if the commissioner goes to a certain place and holds an inquiry into two, three or four cases on the one day, he is only entitled to the sum of $15?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
That is entirely a matter
for the Auditor General. When we receive an account we certify that the order was issued for the holding of the inquiry, that the inquiry was held, and it then goes to the department of the Auditor General, who sees that the terms of that resolution are carried out.

I think the minister
has a duty to discharge to the committee and to all of us as to how he understands this Order in Council.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: That is the way it i,s done. It is more a matter for the Finance Department. I think that the Minister of Finance speaks for the Auditor General in this House. I certainly have no authority to speak for him. I think that the language of the order is pretty plain. We are simply responsible for certifying that the order issued for holding the inquiry, that the inquiry was held and then it is for the Auditor General's Department to see whether the number of days charged for is correct or not. The account is not paid until he certifies to it.

The question of the
continuing in office or not of the commissioner is a matter not for the Auditor General but for the minister. The question as to how the commissioner conducts himself and how he comports in his conduct with the order appointing him is a matter for the minister. If the commissioner does not comply with the law I should think that it would, be a matter for the head of the department to enquire into and not the Auditor General.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: The Auditor General could refuse to pay him.

He could refuse to
pay him? The minister says that it is the same kind of law for all the departments, that it covers them all.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
I will read the Order in
Council under which my authority comes:
The' Committee of the Privy Council advises that the Minister of Marine and Fisheries be authorized to appoint, in accordance with the provisions of part 2 of the Inquiries Act, a commissioner, or commissioners for the province of New Brunswick-
I am just taking this one, but it is the same for Nova Scotia.
-to enquire into and report upon any charges of political partisanship which may be preferred against any officer, clerk or employee in the outside service of the Department of Marine and Fisheries in that province.
I have nothing to do with the payment. That is a matter that rests entirely with the Department of Finance, subject to the audit of the Auditor General.

I want to know from
the hon. minister if this order which I have just read is the law or regulation governing the Auditor General in making this payment?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: I would say it undoubtedly is.

There is no authority
which governs him in ascertaining how much is due to any commissioner, except this order?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: Not so far as I know.

I am not anxious to
go after any personage in particular, but we are told by the hon. minister to-day that he does not believe our statements-

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: No, I did not say that.

-as against this commissioner. I want to tell the minister that on the 6th day of September, 1912, this commissioner, Mr. Duchemin held six investigations between three o'clock in the afternoon and six o'clock in the evening in a house at New Uampbellton or Big Bras D'Or in my county. He examined six individuals; and for his work he sent in six separate and distinct bills, amounting to something over a hundred dollars for about three hours' work. These bills are on file. They are probably paid, and paid under the terms of this authorization. Unless there is some clear, distinct and satisfactory explanation from this commissioner, I think that moneys are paid out of the funds of this county which are not earned. I submit that any work that a commissioner can do in half an afternoon is paid for by the $15 and other incidentals. I mention this' simply in order to show that the minister should not be so particularly strong in flaunting the word of this gentleman in our face, when I am prepared to prove to the hilt that this is the way in which things are done, so far as the money end of it is concerned. When it comes to a matter of

getting the hard cash of the Government without earning it and in direct violation of the order appointing a commission in the service of the Government, I should hesitate a little, if I were in the position of the hon. minister, to tell hon. gentlemen that I did not believe sworn affidavits which differed from his statements of fact. One irregularity may cause another. If I find a man getting money which he has no business 'to get, and making false returns for the purpose of getting it, I would have some hesitancy in accepting his statement as fact.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: Does the hon. gentleman say that these investigations were all held on the same day?
The same day between three o'clock in the afternoon and six o'clock in the evening.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: The hon. gentleman knows that of his own knowledge?
The returns show it.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: They are all dated on the same day. Does it follow that they were all held on the same day?

I have a letter here
from one of those whose cases were investigated.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
The matter is one that
the Auditor General is responsible for. Is that in the Department of Marine and Fisheries?

No, it is in the Department of Customs.
I see my hon. friend from Rimouski (Mr. Boulay) smiling broadly and laughing over the fact that this irregularity was in the Customs Department, and therefore it does not matter at all. There is only one Auditor General in this country, who pays the money. The money comes out of the same fund, the money of the people. My hon. friend from Rimouski need not laugh if he finds irregularity in the Customs Department. I have observed from the returns that his dealings are with the Department of Railways and Canals, for, ties and things of that sort.	[DOT]

When a charge of this
nature is made to the hon. Minister of Marine and Fisheries, do I understand him to say that the only recourse is that the Auditor General shall not pay the bill? Does he not think it up to him to have had this matter taken up by counsel and had the man dismissed from his position?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
If any charge had been
made to me, I would certainly have had it investigated. No such charge has been made to me, and no such charge would Mr. McKENZIE
be made to me, because it was not in my department that this occurred. It is the duty of the Auditor General, when these accounts come in, to order payment if they are correct. If they are not correct, he should not order payment. If he refused to order payment on the gTound that there was dishonesty, the matter would be brought to the notice of the Government and the facts ascertained. So far as I am concerned, the incident referred to by the hon member for Cape Breton (Mr. McKenzie) has no relation to my department at all.

I think we can show
similar instances in the department of my hon. friend. He cannot escape responsibility by any reference to the Auditor General. My hon. friend sends these bills to the Auditor General. It is his duty to send nothing to the Auditor General unless it is right and should be paid. It is for my hon. friend to investigate these matters and to see whether his commissioner is charging too much or not. If he will investigate matters, he will find conditions of this nature. It is impossible for anyone to understand accounts sent in by Mr. Duchemin. It is impossible to say how many days he took in these different places. He does not give the time that he spent in any one particular place, but he rambles from one place to another and combines three or four of these places together, which may be many miles apart. Then he sends in a bill for so marfy days. It is the duty of the hon. minister to get clear and distinct accounts from this commissioner as to how many hours he spent in each particular place and on what particular days he conducted any investigation.
I have a letter on my desk from the department of my hon friend which requires some explanation. I asked the following questions a few days ago, and the following answers were given:
Q. 1. What is the date of the appointment of H P. Duchemin, investigating commissioner for eastern Nova Scotia?-A. So far as the Department of Marine and Fisheries is concerned, 5th January, 1912.
Q. 2. How many days has he been employed by the Government since his appointment?- A. 73} days.
Q. 3. What is gross amount paid to Mr. Duchemin as an allowance for his services, excluding travelling expenses or other outlays?-A. $1,121.25.
Q. 4. How much has been paid to Mr. Duchemin to date for travelling expenses, living expenses, witness fees, and other sundry expenses, respectively?-A. Travelling expenses, $76.28; living expenses, $193.75; witness fees, $26.76; sundry, $273.12.
What is this ' sundries ' of $273.12 made
up of?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: It is a pretty long stateoent including a great irany small items of telegrams, postage, fees for serving witnesses, and one item of $2 for the use of a hall in which to hold an investigation.

The hon. gentleman
might leave that statement with the clerk.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
I shall be glad to do so.
Now, with regard to the question raised by the hon. member for Cape Breton North (Mr. McKenzie) about the way these accounts are dealt with in the department, I find on the file a memorandum of May 8, 1912, by the deputy minister to the chief accountant, as follows:
I am unable to find on the files any reference to the arrangement concluded between the Auditor General and yourself, respecting the payment of accounts rendered by the various commissioners inquiring into charges of political partisanship against employees of this department.
A. Johnston.
And there is the reply of the accountant to the deputy minister:
Referring to arrangements verbally made, with the Auditor General in regard to accounts rendered by the commissioners appointed to inquire into and report on any charges of political partisanship preferred against civil servants, I beg to report as follows :-
When the Order in Council of the 20th December last approving of appointments of commissioners was received in the department, it was noticed that there was the vote out of which the expenses incurred on account of such investigations were to be paid.
I, therefore, went to see the Deputy Minister of the Finance Department to see wThat arrangements could be made, as commissioner L. C. Beaubien was then pressing for payment of his accounts for investigations. I was informed that these expenses were to be paid out of contingencies (Finance Department), and that the Auditor General would examine the accounts and authorize the issue of the cheques in payment thereof.
Later I interviewed the Auditor General, and it was agreed that, when accounts were rendered by commissioners in connection with investigations, this department would certify that said investigations had been authorized and reported on. The accounts were then to be forwarded to the Auditor General to he examined and checked in accordance with the provisions of the Order in Council of the 3rd January last.
None of these accounts came under my notice; they were dealt with in the department by the accountant and the deputy minister in the usual way.
How many commissioners has the minister employed in the whole of Canada to investigate?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
In Nova Scotia, there were Mr. Duehemin, Mr. Macdonald and Mr. Lane. I think that Mr. Macdonald has not
done any work for some time. In New Brunswick there were Mr. Knowles and Mr. Legere. In Quebec there were Mr. Bergeron, Mr. Beaubien and Mr. Shurtliff and Mr. Flynn. In Prince Edward Island there was Mr. Heath Strong.
Ocean and river service-maintenance and repairs to Government steamers and icebreakers, $1,000,000.
Will the hon. minister please explain this item?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
This is the usual vote
which has been passed for years-and it is the same amount as last year-for the maintenance and repair of government steamers and ice-breakers. I have here the details of expenditure of all the vessels we have in commission, including salaries, fuel, hoard, repairs, etc. The list would be lengthy to read, but if there is any special information desired I shall be glad to give it.

Are there any new
ships?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
There is the Estevan,
which was under construction at Col-lingwood when I oame into office. She was finished this spring and has gone around to British	Columbia-has arrived there. She will be employed in the buoy service in British Columbia. The Dollard was under construction also at Collingwood, and it is expected that she will he completed and put in commission very soon. The Dollard will take the place of the Shamrock, which was used up. It will be remembered that there was an explosion on board the Shamrock some years ago. We have twenty-seven vessels, of which twelve are in commission during the whole year, and fifteen are in commission during a part of the year. There are all sorts of boats including the Earl Grey and the Minto which run between Prince Edward Island and the mainland, the Lans-downe, the Aberdeen, La Canadienne and the others.
The Dollard was the one we saw at Kingston?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: Yes, with the Bellechase; they were both there at that time.
The Princess is still on the Baie des Chaleurs route?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: Yes.
Always under the command of Commander Wakeham?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
Yes.
.Mr. LEMIEUX: I am bound to say that Commander Wakeham has always given satisfaction to the people in that district.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: I wish I had more officers like him.
Were there any icebreakers in commission in the province of Nova Scotia last year? I have special reference to the service in Sydney harbour.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
We had no ice-breaker
available among our boats to do work in Sydney harbour last year. At the time the ice-breaker was required at that port, the Stanley, which has been doing the work in that district, had met with an accident and was laid up for repairs. There was a requisition made for the services of an icebreaker, and it was a matter of regret to us that we could not comply with it.
Has the department any boats under construction at the present time?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: In the Marine and Fisheries Department the Dollard is the only boat under construction at the present time. There are two dredges for the St. Lawrence ship channel under construction at Collingwood, and some vessels are under construction for the fishery protection service in British Columbia; these come under the Department of Naval Service. Contracts have also been awarded for the construction of some small gasoline boats for the fishery patrol service on the British Columbia coast.
Are these boats equipped with Marconi wireless telegraph system?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: Some of them are. All those that do ocean work are equipped with wireless-boats like the Aberdeen, Stanley, Montcalm and Minto.

I think the captains of the Government-boats should have entire control of the selection of officers and men. When I represented the county of Gaspb, I gave Commander Wakeham a free hand in respect of the selection of his men, and I think that accounts for the excellent service we have had. I have often compared the crews on La Canadienne and the Princess, which were under his command, with those of some other boats in the river St. Lawrence upon which the selection of the men was made rather by members of the House than by the captains of the ships. I think, therefore, that the minister should give his captains a free hand in the selection of the ships' crew, for I am sure he would get a better service in that way.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
As far as Commander
Wakeham's boat is concerned, the system to which my hon. friend has referred has been continued. His is the only boat in the service upon which that system has prevailed absolutely. I agree with what my hon. friend says in regard to this matter, but there are certain difficulties in the way of carrying out his suggestion. As far as the officers on all these boats are Mr. HAZEN.
concerned, our endeavour is, when a vacancy occurs, to promote a man already in the service, provided he is competent.

Has the hon. minister given an increase to the captains this year?
I remember that during the few days I was Minister of Marine and Fisheries, I received a petition signed by nearly all the captains and officers of the various government, steamers, asking for an increase. I had it in mind to give them a legitimate increase, but unfortunately the people of this country deprived me of the opportunity of carrying out my good intentions in that respect. I hope my hon. friend has complied with this iequest which was made by the officers of the staff. The salaries have not been revised for many years, and the officers, of course, like others, feel the burden of the high cost of living.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
There have been certain,
increases made for the purpose of equalizing the salaries, but that does not altogether fill the bill. The officers of the department are at the present time preparing a schedule, so that when a man is appointed to a position in the service he will know what his increase and maximum will be. This schedule, which will certainly give an increase to these officers, will, I think, be ready for my approval in a very short time.

Does the department intend
to build any new boats within the coming year besides those mentioned by the hon-minister? If so, I would like to say that we have in Yarmouth a ship-building plant that could construct the small steamers necessary for the service of the department.	.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
In the future, so far as my department is concerned-and I hope the same system will be adopted by the Government generally-I think it would te fair, in asking for tenders, to stipulate that the boats shall be constructed in Canada. I may say frankly that one difficulty experienced in the contracts we have made in the past for the building of boats in Canadian shipyards, is that they are never delivered at the time they are undertaken to be completed, and other difficulties are experienced which are not met with when the contracts are taken by firms of established repute on the other side of the water. The tenders offered by firms on the other side are very much lower than those of the Canadian shipbuilder, and it is impossible for the Canadian shipbuilder to compete, but in calling for tenders for these ships I think it would be fair, as a matter of policy, to ask that they be built in Canada. The result of that would be, I think, that the shipbuilders on the other side would establish plants in Canada, and do the

work here, employing the labour of our own people. I may'say in passing that if there is at Yarmouth a ship-building establishment which can compete successfully for the building of vessels, I would be glad indeed to see them get the contract. We have in the estimates a provision for a first-class ice-breaker for the river St. Law-icnce. The ice-breaking on the river St Lawrence is done at the present time by the Montcalm and the Lady Grey. These are boats that do ice breaking in certain portions of the year and at other times are used for general work in the rivers in connection with the Marine and Fisheries Department. That is not found altogether satisfactory. The work of breaking ice is of a very heavy character, and is very hard on the boats. They have to be equipped with a great deal of power, and this makes them very expensive to use in the summer for the general purposes of the department on the river. We are asking in this vote for a sum that will enable us to purchase a modern, up-to-date ice breaker for the St. Lawrence river. I consider the ice-breaking on the river of very great importance. If it is not broken at the proper time there are great floods, with consequent inconvenience and damage, and the result of the breaking of the ice has been to open navigation to Montreal at a very considerably earlier date. That is the one boat which I contemplate asking for this year.
Will this boat be built in Canada?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: I hope to be able to get it built in Canada.

I am glad that the minister contemplates adding to the flotilla of ice breakers. As my hon. friend knows, there was a great deal of prejudice in and around Quebec city against this ice breaking at Cap a la Roche. When I was a mmister, delegation after delegation from Quebec came to me protesting against the use of those steamers, under the pretext that the ice breaking at Cap a la Roche was jamming the harbour in front of Quebec and preventing the ferries from performing their service. There was a certain element of truth in that; but, as a matter of fact, the floating ice, although it seriously hampered the boats, never actually prevented them from carrying on the service. But, as my hon. friend says, even if we were not to consider the immensity of the service rendered to navigation by opening it at least three weeks before the ordinary time, the presence of those ice breakers and the work performed by them prevents the flooding of immense areas on both sides of the river St. Lawrence from Cap a la Roche up to Three Rivers and lake
St. Peter. My predecessor, Mr. Justice Brodeur, and his predecessor, the late Hon. Mr. Prefontaine, are entitled to great credit for the work they did in that connection. For several winters they had engineers on both sides of the river watching very closely the movements of the ice and tides. It was noted that as soon as the ice breakers began to perform their work at Cap a la Roche, practically all the floods ceased in the upper district. As regards the trade of the country, it is, as my hon. friend says, of immense value commercially, financially and economically, and three boats are not too much for that work. The number of boats plying between Canada and Europe is increasing every year, and the sooner you get the channel open in the spring the better for the trade of this country. I sincerely congratulate the department on acquiring the new boat, and I hope it will be built in Canada. My hon. friend visited with me last year the shipyards at Kingston, where we saw the Dollard and the Bellechasse. The Mont-magny was built in Canada, at Sorel. It may have cost more than it could have been purchased for in England, but if you want to have shipbuilding encouraged in this country you must not be afraid at first to pay a little more than you would have to pay in Great Britain. There is a beginning to everything. I daresay that the first icebreaker built in Russia, the famous Ermaak, cost a considerable amount; but since that time Russia has been building icebreakers for other countries, and, by encouraging that shipbuilding industry, it has created one of the greatest industries in the world. If my hon. friend would take as his motto Canada for the Canadians, and encourage exclusively our shipbuilding yards, he would be entitled to great credit. I read the other day in a paper that a Canadian shipbuilding firm at Collingwood had been awarded the contract for building the largest steam vessel afloat on the great lakes. Surely if a Canadian firm at Collingwood, with its men, equipment and material, can built the largest vessel for the lake service, the Department of Marine and Fisheries can afford to assemble at Sorel or at Kingston or in the maritime provinces the material and the men necessary to build his flotilla of steamers. If I mistake not, a delegation came here during this session and interviewed my hon. friend and the Prime Minister asking that the uovernment encourage shipbuilding in Canada. This is an excellent occasion -for doing this. If we are not able to do all of the work of building those ships, we have only to import from Great Britain the men who are able to direct our own people. Take, for example, what the firm of Vickers, Limited have done in

Montreal. It is true that this immense floating dock has been imported from Great Britain, but Vickers have agreed to have that floating dock in Montreal and to erect immense sheds on both sides of the dock for ships to do the repairing of vessels, general chandlery WQrk; and at the sametime the firm is ready to build in -Canada ships of a certain tonnage. It is a British firm, but it becomes Canadian, and because the firm is Canadian it remains British. If Vickers, Limited, are encouraged at Maisonneuve, I am quite sure that within a very short space of time we shall have an immense shipbuilding industry in the immediate vicinity of the city of Montreal. I would ask my hon. friend not to be too chary in the amount which he will be prepared to pay in Canada fox the building of his steamers. It might be fifteen per cent or twenty per cent more, but the people will not begrudge the payment of that slight increase in the price, as compared with the English price oecause, after all, you are building up a Canadian industry, and are ensuring for the future work which will be to the credit of Canada.

The minister could
scarcely expect the work to be done with the same speed as it can be done in the better equipped yards of the old country. If you give a Canadian ship-builder the opportunity to build one of those vessels, after he gets a plan and understands what is required, he will have to order a good deal of material from the other side. He has to send his specification over, and it takes sometimes weeks or perhaps months to get it filled. Allowance must be made for that, if the Canadian shipbuilder is to have a chance. The minister must remember that a good many articles which enter into the construction of steamships are heavily taxed. He cannot expect ships to be built at the same price as in a free trade country like England.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: The principal difference is in wages.
I do not think so.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: Yes, I have had the figures furnished to me by ship-building firms in this country, and according to them, the principal difference is in regard to wages; it is a difference of forty-five per cent.
If the minister inquires among the ship-building yards in Canada, he will find that they do not look upon wages as the most important item.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: That is what I inquired of them, and I got that statement.

It is contended that Canadian workmen can do more work in a day than British workmen, that they can turn Mr. LEMIEUX.
their hands to so many different classes of work that they are more profitable than the workmen employed in the British yards. Then the cost of material is a very important item. Some few years ago I had occasion to investigate this matter, and I visited the yards at Collingwood and Toronto, and collected information which I can give to the minister. From the inquiries I made it appeared that it cost something like six dollars a ton more to build in Canada than to build in England, that is without allowing for any profit. The additional expense was something like six dollars for each ton of the ship that was constructed in Canada. The minister will have to make allowances for these important phases of the business, if he expects the Canadians to have a chance at all. Delays also occur in the department. We are now well on in the Spring, whereas, if the minister had brought down his estimates four or five months ago, had secured his money, and had had his plans ready, the Canadian builders would have had a chance months ago to send their specifications across, and would have had a much better opportunity to do the work, if he expects to get it done this year. However, I am much pleased that the minister assures us that his policy is to build those vessels in Canada if it is possible to do so.

I am glad to have the
opportunity of corroborating what has been said by the hon. member for Rouville (Mr. Lemieux) so far as Commander Wakeham, of the Princess, is concerned. I have had the pleasure of seeing him at work in the gulf of St. Lawrence for twenty years or more, and no more efficient officer is to be found in the service of the department. It is generally hoped in the district that he will continue long in the service of the department. I was glad to hear that Commander Wakeham had been given a free hand in the choice of his boat. I would like to be informed whether the same principle will apply to the other Government boats in the gulf and river St. Lawrence, or whether the patronage system will be applied.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: We are following practically the same system that has been followed for a number of years. Commander Wakeham is the only one who has an absolutely free hand. We try to promote officers when vacancies occur.

I have had complaints'
of men employed on Government boats on the St. Lawrence being summarily dismissed on the change of Government.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: Not on these boats.

Has the minister any
idea of the number of men who were dis-

missed from the Government boats on the St. Lawrence?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
No. I think there were
very few. They are men who are shipped for the season. They sign articles for the season, and very frequently do not go back. There are changes going on every year.
When vacancies have to be filled are the appointments left to the members of the various constituencies?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: If there are vacancies.

Are lightships included in
this vote?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: No. They are under a different vote.

In Nova Scotia and
in the maritime provinces, we recognize the great importance of the river St. Lawrence, the great artery of commerce of Canada. But there are seasons of the year when ice-breaking is of no avail in the river St. Lawrence, when it cannot be done, and we have in the harbour of Sydney a place where ice-breaking will be of benefit when it is of no avail on the river St. Lawrence. I have had in view the proposition to utilize the cable boat during the winter time. The cable boat made the harbour of North Sydney her home for a year or so, and the proposition was that it could be converted into an ice-breaker in winter. She has nothing else to do during that season, for she is laid up.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: To whom does it belong?

The Department of Public Works. The cable boat has been removed from North Sydney, and it is most desirable that we should have an icebreaker there during the three or four months of the year. The ice-breaker required to do the work there need not necessarily be of a very powerful type, because the ice that comes to the mouth of the Sidney harbour	is	never very heavy.
I wish to point out to the minister the great importance of keeping a track open for about five miles from the mouth of the harbour up to North Sydney, or perhaps four miles farther up to the pier. We have at that harbour that tremendous plant of which we are all so proud, not only in Nova Scotia but in the whole of Canada- the plant of the Dominion Steel and Coal Company representing from $50,000,000 to $60,000,000 of money-coal and steel combined under one control and management. They could send their product out of the harbour all the year round if it were kept open. But, perhaps more important than sending their products out is that their material is brought in from Newfoundland. Their ore is brought in from Newfoundland
and I understand that they are now starting to bring their limestone from there. The bringing in of ore and the taking out of steel are also equally important in connection with the Nova Scotia Steel and Coal Company. On that account I submit to the minister that this question-if I could get the attention of the minister-

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: I beg the hon. gentleman's pardon.

I submit that this
question is sufficiently important for my hon. friend from Halton (Mr. Henderson) to permit the minister to listen to me for a moment. I am talking about two of the biggest industries in Canada, industries in connection with the Dominion Steel and Coal Company and in connection with the Nova Scotia Steel and Coal Company, I am talking upon a subject that is of vital importance to these two concerns and I am suggesting that something should be done to keep	Sydney harbour open all	the	year
round. The minister and the hon. member for Halton both know the harbour of Sydney.
Mr.	HENDERSON:	I	beg	my	hon.
friend's pardon; I did not just catch what he said.

I said that the minister and my hon. friend from Halton know Sydney harbour well.
Mr.	HENDERSON: Oh,	yes.Mr.	McKENZIE:	And	they	know its
grandeur, its magnificence and its beauty.
I was there once.

They will understand what an important thing it is to provide for keeping it open if it can be done by ordinary expenditure. There is no present means of keeping it open and I was point-ting out to the minister that our coal, our steel rails and all the products of the steel works could go out all the year round if about four miles of ice 'were kept open. Not only would these products go out but the iron ore for the Nova Scotia Steel and Coal Company and for the Dominion Steel and Coal Company, could come in from Newfoundland if they could get in with their steamers. As it is now they have to rush things during the summer and, at great expense, to pile up this ore and store it, whereas, if they had the opportunity of bringing the ore during all the year, it would greatly facilitate the operations of these large concerns. Limestone is now about to be brought in by the Dominion Steel Company from Newfoundland and it is highly important that communication be kept open all the year round for the bringing in of this commodity as well as

the sending out of the coal and the products of the steel companies.
North Sydney is the Atlantic terminus of the Intercolonial railway, and from that terminus we have connection with the island of Newfoundland. The trade has developed enormously during the- last ten years. Ten years ago there was no communication at all. Since that, instead of one boat, there are two boats and instead of a few passengers there is a tremendous traffic, an enormous trade, ten times, aye, one hundred times, greater than it was ten years ago; it is continuously increasing. The Reid Newfoundland Company are battling with the ice and doing the best they can to keep their boat on every day during the winter. They are doing very well, missing only a few trips, and I submit to the minister that in view of the abundance of the surplus and the money which the Government have, and in view of their desire to develop every industry and assist transportation everywhere, it would be a very justifiable and legitimate expenditure to provide for placing in the harbour of Sydney this cable boat that I speak of, convert it into an ice-breaker, or build an ice-breaker for the purpose, which would be kept at Sydney harbour all the time. It would be through with Sydney harbour before it would be required on the St. Lawrence where I understand ice-breaking is required to be done in the early spring and therefore, after the ice-breaker had done all the work necessary at Sydney, it could be taken to the St. Lawrence. I can assure the minister that he could not possibly use the money that would be necessary in a better way in the general interests of the country. I am not talking politics. I am not trying to make votes or trying to deceive him in any way; I am talking about a big proposition with respect to Dominion industries which are of importance to every part of Canada and I am suggesting something that would contribute to the expansion of those great plants.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
I appreciate the importance of the matter to which my hon. friend (Mr. McKenzie) has referred and the desirability of having Sydney harbour kept open during the winter months so "that vessels could come and go. With the building of the new ice-breaker for the river St. Lawrence I think there will be no difficulty at all in meeting the position of affairs. In the first place, it will relieve the Montcalm, which, I think, can then be brought down during the winter season to Sydney and in addition, with the building of the car ferry across the straits of Northumberland connecting the island system of railways with the mainland, there will be two boats which will be available as ice-breakers-the Earl Grey and the Minto. In the course of a couple of years I think we will have plenty Mr. McKenzie
of ice-breakers to look after the harbours on the Atlantic coast as well as those of the St. Lawrence and others to which our attention has been called. In previous years we were able to do something at Sydney with the Stanley, but unfortunately this year the Stanley met with an accident and she had to be laid up just at the time her services were required.

I might call the attention of the minister to the fact that there are ports on the Baie des Chaleurs in which these ice-breakers might be used to advantage. The navigation of the Baie des Chaleurs is held up very often because the ports of Dalhousie and Gaspe are closed with ice. An ice-breaker could be very well employed there.

How many boats has the
department employed in the buoy service in Nova Scotia?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
There are two in Nova
Scotia, the Lady Laurier and the Stanley; there are two in New Brunswick, the Aberdeen and the Lansdowne. During the winter season the Montmagny is used there.

It has been thought for some years that the department has not steamers enough to look after the buoy service properly. Of course, the minister knows that the coast of Nova Scotia is the roughest coast, I suppose in the world, and the hardest place to keep buoys in position. I have noticed for several years that during the winter season a large number of these buoys are adrift and, the department not having a boat near Yarmouth, the buoys that go adrift have to wait until the steamer comes from St. John to get them. If the department made an arrangement, at a reasonable price, with a firm in Yarmouth to look after these buoys when they go adrift, I think it would be a good thing for the department and also for the safety of navigation. The boats running between Yarmouth and Boston make better time than the railway trains do. When these buoys are out of position, hundreds of lives may be in danger, and it is very important indeed that they should be replaced as quickly as possible. The hon. minister understands that, when a buoy goes adrift, it probably takes twenty-four or forty-eight hours for the matter to be reported, and a couple of days for the steamer to get from St. John to the vicinity of Yarmouth; or, if tshe engaged in some other business, it may be several days before she can hunt for that buoy and find it. If the hon. minister made an_ arrangement with the regular boat people in Yarmouth or somebody else there, I have no doubt that a lot of time would be saved, and the safety of the mariners, who have to visit that very rough coast during the

winter time, would be much greater than it is at present.
Can the hon. minister tell us how the supplies for these boats are obtained? Are they offered for tender?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: I suppose the hon. gentleman means the food that is furnished. Contracts are entered into with the stewards on board the boats, at an amount fixed by the department, and the stewards supply the food. That system was adopted a few years ago. Before that, the stewards used to buy the provisions and charge them to the Government. That system was not found satisfactory. The opinion of the department is that the present system is much more in the interests of the department and the public service than the old system was. The stewards enter into a contract to feed the men at so much a day, and the officers at so much a day.
Is the steward free to go to any merchant?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: Absolutely free.
There are no parties recommended as people from whom he should purchase?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: None.

In case the stewards do not
pay the bills, does the minister have them under bond?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: We have them under bond. The bonds are personal bonds, because we could not get a bond company to guarantee the stewards. We have public notices in the press in the different localities to which these ships go, informing the people that the Government are not liable for these stewards. We are holding them as far as we can by these personal bonds, but, no matter what care the purchasing agent may exercise, some of these bonds cannot be recovered. As a matter of fact, some stewards have resigned because they have been unable to furnish any bonds at all. Every effort was made by Mr. Doutre and the deputy minister to get bonds that would be approved of by the Department of Justice.
How is the coal supplied?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: By tender and contract.

The arrangement made between the stewards and the department may be a very good one; but it is hardly fair for the butchers, grocers and others who supply these stewards from time to time, when they cannot get their bills paid. These boats go into small places; a steward, with a gold band on his cap, goes into a butcher shop or a grocery
store; the man gives him the goods and charges them, supposing that the Government will pay the bill.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: We are spreading the information as much as possible that the Government is not liable.

I think some percentage
should be kept back from each man _ so as to guarantee that those who furnish supplies and provisions for the Government boats will be paid.
Examination of master and mates, $16,500.
Mr. LEMIEUX- Where is your board of examiners-at Quebec ?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
The list of examiners is:
Charles Eddy, William Lugar-I see by the newspapers that Mr. Lugar is dead,- Captain H. W. King, Alexander Cameron, John E. Murphy, James Sutherland, A. J. Wolf, James Gaudin, George C. Coles, M. Thodarson, Angus Grant, G. Hallett. The amount was $5,000 for last year; the additional $5,000 is for contemplated extension of the service. Very great complaint has been made to us in regard to the inconvenience masters on the great lakes are put to in attending these examinations.
Where have they to sit-in Ottawa ?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: No, in different places. Captain King is in Toronto.
Whom have you in Quebec ?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: Captain Lachance. The additional $5,000 is for contemplated extensions of the service as follows: Examiner at Toronto, $1,800; examiner at Quebec, $600; Captain Lachance also receives pay for conducting a marine school; his total salary Is $2,400. Examiner at St. John, $600; office rent, $500; extension of service, Quebec and Ontario, $1,000; examinations in Yukon, $500. In addition to their duties as examiners of masters and mates, the above officers are required to conduct preliminary investigations into wrecks, to deliver lectures in marine schools, and to do other work that the department may assign to them.

I noticed in the press_ that the department was taking into consideration the changing of the examination centres for masters and mates, and of having one head centre in the maritime provinces. Is this so ?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: We' have had Captain Lugar, who has been chief examiner of masters and mates in Nova Scotia; then there are local examiners in addition to him.
Masters and mates are still examined at the port of Yarmouth by Captain John E. Murphy ?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: Yes.
Is it proposed to make any change ?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: No. Rewards for saving life, including life-saving stations, amount to $110,000. There is an increase caused on account of new stations at Long Point, Point Pelee on Lake Erie, Bay View, Digby, Toronto, Cheticamp and Richi-bucto.
Is there anything in the estimates for a life-saving station at Mud Island ?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: No.

Objection is taken to
the way in which the minister has dealt with the life-saving stations since he came into office. I was much surprised to learn, m answer to a question asked in the House, of the large number of coxswains and crews of life-saving stations who had been dismissed, many of them without investigation. The life-boat service was always supposed to be free from political bias; this service was not looked upon-at any rate in the part of the country from which I come-as a political matter. It was the custom for one of the best men in the harbour to take charge of the life-boat and he selected his own crew, taking the best oarsmen and the most athletic young fellows in the harbour. It was a great surprise to the House and the country to find that even this service does not escape the spoils system that the minister has established. In answer to the question I have referred to, the statement was made that there are nineteen life-saving stations on the coast, and the officers of twelve of these have been dismissed, seven of them without investigation. One of those dismissed is a man in my own constituency who has done good work in this service in the past.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: How many stations did the hon. gentleman say there were?
The answer I have here is that there are nineteen. This was when the hon. gentleman became Minister of Marine and Fisheries.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: Yes; there are twentyseven now.

I, for one, enter my
strong protest against dealing with the lifesaving service in the manner I have indicated. The men who have charge of these stations undergo great risk and hardship, and those composing the crew are generally the best oarsmen in the harbour. In my own constituency the Government dismissed Mr. Hugh P. Munro without any Mr HAZEN.
investigation whatever and appointed a man in his place who was away from the district at the time. The whole life-boat service of that coast was demoralized for several weeks on account of the change that took place. This was done without excuse. At least, I have never been able to get any excuse from the minister, and if he has any now to give, I should like to hear what it is. I was surprised to find that a man who had served in the department so well as Mr. Munro for so many years had been dismissed. I think he was in office nearly as long as the other Mr. Munro to whose case I drew attention this session. He was appointed if I remember well, by the Conservative party before the change of Government in 1896. The Liberal Government did not dismiss the life-boat coxswains along the coast so far as I can leam, at all events they did not do so in the part of Nova Scotia from which I come. Mr. Munro as I understand, occupied his position from 1896 and held office all through the regime of the late Administration. He did his work well, and certificates have been filed with the department approving of things done by him and bis crew on more than one occasion. I have on my desk a statement of Lloyd's agent and others stating that they were a very capable and satisfactory crew. Before this man was dismissed, I wrote the minister that certain people were endeavouring to obtain his dismissal and asking him to give Mr. Munro a fair trial if complaints were made against him. I have the reply of the minister dated the 22nd of December 1911, which says:
Before final action is taken in the way of dispensing with Mr. Munro's services, he will be given an opportunity to be heard in his own defence.
But he was not given an opportunity to be heard in his own defence; for the next letter on the file is one from Commander Thompson that his services have been dispensed with and asking him to hand over the key to the boat-house and all the property under his control to the man appointed to take his place. That is a case in my own constituency, and there were in all 12 dismissals along the coast, seven of them being without investigation.

I would call attention also to the dismissal of the captain of the life-boat service at Yarmouth. I asked the minister some time ago if any dismissals had taken place, and understood him to say that so far as he knew they had not. I bad heard rumours of the dismissal of Captain Albert Caines, but after the minister's answer, I rested easy, until I went home a short time since and found that his dismissal had taken place without investigation, and there was no notice of dismissal until word

came from the department. 1 agree with the hon. member for Guysborough that petty politics have got down in this country to a point where members of life-boat crews are dismissed, because they happen to be Liberals or Tories, and the sooner it is done away with the better for the people whose life, when in danger, these crews are established to save. 'Captain Caines has been a faithful and efficient officer. He was one of our most respected ship officers at Yarmouth for many years, a man of ability and he lived near the life station. To dismiss such a man without investigation, I say, not wishing to use any stronger language, is a very small piece of business.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: Captain Albert Caines was dismissed on the advice of the officers of the department on account of his age, he being over 72 years of age.

I have seen men of the age
of seventy-two years who are far more active than the hon. member for Annapolis, (Mr. Davidson), who is applauding so loudly. Captain Caines was a capable officer; he was aS' competent to take charge of a life-boat as any man I know, and the assertion that he was dismissed from office because of his age is a very paltry excuse. I would have respected the hon,. minister more if he had said that he turned the man out because he had been a life-long Liberal. I still insist that his dismissal under those conditions is a small business, and does not add to the dignity of the Minister of Marine and Fisheries. Might I ask the minister whether a new life-saving station has been built at Point Prim, Digby county?

There is a new station at
Bay View, Digby.

Was it built by tender and
contract?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: Yes.

Who were the tenderers?
Mr, HAZEN:	I have not that information before me, but I shall be glad to get it for my hon. friend at any time. The files of the Department are always open for his inspection.
Mr, CHISHOLM (Inverness):	Has the
station at Cheticamp been opened?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: Yes.

Who is the coxswain
there?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
Michael Maillet. He was
appointed on October 15, 1912, when the station was opened.
Was he the first man recommended for the position?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: So far as I know, he was.

I recommended for
appointment a man by the name of Doucette. Does my hon. friend know whether his name is in the department?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: I have not his name here.
He was recommended for the position; I understood that he was appointed.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
I do not think that any
appointment was made before the one I have mentioned, although I do not speak positively on the matter, because I have not the information here. I take it for granted that the hon. gentleman wrote a letter to the department recommending for appointment the gentleman mentioned by him, and that letter will be found on the files of the department. I shall be glad to give the hon. gentleman any information he desires on the matter.
Are there any life-saving stations in the province of Quebec? I think that enough wrecks take place in the lower St. Lawrence to justify the establishment of a life-saving station.

I would like to corroborate what my hon. friend the member for Bonaventure says. Either at Gaspe _ or Paspebiac there should be a life-saving station. On the portion of the peninsula which faces the Atlantic ocean, the coast is very often swept by terrific storms, especially during the months of September, October and November, and during the last ten or fifteen years great losses have occurred, in vessels as well as lives. I think my hon. friend should consider the advisability of establishing a life-saving station in that neighbourhood.

There might be two or
three life-saving stations along the coast of Gaspd.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
It is an extraordinary
thing that there are no life-saving stations in that district, and I will certainly give attention to the matter.

The minister has given us no explanation of the fact that he wrote me stating that Mr. Hugh P. Munro would have an opportunity of being heard before his dismissal, and that he then declined to give him that opportunity, and dismissed him without an investigation. It is an extraordinary thing for the minister to do, and if he has an excuse, I think it would be polite for him to say so.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
When I wrote that letter
I presumed my hon. friend had reference to charges that had been made against Munro in connection with political partisanship. But Commander Thompson reported to the department that Munro was seventy years

of age, and that he was entirely too old to be entrusted with the charge of a life-saving station.

If Commander Thompson made such a report, I wish to say that the minister will find by reference to his files that he recently made another report contradicting the previous report. Complaint was made against this man prior to the defeat of the late government by certain persons who wished to obtain his position, and Commander Thompson was sent to White Head to investigate the case. After making a very thorough investigation, Commander Thompson reported to the department that Mr. Munro, although seventy years of age, was a very active man and quite able to carry on his work as coxswain of the life-boat crew. If Commander Thompson made a report contradicting his former report it simply shows that Commander Thompson was not allowed to have a free hand in regard to the matter, but that he had to do what he was told.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: Is Munro alive now?

Certainly. He is a
very energetic man; there is no finer physique to be found on the coast of eastern Canada. He is erect, tall and athletic, and Commander Thompson personally informed me that he was surprised to find a man of seventy years of age so strong and active. He reported to the department that the attempt to have Munro dismissed on account of his age was altogether improper, and that he was well able to carry on his work as coxswain of the life-saving crew. I would ask the minister to produce the second report which is said to have been made by Commander Thompson, so that the committee may see how he has dealt with the matter.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: I have not that information here but I shall be glad to find out what it is. On general principles I think that no man of 70 ought to be a member of a life saving crew. I think it is absurd to say that a man of 70 can go out in the heavy storms and do the work necessary in order to rescue people on a ship in distress.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: I do not admit that at all.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: My right hon. friend, perhaps, is trying to rescue a ship in distress now.

How
many officers are at Cheticamp station?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
A cockswain and a crew of seven. The cockswain receiving $75 a year and the crew smaller amounts.
Investigations into wrecks, $18,400.
Mr. LAW How is this amount expended?
Mr. HAZEN.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: This is exactly the same amount as last year. It is expended as follows: Travelling expenses of the chief wreck commissioner, $3,500; travelling expenses of the wreck commissioner of British Columbia, $1,000; travelling expenses of witnesses, $1,000; salary of the British Columbia wreck commissioner, $1,000; stenographers' fees, $3,000; legal services, $2,000; services of nautical overseers, $1,500; services of interpreters, $200; reporting and typewriting, $200; printing and unforeseen incidentals, $1,000; expenses of preliminary enquiries, $2,000. This does not include fees which may be granted to acting wreck commissioners for which an additional sum of $1,500 may be added.
Is there a wreck commissioner for the province of Nova Scotia?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: There is no wreck commissioner for Nova Scotia. The chief examiner of masters and mates acts on pre-Jiminary enquiries and also as wreck commissioner at times. When Captain Lindsay cannot act, the chief examiner of masters and mates is called on to act without additional salary.

It seems to me there should be a commissioner in an important province like Nova Scotia. It is well known to the minister that Nova Scotia has a very rough coast, and there are many wrecks on that coast.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: We do not seem to be crowded at all with the present stag, they are able to take care of it. I suppose that is largely because, owing to the lights and aids to navigation that have been placed there, the coast is so safe to navigation that there are very few wrecks.

I have no doubt that is the case, that after fifteen years of Liberal administration, owing to the improvements in the buoy service, wrecks have been minimized.
Expenses of schools of navigation, $8,000.
Where have you those schools?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
At present there are
schools at Yarmouth, N.S., North Sydney, Quebec, Collingwood and Victoria. Last year the vote was the same, and our expenditure was only $970. The officer who has charge of this matter recommends that we adopt a different policy from that which has prevailed in the past. Hitherto we have depended largely on a system of lectures. But the officer reports that while that system may have a tendency to stimulate increase among fishermen and seafaring men it is almost worthless as a means of preparing seafaring men to take

their certificates as masters and mates of vessels. The suggestion now is to discontinue the lecturing system and to establish schools of navigation where these men will receive such instruction in seamanship and navigation as will prepare them to qualify for masters and mates. It is also proposed to assist private navigation schools if necessary.
Is the minister providing for any additional schools?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: We are prepared, whenever it is made apparent to the department that a necessity exists for the establishment of these schools, to assist them.

But what would have
to be done?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
At Collingwood there is
a gentleman who established a school himself. He says to the people: You want instruction in navigation, I am here for that purpose. He gets some assistance from the department, an annual amount to help him with his school. At Halifax, Captain Lugar, a paid official of the department, who receives a salary nf $1,800, has conducted a school without any additional salary.

I suppose
no successor has been appointed to Captain Lugar?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
No. I do not think we
have yet received official notice of his death, although we have seen it in the newspapers.

What steps would need to be taken to secure the establishment of a school in a small town like Canso, where there are some two thousand seafaring and fishermen engaged in the fisheries in the summer, but not very busy for a couple of months in the most severe part of the winter. They could very well attend a school if one were established iai, ;that town. I have no doubt that the minister .could co-operate with the school board and the town authorities in order to get the use of the school room and such facilities. If the people there knew what was necessary to be done I have no doubt there are many places in Nova Scotia where advantage would be taken of this vote. The great trouble would be to find a properly qualified instructor. I would be glad if the department would let it be known in these little towns where they are anxious n to have schools of navigation that assist ance will be given by the department

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
We are trying to work out some better system than that which exists at the present time. We have officers directing their attention along that line. If in any of those towns there were a
reasonable number of young men who wished to get instruction sc that they could qualify for masters' or mates' certificates, we would be very glad indeed to give generous assistance. The officers of the department tell me that in the past applications have been made for the establishment of schools, and that the department helped in such cases, but they did not prove successful. A few years ago they were asked to provide an instructor for a school in Montreal. They were told that a large number of students would attend, and an instructor, a very competent man, familiar with both languages, was appointed. A good many students attended the first night, but on the third night there was not a student present, and the results were very disappointing. It is only men who have made up their mind to follow a seafaring life who attend these schools, but if in some of the small towns of Nova Scotia there were eight or ten young men who wanted instruction to enable them to follow a seafaring life, I have no doubt that out of this vote we could give assistance, and if there were co-operation with the school board, if we could get accommodation in the schools, it would help very much. We would be prepared to entertain any application along that line, and give it the most sympathetic consideration.

Would the technical
school at Halifax be at liberty to apply for some assistance in the way of establishing a branch?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: There has been correspondence with both the Prime Minister and his colleague from Halifax, I think, about the matter. We have had communications from them, and the matter is now receiving the attention of the officers of the department.

With reference to young men not attending those schools, I may say that my experience is quite different from that of the department. In Canso, a few years ago, a school was established for one winter, the head teacher of the public school being in charge of it. He was a man who knew something about navigation and could teach the theory of navigation, and the school was attended by a large number of young men during the winter months. It was very successful indeed. But the teacher removed from the place, and the instruction ceased. I suppose that the next teacher was not capable, or perhaps he did not care to take up the work. The main trouble I think is to find a suitable man to give the lessons. If the minister could discover some suitable man to go from place to place on the coast and spend a few weeks with the young fellows desirous of getting lessons on navigation

he would assist greatly. Those young men cannot go to Halifax. It is impossible for them to take long journeys and to live in those expensive places, but if the instruction were brought to them it would be of great importance.

I entirely agree with my hon. friend from Guysborough when he says that the young men who are interested in the matter should receive some assistance in maritime instruction. As he says, they cannot afford to attend a central school at Halifax. I entirely agree with his views, and I may say that I have made representations to the minister along the same lines. I trust that the department will be able to work out some system that will be more satisfactory than the one heretofore in vogue whereby these young men in the different parts of the maritime provinces would have an opportunity of acquiring an education along the lines suggested.
Registration of skipping, $1,500.
What is that?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
This is to cover the expense of the registration of shipping. After a careful estimate of the probable items of expenditure, such as the purchase of a new register, books, forms, certificates of registry, the officers are of opinion that $1,500 would be ample for this branch of the service this year.
Removal of obstructions in navigable vvaters, $20,000.
The removal of an obstruction is at the risk of the party responsible for it, is it not?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: Yes.

I understand that in
some oases where the party has failed to remove the obstruction, the department is in duty bound to clear the channel. I suppose this vote is to provide for such contingencies.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: Yes.

I have a case in mind. Last year on the river St. Lawrence, not far from Montreal, there was a wreck of a steamer plying between Montreal and Valleyfield, and I understand that the wreck remained in the channel for some time. Several persons perished, and the captain was practically ruined. I suppose that in a case like that the department would have to remove the obstruction?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
Yes. In that case we
were unable to have the wreck removed before the close of navigation. We got into communication with people at Kingston who have a wrecking plant, but they were unable to get the plant into operation Mr SINCLAIR.
in time, and the wreck had to remain until this. year. If the people responsible are not financially able to remove the obstruction, the department undertakes the removal. Twenty thousand dollars is practically the same amount as last year. Last year the total amount expended was about $11,000. There were some cases where the work was very heavy, but in those cases the parties who owned the boats were able to bear the burden.
Winter mail service, $11,000.
What is that?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
It is for the letter mail
service between Prince Edward Island and the mainland. I think my hon. friend has had the pleasure of crossing over there in an open boat. There are some winters when the ice becomes so heavy that it is impossible even for the ice-breakers to get through, and people have to cross in open boats. This vote is for that service. The boats are kept in repair to convey people across, and to take the mails in the event of that condition prevailing. Of late years the expenditure on the service has been light, because the Earl Grey and the Minto are both very good ice-breakers, and have been able to maintain a service during the winter. During last winter I do not think that these small boats were required at all.

I would like the minister to consider the advisability of utilizing one of the boats, say on five or six occasions during the winter season, for the purposes of a mail service to the Magdalen islands. As he knows, the last mail packet from Pictou leaves at the end of November, or the beginning of December. I am informed by people of the Magdalen islands that at least three or four, and sometimes five trips can be made during the_ winter between the mainland and the islands. From December until April they are closed in, and get only such news as can be transmitted by cable, or by the Marconi wireless system. That is not satisfactory at all, when a boat could easily be sent from Georgetown to Sydney. I had occasion some years ago to speak to the captain of the Stanley and, as regards the practicability of it, he saw no item of chance at all; he said that he could make the trip very easily at certain periods of the winter. But there were strong objections taken by the department, although the captain, himself, had none. Of course, he had to obey orders. I think that my hon. friend this year, or last year, overlooked the hesitation of the department and managed to send a boat once or twice, much to the benefit of the islanders, I would like him to consider this as a permanent affair for future years.

I beg to make the same request for the people of Anticosti. I do not think you can make five or six trips, but you can make two trips there during the winter. There is a boat at present subsidized by the Post Office Department which makes one or two trips to Labrador. I would not risk that boat about Anticosti, but your icebreakers could certainly be sent to the island. Anticosti has been settled of late by Mr. Menier, a very wealthy Frenchman, who has acquired that island. There is a population of nearly eight hundred very thrifty and industrious people. The island is like a European park. There is at Ellis bay, a beautiful castle, the residence of Mr. Menier himself. He has established splendid roads all through the island. There is a magnificent lobster and salmon canning industry and he is exploiting the lumber on a scientific basis as they do in France and Germany. The settlers are all Canadians, they are not foreigners. He has built a handsome cottage for each family. There is also a savings bank, a church and an hospital with the most modern equipment, which I visited some years ago. In fact, it is an ideal life for the settlers who are there. Quebec has become quite a feeder for Anticosti. The traffic between Quebec and Anticosti has increased by leaps and bounds during the last ten years. Therefore, Mr. Menier is entitled to fair and generous treatment from our Government. He has established a small Deeauville railway on the island and he has built, at his own expense, large deep-water piers whidh are utilized by the Government steamers free of any charge.
One mile long.

He has provided a
number of lighthouses, in fact he is a public benefactor and I am told that he has offered the Government of Canada the opportunity of fortifying some points on the island. There were fears expressed some years ago that such a large portion of our territory might pass to a foreign power, hut Lord Grey, our former Governor General, visited the island, was received by Mr. Menier, and after that he was very well pleased with the genial foreigner. Under these circumstances, I would like my hon. friend to consider the possibility of sending twice during the winter at least one of the Government steamers for the carrying of the mails. It is an important point in the river St. Lawrence and one which has attracted the attention of Europeans of late years. Mr. Menier has brought very many of his friends from Europe and, coming to Anticosti they have been struck with our country-some have already invested a good deal of money in western Canada. As you know, Mr. Menier is the 'chocolate king.' he is one of the
wealthiest men in Europe. A brother of his is one of the most influential public men in France, and the Dominion Government would be doing good business by encouraging him in the work which he is carrying on at Anticosti. Ganada needs such good friends in Europe and France particularly.

I am very glad to be able, to substantiate what my hon. friend from Rouville (Mr. Lemieux) has said regarding the importance of Anticosti island. It is largely peopled by settlers from th* Gaspesian peninsula, Chicoutimi and Saguenay. The Montreal Board of Trade, realizing the importance of the island are to visit it in June next when a large excursion party is going down on one of the Richelieu and Ontario Navigation Company's boats. There is no regular boat calling at the island.
