There is no difficulty in carrying out the suggestion of my hon. friend from Rouville, as the service could be performed by the ice-breakers which go to Seven islands, only a few miles from Anticosti.	I would be glad if some
measures were taken to bring Anticosti more into touch with the political life of Canada. Mr. Menier is a great Frenchman, he has also big ideas and he is the benefactor of those who come in contact with him. The island, though belonging to the constituency of Chicoutimi and Saguenay, has remained somewhat out of the political life of the province. I understand that a poll is hardly ever opened there. Surely it would be possible for the minister to make an arrangement, either in connection with the lighthouse service or in connection with the subsidized steamers calling on the north shore of the St. Lawrence, for a limited service connecting with the island of Anticosti. One of the most notable things that Mr. Menier did in the early days of his occupation of the island of Anticosti was to abolish the mosquito. Mosquitoes in the earlier days infested the island to a great extent. He drained out the swamps, took the gravel excavated from those drains and built a magnificent system of macadamized roads all over the island, and at the same time did away with the mosquitoes. He erected just next to his magnificent residence, a statute to Gamache, one of the earlier smugglers on the lower St. Lawrence, about whom a great many folk lore stories have been told. The island ,of Anticosti is a very interesting place, and I am sure that the Government would be well advised if they brought the island into closer touch with the people of the St. Lawrence and of Canada generally. Mr. Menier has shown himself well disposed to submit to our laws. There is a customs agent on the island. Mr. Menier has telephone and tele-

graphic services. He has always been glad to entertain the Governor General and ministers who have gone down to see him. No British fleet ever passes without visiting the island. Admiral Blake, some years ago, went there to inquire into the story published by the New York Herald that Anticosti had been acquired by France for the purpose of fortifying it and making it a stronghold to be used for the recovery of Quebec. Admiral Blake went over and found that what was supposed to be the magazine was full of potatoes. On the square that Mr. Menier had opened in the middle of the town, he found one of the old guns which had been put into proper shape. The island is a most interesting place, and I am sure_ that the minister would be doing a public service if he could assist Mr. Menier in bringing the people of the island into more general touch with the people of the St. Lawrence and of Canada generally.
In the cellar of the Gouverneur-really the superintendent my hon. friend will find excellent French wines; but, of course, he is not interested in that if he is a teetotaler.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
Last winter we sent the
Montcalm twice to Anticosti. In regard to the Magdalen Islands, during the *winter of 1911-12, we were able to send the Stanley there on two occasions. Last year we were able to send her only once, because she was laid up a long time for repairs. When we have Canadians living under such conditions as they do in Anticosti and the Magdalen Islands, we ought to do all we can to make their lives endurable and to keep them in touch with the outside world. With the boats we have available at present, it is impossible to say whether we can have regular trips during the summer months. As soon as the car ferry is established between Prince Edward Island and the mainland, with the Lady Grey and the Minto, we hope to be able to give better service to Anticosti and the Magdalen Islands than we have been able to do in the past. My hon. friends, the member for Rouville (Mr. Lemieux) and the member for Bonaventure (Mr. Marcil), have drawn such alluring pictures of Anticosti that I think I shall have to take a trip there during the coming summer.

I shall give you the
name of the gouverneur of Anticosti. The word gouverneur has not the same meaning as governor. Gouverneur in the present instance means the superintendent. The name has caused some people to think that Anticosti is held by the French. The name of the gouverneur is Mr. Martin Zede. He is a most charming official; all Mr. MARCIL.
his friends are Canadians, and my hon. friend will enjoy true French hospitality if he goes to Anticosti.
Inspection of live stock shipment, $5,000.

Does that come under
the Department of Marine and Fisheries?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: The duties of these inspectors are to inspect the cattle ships for the purpose of seeing that they are fit for the shipment of cattle and that the cattle have sufficient accommodation.
Where is the inspecting done?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: Almost entirely at Montreal. It used to be done at St. John, but there is hardly any necessity for inspection there now.

Does my hon. friend expect that Canadian cattle will ever pass at Liverpool without the stigma which England has put upon them? I have a motion on the OrdeT Paper which unfortunately has not been reached, asking for the removal of the embargo on Canadian cattle. Now that the Government is generous by voting $35,000,000 to the Admiralty, do you not think, Mr. Chairman, that my good friend should ask the British authorities to remove the embargo on our cattle? It is admitted by everyone-and by no better authority than Sir Charles Tupper-that this is a libel against Canadian cattle.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
I think the embargo is
only a measure of protection. The matter, however, is one which is under the Department of Agriculture. When the estimates of that department are taken up, my hon. friend will get more satisfaction than I am able to give him.
To continue thq subsidy for wrecking plants in Quebec, Maritime provinces and British Columbia, $45,000.

Would the minister give us
a memorandum of those?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
Up to the past year this
vote was always $30,000-$10,000 for wrecking plants in British Columbia, $10,000 for wrecking plants with headquarters at Quebec, and $10,000 for wrecking plants in the maritime provinces. These wrecking plants have been owned by the Dominion Coal Company at Sydney. Last year Mr. Davy, who had the contract at Quebec, refused to renew it, stating that, even with the subsidy of $10,000, he was losing money, because there had been so few wrecks on the St. Lawrence river for the past three or four years. He had to keep a tug boat equipped with pumps and wrecking apparatus, with its fires constantly banked, a large schooner and men to man them. The shipping interests felt that there must be

a wrecking plant on the St. Lawrence. Therefore a company was formed by the different steamship interests with whom we made a contract. They bound themselves to equip their tug boat with wireless telegraphy, as had not been the case with Davy. In consideration of their doing that, it was agreed that they should be allowed, within a certain limit of space on the river, to do certain work in the way of towing of ships, because, with their wireless apparatus, if a wreck occurred, they could be notified and get to the scene of the wreck almost as quickly as if they were lying at Quebec. They refused to take up the work at $10,000, and we agreed to give them $25,000. There was an agreement in the contract that, after they paid on their equipment a valuation that was fixed-I think it was six per cent-the balance of the profits, if they had any, were to be divided between the Government and the company. Last year, as hon. gentlemen know, there were a number of wrecks; and the result is that, while we paid the company $25,000, there had been paid back into the Consolidated Revenue Fund of Canada about $12,5ui) as the share of the Government in the partnership into which they entered. The arrangement will work out very well. Everyone will admit the necessity of having a wrecking plant, and it seems impossible to have a wrecking plant without aid from the Government.

It is recommended by
the shipping interests?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
Yes. They realize they
must have a wrecking plant on the St. Lawrence.

I have no objection to the
vote, but I think tne western part of Nova Scotia should have one of those plants.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
It has been put forward
every now and then that the wrecking plant ought to be in the Maritime provinces, so far as the winter months are concerned, at some point nearer to the bay of Fundy and the south shore of Nova Scotia.

Somewhere around St.
John.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: No, I think the matter can be met by the arrangement that will be made for this year by having that plant remain at Sydney during the Summer months, and then they are going to have some of their plant at Halifax or some point west of there, where tney will be available near the bay of Fundy during the winter.

Are the parties having the
contract allowed to charge anything for salvage?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
Yes. If they were not
allowed to do that, the amount the department would have to pay would be increased. The rates are of course subject to our approval.

Before my hon. friend
proceeds to another item, I should like to speak about a matter which perhaps is not germane to this. This patrol which was organized in the north Atlantic was with a view to preventing wrecks and accidents?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: Yes.

(Translation.) Mr. Chairman, I fully concur in the remarks just made by the hon. member for Rouville (Mr. Lemieux), with respect to establishing salvage stations in the region of the gulf, in order to bring efficient relief to ships in peril. Those stations should be established at Gaspe or at Rimouski. Either of those two ports would be a good centre where to establish one of those stations _ which could send out some help to ships in distress.
I think this matter has been too much neglected in the past and that the Government should do something in this direction.
As to the remarks made by the hon. member for Rouville with respect to carry-

ing the mails over to Magdelen Islands, I think that they are very appropriate. Those people are deprived of means to communicate with the mainland during all the winter and the Government would be doing good work by granting them a better service with respect to carrying the mails.
As far as naval schools are concerned, I am glad to hear from the minister himself that he is ready to help some of the students who would like to become conversant with matters pertaining to navigation. In our counties which are located along the sea, like Eimouski, Gaspe and Bonaventure, we have numbers of fishermen, of excellent seamen, and what they lack and what they want in order to improve in their art is naval schools.

the salaries of fishery officers are under discussion, I wish to have the minister ready if I decide to bring up the case of A. R. McAdam, fishery officer at Malignant Cove. I have about come to the conclusion that the political virtue I have ascribed to hon. gentleman, which I Mr. BOULAY.
thought existed in this benevolent-looking man and smooth-talking minister, as a matter of fact does not exist in him. It comes down to this-he has made up his mind that he will be like his associates and will fire any Grit who is in office. On that account, I may not bring the matter up at all.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: I am sorry to have disappointed my hon friend.
I expect to call the attention of the minister to the dismissal of Captain Norman L. Trefry, shipmaster at Yarmouth, and Dr. Carl A. Webster, Port Physician at Yarmouth.

Before the committee rises for the six o'clock recess, I wish to say a word. I have been absolutely disgusted with the corruption that goes on in Nova Scotia and the call there has been for so many dismissals. What kind of people are they? In my county there has not been a dismissal of an officer for fifteen or twenty years. We observe the law there in election time; we do what is right; there is no cause for dismissals. I cannot but think that if hon. gentlemen would serve their constituents fairly, they would not air their grievances as much as they have been doing. The reputation of the whole province of Nova Scotia is being destroyed. I had the idea that Nova Scotians were respectable people, law-abiding people. But it turns cut, from one thing after another, that there is hardly a man in the province but is guilty of something in connection with elections. I really think that hon. gentlemen would be doing a favour to their province if'they would drop this miserable talk about dismissals and bringing to the notice of the whole country the actions of the people of that province. On the whole, however, I cannot believe the people are half as bad as they are represented. I have too much respect for them to think otherwise. To my mind the time has come when this talk about dismissals can very well be dropped, at anyrate for this session.

I would suggest to the hon. gentleman that he make that suggestion to tile minister.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works
speechtext:
This is a Bill prepared
by Judge Robson, now Utilities Commissioner for the province of Manitoba, for the purpose of taking the water from Shoal lake, a portion of which is within the province of Manitoba and a portion of which is within the province of Ontario. By reason of the fact that the lake is situated in both provinces it was found necessary to have this Bill. A similar Bill relating to the city of Ottawa was passed by this House the other day. The Bill has been very carefully prepared, it was presented to the Senate by Senator Young and passed by that House. It has passed the Private Bills Committee of this House. The city of Winnipeg has obtained its domestic water supply from artesian wells, but these have not been found sufficient for a great and growing city and it is now desired to bring water from this lake. There is no objection from the Government of Ontario.
On section 7-application of sections of Railway Act:

What are these provisions of the Railway Act?
Mr. AIK.INS:	They relate to the expropriation of land through which the conduit may be carried. The purpose is to modify the Railway Act to such an extent as to make it applicable. So instead of Minister of Railways it says Minister of Public Works. The expropriation which is provided for of course calls for compensation.
It would seem to me that the legislation of this Parliament would hardly b9 sufficient under the circumstances.

Under the British North America Act any work extending from one province into another or connecting twi provinces necessarily comes within the jurisdiction of this Parliament. The works authorized by this Act refer specifically to taking water from Ontario.

This is not the kind of work that is contemplated by the British North America Act. I am not objecting to the Bill, but merely pointing out that this is a case where we may be taking the property which belongs to the province of Ontario, or the property of some individual. I submit that the Government of the province of Ontario should be consulted in some way as to this Bill.
Mr. LANCASTER.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works
speechtext: The province of Ontario had due notice of this Bill, and it has been before the Senate and advertised in a public way for some weeks. I know that the Government of the province of Ontario have had full knowledge of it, and there is no objection from any quarter. This lake is in an outlying district, and the Bill cannot affect or disturb anybody.

The minister's statement does not cure the point of law I am making. I do not know what view the Government or the people of Ontario may take of it, but the water of that lake is as much the property of Ontario as part of a forest or a deposit of minerals would be.

There seems to be some misunderstanding. This Bill does not provide for the taking of water from any special place. It provides for getting water from waters that are under the control of the Parliament of Canada. It does not provide for going into Ontario or any other province. If they do go into Ontario and take water, they will certainly have to make an arrangement with the Ontario Government. This Bill is only to give the city of Winnipeg power to take such waters as are under the control of the Parliament of Canada; it does not specify any lake.
Does it provide for expropriation ?

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works

Yes.

speechtext: It is estimated that the total number of cubic yards to be removed in the north channel below Quebec, to obtain a channel thirty-five feet in depth at extreme low tide and 1,000 feet in width, amounts to 16,153,173 cubic yards. I desire to call the attention of the Minister of Marine and Fisheries to

certain dismissals in the lighthouse service made in the county of Richmond during the last year. Mr. Duchemin, the gentleman entrusted with making recommendations for dismissals, has become emboldened no doubt by the encouragement he receives from the minister. From time to time during the present session, as well a.:' during the last session the attention of the House has been called to the absolutely unfair and unjustifiable recommendations which have been made by Mr. Duchemin for the dismissal of public officers throughout the province of Nova Scotia. As I have said, owing to the defence made for him on the floor of this House by the ministers and their supporters, he is keeping the even tenor of his way, and is becoming less and less disposed to observe the ordinary rules and principles of fair play which characterizes the lowest and most inferior courts in the land. I have here the papers with regard to the dismissal of Mr. Michael O'Brien, keeper of the light at Bear island. Mr. O'Brien received notice to appear before Mr. Duchemin to answer to the charge of political partisanship, and that notice is as follows:
Mr. Michael O'Brien,
Bear Island, N.S.
I beg to notify you that I have been instructed by the Minister of Marine and Fisheries, to investigate the charge of political partisanship, that has been preferred against you, for acts committed while you were in the employ of the Dominion Government, in the capacity of lightkeeper.
The investigation will be held in Edward Malcolm's house, at Port Malcolm, N.S., on Thursday the 20th day of February, 1912, at two o'clock in the afternoon, when you are t equested to be present, and to have any witnesses there who can testify in your behalf.	,
Dated, Sydney, N.S., the 17th day of February, 1913.
H. P. Duchemin.
Commissioner of Inquiry.
This notice, it will be observed, requested the attendance of Mr. O'Brien at Port Malcolm for the purpose of answering the charge. But instead of Mr. Duchemin holding the court at Port Malcolm upon the day fixed by him, he held court eight miles away in another county, and of the holding of that court Mr. O'Brien had no notice. Yet Mr. Duchemin proceeded to investigate the charges as if Mr. O'Brien had been properly summoned before him. I have here the affidavit of Mr. O'Brien setting forth the facts:

30th December, 1912.
Dear Sir,-I have yours of the 21st instant, in which charges of political partisanship are preferred against Michael O'Brien, keeper of the light on Bear Island, Richmond county, N.S.
