I pointed out that Mr. O'Brien was summoned to appear before Mr .Duchemin to answer to the charge of political partisanship at Port Malcolm, in the county of Richmond, on February 20, 1913. Mr. O'Brien did not receive his notice until February 22, 1913, and, in addition to his not receiving notice in time to appear before Mr. Duchemin, the extraordinary feature of the matter is that Mr. Duchemin changed the place where the investigation was to have been held, and where O'Brien was notified to appear, to Port Hawkesbury, a point eight miles distant from Port Malcolm, and the investigation was there held by Mr. Duchemin without giving O'Brien an opportunity to appear, because O'Brien received no notice to appear at that place. I have before me the report which was sent by Mr. Duchemin to the Department of Marine and Fisheries, upon which Mr. O'Brien was dismissed. In the earlier period of Mr. Du-chemin's investigation of these charges, he always forwarded a copy of the evidence which was taken before him to the several departments which had instructed him to hold the investigations, and when the papers were moved for, not only Mr. Duchemin's report, but the whole of the evidence was available. It would appear, however, that Mr. Duchemin has profited by experience, and he is not now forwarding copies of the evidence upon which he bases his report for dismissals. It would be perfectly obvious, upon a comparison of Mr. Duchemin's findings with the evidence upon which he based them, that his recommendations had not been justified by the evidence. Mr. Duchemin, therefore, has not recently



an instrument for the purpose of bringing about dismissals which are bound to come anyway.
There is no circumstances in connection with this dismissal of Mr. O'Brien that can be justified for a moment. Mr. O'Brien did not receive a notice of the investigation until two days after the date of the investigation; the investigation was held at a place eight miles distant from the place where he was summoned to appear and therefore he had no opportunity whatever of appearing before the commissioner.
It has been disputed by hon. gentlemen opposite as to whether the statement which has been made by hon. gentlemen on this side is correct that Mr. Duchemin is not allowing counsel to be heard on behalf of persons charged. That is a small matter, grave as it is, compared with the fact that men. are taken unawares, are sent notices which are absolutely deceptive, are given notices which are intended to deceive them and to render it absolutely impossible for them to be present at the inquiry. If Mr. O'Brien had been present at that inquiry, although I submit it would not have availed in the mind of Mt. Duchemin, he would have had the satisfaction of going upon the witness stand and pointing out the respects in .which the evidence adduced against him was absolutely without foundation. As a matter of fact, Mr. O'Brien was not the agent of the Liberal candidate in the last provincial election. He has not been an agent for any candidate either before or since his appointment to office, so far as I am aware. The fact that Mr. O'Brien went into the poll on election day and asked the presiding officer to mark his ballot would no doubt have been explained had an opportunity of appearing before Mr. Duchemin been given him. So I say, in view of all the circumstances, that Mr. O'Brien's dismissal is one of the most dastardly and indefensible dismissals in the province of Nova Scotia in eighteen months-and there has been a record in Nova Scotia of which neither Mr. Duchemin nor the Minister of Marine ought to be proud.
What is my object in bringing this matter before the committee? I certainly do not expect that the minister will reinstate Mr. O'Brien. Should the minister grant another inquiry, and give Mr. O'Brien another opportunity to appear before Mr. Duchemin, the commissioner would no doubt so garble the testimony as to make an apparent justification for his dismissal and the only result would be that another $30 or $40 of Government money would find its way into his pocket. My purpose in bringing this matter before this committee is to give publicity to the infamous manner in which these investigations are being held, For fifteen years the Liberals were in power in this coun-Mr. KYTE.
try and only in two cases were there dismissals for political partisanship^ in the county of Richmond and these dismissals were made after inquiry, not by a political partisan but, as is well remembered, by a commissioner appointed by the late Government to make inquiries into political partisanship in Nova Scotia, a gentleman who held a high position in the public service of this country, who had had very long experience in holding judicial inquiries. I refer to the late Captain Douglas. No one would dare to attempt to influence Captain Douglas as to the decision he ought to give to any inquiry before him and, as a matter of fact, I know many instances where in quiries were held before him and he dismissed the charges of partisanship alleged against the official. Never in the history of Canada have there been so many dismissals as have been made in all the departments of this Government since they came into power. This afternoon the hon.. member for Halton proceeded to read a lecture to members from Nova Scotia for the time they were taking up in discussing the matter of dismissals in that province. He said it was a disgrace to the province of Nova Scotia. I quite concede it is a disgrace to the province of Nova Scotia, a bitter disgrace to the Government which the hon. member supports so loyally. If there is any person disgraced and degraded before the country in respect of these dismissals it is not the unfortunate officeholder who has been hounded to death since the change of Government in order that his position might be given to a partisan; the disgrace lies at the doors of the members of this Government who countenance these unfair dismissals and will resort to the subterfuges to which they do resort in order to bring them about. On another occasion, when discussing the question of dismissals in this House during the present session, I read the declarations of the Prime Minister as to what the rights of an official were with regard to participating in public discussions. The right hon. gentleman stated that public officials had the right not only to attend public meetings but to speak at public meetings provided they did not give offence to any person in the community. But, like every other principle which the right hon. gentleman espoused when he was in office, it has been cast to the winds, and, with every colleague he has in the Government, he has degenerated to the verv lowest depths to accomplish the ruin of officials who have been public servants during the last fifteen vears. On other occasions during this session, we have had cries of sympathy from hon. gentlemen opposite. When complaint was made in this House that a man named Andrew

Landry had been improperly released from jail in order that he might enjoy the emoluments of publio office, the defence was that he had a large family, and that it was a most cruel thing for him to be kept in jail. The hon. Minister of Marine and Fisheries and the Minister of Justice both declaimed against hon. gentlemen on this side of the House on the ground of their hard-heartedness in seeking to have this man Landry kept in jail to serve out his sentence, when a family depended on him. But 75 per cent of the men who have been ruthlessly driven from office have large families depending on them. They are men who gave up whatever employment they previously had to accept employment under the Government, and they have been turned out of public office without any means of livelihood. The sympathy and charity of hon. gentlemen opposite are only to be extended to Tories who are seeking office, or who are seeking liberty from the public jails. There is no sympathy to be shown for the official who happens to have been appointed by a Liberal, but if he has been guilty of voting for or has been suspected of voting for a liberal candidate, he must be cast to the winds, and their own heelers must be given the position. I am -anxious to hear what defence the Minister of Marine and Fisheries has for the dismissal of Mr. O'Brien, in view of the circumstances which I have stated, and in order to give the minister an opportunity of making a defence I shall give the floor to him, and continue my remarks later on.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
My hon. friend has worked himself into a fine state of frenzy over this matter. He has used a -wonderful vocabulary of adjectives. 'Gruesome,'
' blood-thirsty,' and other adjectives of the most extraordinary character have been indulged in by the hon. gentleman-adjectives which I think are entirely misplaced. What are the facts in connection with this matter? The facts are that charges were made to the Marine and Fisheries Department to the effect that this man occupying a Government position, had been an active partisan in recent elections in the province of Nova Scotia. Mr. Duchemin, who was the commissioner appointed to investigate charges of that sort in the eastern part of the province of Nova Scotia, had this matter referred to him for inquiry. Mr. Duchemin, after inquiry, submitted his lenort to the denartment, and in that report, which is the only matter we have on record with regard to it, Mr.. Duchemin states that Mr. O'Brien was duly notified of the time and place of examination, hut that he did not appear thereat. That is the only statement we have with regard to
340}
the investigation. It is the statement of the commissioner appointed and sworn to do his doty, and that commissioner states most emphatically that Mr. O'Brien was notified of the time and place of investigation, but that he did not appear thereat. Now, it is a very strange thing to me, if that investigation was held, as it was held away back in the month of February last, thfit no communication of any sort was ever addressed to the department by Mr. O'Brien, or by anybody acting on his behalf, stating that he was not notified of the time and place of examination and had no opportunity of attending, if such were the case.

Mr. O'Brien immediately
sent me a copy of his declaration, and I moved for the papers, and I got them only a short time ago.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: That is no answer to the statement I made. I say it was a surprising- thing, if my hon. friend is correct in saying that O'Brien was not properly notified of the time and place of investigation, as Mr. Duchemin says he was, that after all these months had elapsed, no communication was addressed to the department stating that he had not been notified.
Does the minister say that O'Brien committed perjury when he made this declaration ?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: My hon. friend had better not get excited.
I am not excited at all.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
He is the most excited man I have seen in the House this year ?'
^Mr. KYTE: Nothing of the kind.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
I -repeat to my hon. friend that it is a most- extraordinary thing-I repeat it for the third time-if that statement of Mr. Duchemin's that O'Brien had been notified of the time and place of examination, is not true, and Mr. O'Brien was not notified of the time and place of examination, that all those months should have elapsed without any representation having been made to that effect to the department. My hon. friend says he moved for the papers. That is no answer to what I have said% He moved for the papers which were in the department, and they were brought down. Every paper bearing on the matter was brought down, and there is nothing in those papers showing that any complaint was ever lodged with the department- claiming that Du-c-hemin's statement that he had notified O'Brien of the time and place of examination was an untrue statement, or declaring that O'Brien had not been so notified. I agree at once

that if he was not notified, it was a most improper proceeding, and I further say that if he was not notified, and if in that report, Mr. Duchemin was stating what was untrue, and deceiving the department, it was a most improper proceeding, and one not worthy of an official occupying the position of commissioner under the Act. But all that we have on our official record is that statement of Duchemin that O'Brien was notified of the time and place of the investigation, and until there is satisfactory evidence to show that^ that statement is not correct, I think it is my duty to stand by that statement made by Mr. Duchemin in the official -report which he made to the Department of Marine and Fisheries. I must accept and stand by this man who was appointed by the department to act as commissioner until the contrary is shown, as I shall stand by any official of the department until it is shown that he is not worthy of confidence. The investigation was held, and it was shown that O'Brien was a lighthouse keeper who was interested in an election, that he attended the nomination _ meeting, that he was away all day and night, and did not return to his lighthouse until the following day. That is stated in the evidence by a man named Morgan, a fisherman-farmer living at Bear Island. It is further shown that Mr. O'Brien was a voter in the provincial election of 1911, and under the rule laid down by the right hon. the leader of the Opposition, interference ' in a provincial election is just as much a cause for dismissal as interference in a Dominion election. It is shown that in the provincial election of 1911, after the Dominion election, O'Brien went to vote, and that although he was able to read and write he insisted on having his ballot marked by the returning officer. "What could his purpose be in doing that ? He wanted to show his zeal on behalf of the cause of the party he was supporting, what a keen and active partisan he was, and what a keen part he was taking in the elections. Then we have the further statement, that he also talked in strong language	in	regard to
the Conservatives. According to one witness, he said: ' When the Tories were in power they did us no good, and, if they got in now they will ruin us. Certainly the Liberals will get in.' The one statement may have been correct from a certain standpoint, but he was not a good prophet with regard to the other. If that statement is correct, and Duchemin says that is the evidence before him,- I ask any hon. gentleman if that is not sufficient to justify O'Brien's dismissal on the ground of offensive partisanship. No hon. gentleman will contend that it is not, and having that report made by an official api Mr. HAZEN.
pointed for the purpose of investigating this matter, and no report having been made to the department that there was anything wrong with regard to it, I was amply justified in taking the course I did, in recommending O'Brien's dismissal. My hon. friend has referred to the fact that in the province of Nova Scotia under Liberal rule men were not turned out of office in this way. In the county of Queens and Shelburne, far more Dominion officials were dismissed from office after the election of 1896 than have been dismissed since the election of 1911, although there were not so many officials in the county at that time. My hon. friend from Richmond further referred to the fact that the Liberals appointed an official to hold these investigations-Mr. Bloomfield Douglas. In the province of New Brunswick they did not appoint an official; they appointed a lawyer in the city of St. John, a gentleman, I suppose, having a standing at the bar similar to that of Mr. Duchemin, or Mr. Knowles, or the other gentleman who have been conducting investigations of this kind. Mr. Bloomfield Douglas' may have held some investigations but he was not the only commissioner in the province of Nova Scotia appointed for that purpose. I have been informed that in the province of Nova Scotia two other gentlemen, Mr. Bill and Mr. Ross, lawyers practising in the city of Halifax, were appointed to hold investigations and did hold investigations in the province of Nova Scotia. So, my hon. friend is not correct when he says that these investigations were held by officials of the Government because others were appointed just as Mr. McAlpine was appointed in New Brunswick and as other gentlemen were appointed in other parts of the province. All I can say is that I accept the statement of Mr. Duchemin as a correct report of what occurred until the contrary is shown. The hon. gentleman makes the* statement on the authority of a man who has been removed from office. I do not wish to say that that man is not telling the truth, but I will say that he is not an unprejudiced witness and that my duty is to accept the statement that Mr. Duchemin has made to the department without one word to the contrary until months have intervened and with no statement being made to the effect that the man was not properly notified until it is made by my hon. friend to the committee to-night.

The Minister of Marine and Fisheries is inclined to set aside the statement of Mr. O'Brien as to the facts because he says he is not an unprejudiced witness. Very good, but I will remind him that in nine cases out of ten, where he instituted inquiries into charges of partisanship against officials, the witnesses were the men who were looking for their jobs and

trying to bring about their dismissal. Will the minister say that these were unprejudiced witnesses?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: I will say that the statement that in nine cases out of ten the men who gave evidence were looking for their jobs is without foundation.

I will say, speaking for my own county, that in nine cases out of ten the men who appeared as witnesses against officials charged with partisanship were the men who were seeking the offices held by these men and who got the offices afterwards. In seventy-five per cent of the cases the only witnesses called to give testimony were the men who were looking for the offices and who got the offices afterwards. If the evidence of Mr. O'Brien ought to be without weight in the opinion of the minister because he was a prejudiced witness, I ask the minister why he and his colleagues have been dismissing men from office on charges of partisanship when the only witnesses to appear against them were the men who were looking for their places?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: I have not the evidence of O'Brien before me. I have no evidence of O'Brien, he gave no evidence and all we have is the ex parte statement which has been made by the hon. gentleman. All the witnesses who appeared before Mr. Duchem-in were examined under oath.

Why has not the minister the evidence?-because Mr. O'Brien was misled into going to a place eight miles away irom where the inquiry was held, and yet the minister endeavours to make a point that he has not the evidence of O'Brien before him. How could he have the evidence of Mr. O'Brien when this fair-minded, non-partisan and highly-respected commissioner of his sent him off on a fool's errand eight _ miles away from where the court was being held? That is the reason why the evidence is not before the minister. It was absolutely impossible to get the evidence, and Mr. Duchemin well knew that when he sent O'Brien away on a fool's errand. W. J. Malcolm said: 'I have been a Tory for thirty years and I want a public office.' The minister, in view of the report of the dismissal of O'Brien, makes a statement which is tantamount to the well known declaration of the politician in the United States some years ago, that to the victors .belong the spoils. That is the position of the Minister of Marine and Fisheries; we might as well understand it and the taxpayers of Canada might as well be saved the cost of paying Mr. Duchemin for any further investigations which he may be making. The minister says to the committee that there was evidence that this man used offensive language on the street to a voter. Who gave the evidence? It was the wife of the man
who is now the lightkeeper. The two points upon which evidence has been given and which the minister seems to think is a justification for the dismissal could no doubt have been explained by O'Brien had he had an opportunity of appearing before the commissioner. Mr. O'Brien having voted openly, could have been explained, no doubt. I am not complaining so much about the dismissal of O'Brien but I am complaining of the farcical character of the investigation. Mr. Duchemin's conduct in holding investigations in Richmond county, and my experience is not limited to this case, has been such as to cast discredit upon any finding which he may make, and before the Minister of Marine and Fisheries gets his estimates through he will have more instances of the character of the inquiries which have been held. Then the minister endeavours to minimize the effect of the statement I made here to-night by stating that he has not the sworn testimony of O'Brien, whereas we have the solemn declaration of O'Brien, deposed to before a commissioner of the Supreme Court of Nova Scotia, to which is attached the original notice sent by Mr. Duchemin to Mr. O'Brien notifying him to attend for investigation at Port Malcolm on the 20th of February. Yet the minister says there is no evidence that Mr. O'Brien was not summoned to appear before the commissioner at Port Hawkesbury. I have- sometimes admired the ingenuous manner the Minister of Marine and Fisheries has of getting around difficult points in the matter; of the conduct of Mr. Duchemin, but it is apparent to the committee that the minister is driven to the last ditch in his effort to find an explanation for the report which Mr. Duchemin has made in this instance.

My hon. friend from Richmond (Mr. Kyte), has been pointing out a case in which a lighthouse keeper was dismissed on very slight evidence and a dispute has been going on between him and the Minister of Marine and Fisheries as to whether the evidence was sufficient or not. I can cite a case to my hon. friend where there was no evidence at all excepting a letter from the man who wanted to get the job. It is the case of the dismissal of Stephen C. Richards, of Charles' Cove, in the county of Guysborough. Mr. Richards was a good officer, no complaint against him, and he was not a partisan in so far as I know. A letter was written by Mr. Alex. Richard, who wished to obtain the position held by Mr. Stephen Richards, to Mr. Rowlings, the defeated candidate in Guysborough, and Mr. Rowlings forwarded the letter of Mr. Richard to the Minister of Marine and Fisheries. The letter is as follows:

Mr. 6. A. Rowlings,
Sydney, N.S.
Sir,-I beg to report that Mr. Stephen C. Richards now holding the office of lightkeeper of range lights ait Clharlos' Cove, county of Guysborough, N.S. has been an active Liberal partisan and was a worker for the Liberal candidate at the recent election in September, 1911, and I hereby request that he be immediately dismissed.
Yours truly,
(Sgd..) Alex. Richard, per W. J. Murphy.
An illiterate man who is not able to sign his own name makes application through another man of the name of Mr. Murphy, and states that Mr. Stephen C. Richards is a partisan. The letter was sent to Mr. Rowlings, and Mr. Rowlings sent the letter to the minister. Mr. Rowlings' letter is as follows:
Hon. J. D. Hazen, M.P.,
Minister of Marine and Fisheries, Ottawa.
Dear Sir,-Referring to the above I beg to say that I am satisfied from inquiries that I have made that Mr. Stephen C. Richards, the present holder of this position, as stated by Mr. Murphy, is an active Liberal partisan and took an active part in the recent election. I would therefore recommend that the above request be granted and that Mr. Alexander Richard of Charles' Cove, N.S., be appointed to the said position.
Yours truly,
(Sgd.) G. A. R. Rowlings.
The minister will see that the sole evidence on which he dismissed this official was a letter from a man who was expecting to get the appointment, and this letter was forwarded by the defeated candidate. In his letter, Mr. RowliDgs recommends Mr. Alex. Richard, the man who makes the complaint, for the position. Then we have the reply of the minister to Mr. Rowlings as follows:
G. A. R. Rowlings, Esq.,
Sydney, N.S.
Dear Sir,-I am in receipt of yours covering recommendation of Alexander Richard that Stephen C. Richards now holding office of lightkeeper of range lights at Charles' Gove, county of Guysborough, be removed from office.
I note your recommendation that Alexander Richard be appointed to tlie position. In view of your (Statement that you are satisfied from inquiries you have made Itha't iMr. S. C. Richards is an active Liberal partisan, who took an active part in the recent election I will recommend that the cl*inge desired be made.
Yours very truly,
(Sgd.) J. D. Hazen.
There is no necessity for the committee to listen to disputes as to whether evidence has' been taken or not, because there is no evidence here except a letter written by the man who wants to get the appointment himself. If a man can be dismissed on Mr. SINCLAIR.
evidence like that, I submit to the committee that it is a farce to call these proceedings an investigation. Will the minister explain why he dismissed the lighthouse keeper at Charlos' Cove without any evidence whatever, and appointed in his place the man who complained against him?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
Mr. G. A. R. Rowlings,
who was a candidate in the county of Guysborough at the last election, enclose to the department a communication he had received from Mr. Alex. Richard, stating that Mr. Stephen Richards had been an active partisan and was working for the Liberal candidate during the recent election. Mr. Rowlings stated that he had investigated the matter carefully and was satisfied that the information was correct. On his statement, the order was issued a little later on to rerhove Mr. Stephen Richards from his position. I received a letter from my hon. friend (Mr. Sinclair) stating that he thought this was a mistake, and requesting that an investigation be held. At the request of my hon. friend. I ordered that investigation to be held. The investigation was not held as promptly as it should have been. My hon. friend, I think, early in the session, called my attention to the fact that I had given him my promise that an investigation would be held. I looked up the file and found that the department had instructed Mr. Duch-emin to hold an investigation; I think that was towards the end of January Last; but up to that time no report had been received. We instantly communicated with Mr. Duchemin; called his attention to the fact that orders had been issued by the department to hold an investigation, and asked him why he had not done so. We also ordered him to proceed to do so at once, if he had not already done so. I have under my hand the report of Mr. Duche-min which has been handed to me just now by the deputy minister. I did not see it before I came into the House and before two minutes ago, when my hon. friend commenced to speak. The report is as follows:
Sydney, N.8., May 15, 1913. Hon. .T. D. Hazen,
*Minister of Marine and Fisheries,
Ottawa, Canada.
Re Stephen Richards, formerly lightkeeper,
Ohabios' Cove, 'Guysborough county, NjS. Dear Sir,-	.
On the 13fch instant, I conducted an inquiry into the complaints of political partisanship which resulted in the removal of Stephen Richards from the position of lightkeeper at Charlos' Cove, in the county of Guysborough, N.S.
The inquiry took place at Larry's River, Guysborough county, a short distance from the home of Mr. Richards. Due notice had * been sent to Mr. Richards, of the date and

place of the hearing, and he was present throughout the hearing.
Alexander Richard, of Charles' Cove, testified that he had been a voter in that place for 30 or 35 years, and had known iStephen Richard ever since he was a child. This witness described Stephen Richard as having been a strong party man and a worker on his side of politics, for many years past. Witness stated that he remembered the last Dominion election, and that on that occasion Stephen Richard spent a very considerable part of the day around about the polling booth at Charles' Cove. He spent the day- or a considerable part of it-meeting and talking with voters as they came up to the poll to vote. Witness estimated that Mr. Richard was at least two or three hours outside the booth, occupied in the manner described. Witness was there for two or three hours himself, and saw Mr. Richard so occupied, and stated that when he (witness) left the poll, Stephen Richard was still on the ground, occupied in the same manner. Witness further went on to say that on provincial election day, he had known Stephen Richard to spend the day in the same manner outside the polling booth, interviewing and talking with voters, as they came up to poll their votes. He explained that on every election day for years past, it has been the practice of the workers on both 6ides of politics to station themselves outside and near the polling booth. Last election day, for instance, witness was present among the Conservative workers, a.nd he stated that Stephen Richard was associated with the Liberal workers outside the booth. Witness further alleged that it was the custom for Stephen Richard to spend election day in the manner described-either at the poll ait Charlos' Cove, or the poll at Larry's River-some two or three miles distant. Witness also stated that it is a custom in this district for both political parties to endeavour to .have as many as possible of their supporters stationed outside the booth on election day, for election purposes.
On the conclusion of this witness' testimony, I asked Stephen Richard, who was present, if he wished to submit or suggest questions by way of cross-examination. He then asked witness if he knew of his having paid moneys for votes on any occasion. Witness replied that he did not.
Stephen Richard then gave testimony in his own behalf. After having been duly sworn as a witness, he admitted that he was around the poll at Charles' Cove, but was inclined to question the statement of the witness that he had been there for upwards of three hours. In this connection, Mr. Richard said: I admit that I was around the poll at C'harllos' Cove, but I don't think I was there for three hours. I don't think I was there more than two hours. Joe Hatch Richard gave me a drink of rum outside the booth- about a quarter of a mile from the booth, the afternoon of election day, I don't know {whether that was election rum or not.
While witness claimed that he had not done any definite canvassing outside the booth on the occasion referred to, he did acknowledge that he had participated in political discussion outside the door of the booth, and that he had spoken up in the interests of the
Liberals. As witness put it:	J talked up
my. side outside the booth, but did not ask anyone ito vote Grit last election day. Witness also admitted that he was outside the same booth last local election day, and that he had ' talked up his side,' outside the booth on that occasion. He would not state definitely that he did not canvass anyone, but stated that he ' did not remember asking anyone to vote for the Grit side.' Witness did not question the statement of Alexander Richard that it has been his custom for years past, to spend election day outside the booth in the manner described.
In the circumstances I do not think that there can he any question that Mr. Richard violated the rule of the department, prohibiting employees from taking part in elections. It has evidently been his custom for years past to leave the light and spend all, or a considerable part of election day, outside the polling booth at either Charlos' Cove or Larry's River, discussing politics and arguing from the point of view of the Liberal party. This is certainly improper conduct on the part of a public official, and in the circumstances I think amply warranted the action of the department in dispensing with Mr. Richard's services as keeper of the light, at Charlos' Cove.
I have the honour to be, Sir,
Your obedient servant,
(Sgd.) H. P. Duchemin, Commissioner of Inquiry.
I may say to my hon. friend that I would have sent to him a copy of this at once, but I only received it now for the first time.

What does the hon.
minister think of it?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: It seems to me, if he admitted himself that his habit was to stand outside the polling booth on election day, discussing the elections and 'talking up,' as he put it, the Liberal party, that he must have been there for the purpose of helping the Liberal party and that 'he is a partisan.

Not at all. In a little village of that kind they all sit outside the polling booth on election day. My hon. friend knows very well how these elections are conducted. Surely it is not a political crime for a man to chat with his neighbours about the elections, when sitting outside the poll on a fine day. It is a little fishing village, and the day is a holiday for the people. Mr. Richards is an honest man; he tells the truth; he says they are talking about the election. He also says that he was not canvassing anybody.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: He does not say that. He says: ' I talked up my side outside _the poll.' What does that mean? I suppose that ' talking up my side ' meant giving arguments why one should vote for * my side.'

The hon. minister is not so innocent that he does not know what ' talking up my side ' means. He has been long enough around polling booths to know all about it. In a country village, you have fifty or sixty neighbours who have come to the poll. Of course, they are talking election-what are they there for if not' for that? And because an official goes to the poll and meets his neighbours, and they get into discussion about an election and the official says:	I believe my side is
right, is that any reason why the man should be dismissed? We are getting some light on this question to-night. I am very glad indeed to have the Minister of Marine and Fisheries give his answers as plainly as he has done. I have never taken a hand in this question of dismissals except a little talk with the Postmaster Generali very early in the last session. I am safe in saying that three-quarters of the officials in my constituency have been removed from office. I believe that every postmaster of an office with a salary of more than $100 a year has been dismissed, and I am safe in saying that all the customs officers except two or three have suffered the same fate. In one particular case, I got the evidence. I would like to say to the credit of the Minister of Marine and Fisheries-because he has been getting so many hard truths to-night that it would not do him any harm to give him a word of commendation-that in our province he has appointed a gentleman to hold these investigations. In my judgment his principal trouble in Nova Scotia comes from the character of the man-I will not call him a gentleman-who has been carrying on these investigations. If he had appointed a gentleman of the qualifications of Mr. Knowles who acted in New Bruswick he would not have had these difficulties, he would not have had member after member standing up and giving him statements which must shame him until he does not know what to do. I do not think the minister would want to justify such conduct as he has been compelled to justify here to-day. He has not been compelled to justify such conduct in his own province. There' is not an instance brought up within the last two sessions in which we have been compelled to put my hon. friend in a position which he has been obliged, as he has been to-night, to defend conduct of this kind. I have referred to one case in which a man in my own constituency was removed from office. But the man had counsel; he was treated like a British sub-tish; every opportunity was given him to defend himself. The principal evidence against the man was that he was at the polling booth on election day. He was collector of customs, and his office was Mr. ITAZTjN.
not more than five or six rods from the polling booth-just across the street. He was on the street and was seen speaking to myself.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: That was suspicious.

Evidently it was regarded as worse than that-it was sufficient to remove him from office. But I want to say for Mr. Knowles, that he did not recommend the dismissal; he simply took the evidence and referred it to the department and the department made the dismissal. But in Nova Scotia, Mr. Duchemin seems to be the whole department, and not only the whole department but the whole Government. * When they want a man dismissed they simply hand him over to Mr. Duchemin, and he does the job. If he cannot succeed by a fair trial, why he changes the trial place to ten miles away-anyhow, certainly, Mr. Duchemin does the job. I am not going to take any further part in this discussion of dismissals, but I would like to say to the minister that if he wants to play the man, and if he wants the people to believe that he is playing the man-get rid of Duchemin.

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext:
I want to
say just a word in reply to the hon. member for Carleton (Mr. Carvell). There is very little to reply to in what has been submitted by the hon. member for Richmond and the hon. member for Guysborough.
Well, well.

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext:
I think the judgment of
the House will support me in that statement. The hon. member for Richmond is even louder in his exclamations than the Toronto Globe described me as being on an occasion when I spoke, certainly very moderately, the other evening. All we hear from the hon. member is a loud, round and echoing noise.
And sensible, too.

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext:
I do not know what the remark of my hon. friend from Temiscouata may mean; I ignore his statement. With regard to Mr. Duchemin, the hon. member for Carleton said he would call him a man, but not a gentleman. In the province of Nova Scotia, and especially in the eastern part of it where he is best known, among the members of the Bar and the people generally, Mr. Duchemin stands as high in respect of all classes as does the hon. mem ber for Carleton among any people in New Brunswick or elsewhere. When a member of Parliament rises in this House and, behind a man's back, makes an assertion of that kind that he is not a gentleman, it is a pretty small piece of business and shows better than any argument the character of

the member who makes it. We have heard of members of Parliament making statements across the floor of this house, and when given the opportunity to repeat them outside where the honourable laws of this Chamber do not interfere with the due appreciation of a statement of that kind, we have found them shirking the responsibility of their words. I need not refer to any particular hon. gentleman; the House is in possession of the facts in this regard. The hon. member for Richmond says that the witnesses were interested parties, and therefore their evidence should not be taken.
The minister says that.

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext:
The minister stated that
O'Brien was an interested witness. The member for Richmond said that O'Brien gave an affidavit that he was not a partisan. Did anybody ever hear of an investigation in any part of this Dominion where a man came up and admitted that he was a partisan? Did anyone ever hear of an investigation in which the man did not deny it and try to get round it in every way? In my own county, a man insulted me right on the street with regard to the elections, yet he pretended he was not a partisan. He attended a meeting, joined in it, cursed everybody almost on the other side of politics-yet he is not a partisan. In the name of common sense, it would be enlightening to the House to know what definition these gentlemen have of partisanship. A man goes to the poll -and stands outside and talks up his own side, tells the people to vote for a certain candidate. Do you suppose he is asking the people to vote Tory? What the law requires an office holder to do, if he wishes to vote, is to go to the poll, cast his vote and go home and mind his business. But in the counties of Guysborough, Richmond and Pictou-and I will not confine it to these counties-the whole political	machinery	of	the Grit	partywas in	the hands	of	people in	thereceipt of emoluments either from the provincial or Dominion Government. And that statement stands true to-day. The result is that when an investigation is ordered or a charge preferred against a man	in	office,	it	is a safe	bet,that if	he	was appointed to	office
under the late Government, Dominion or provincial, he is a partisan, and a safe bet also that he will deny it immediately the charge is preferred. Hon. gentlemen have raised a great howl with regard to dismissals, but I venture to say they have not won a single vote on the discussion of dismissals, because public opinion knows well the effect of evidence that has been brought to light in Guysborough county for example. It is realized that the men who were there holding office, held office on
condition that they worked for the hon. member for Guysborough and his party. That has been shown from evidence time and time again. The hon. member travels around with an employee of the Government, the employee of the Government solicits support from men whom he meets and the member for Guysborough is there. Yet according to the hon. member for Guysborough that man is not a partisan. The hon. member for Guysborough is personally a very honest and reputable man when he is not engaged in political conversations and arguments, then he loses all the fairness and honesty of which he has an appreciation in private conversation, and immediately discards the whole evidence except that which will help to substantiate his cause. We had evidence here that a man goes to a public meeting in Guysborough and speaks at it, and then proposes three cheers for the member and three cheers for the then Prime Minister, now the right hon. leader of the Opposition; and yet he is not a partisan. In the name of common sense will somebody say what a partisan is in the conception of hon. gentlemen opposite ? The country is entitled to know. But that is not all that took place in the county of Guysborough. A man comes up and gives his evidence under oath that such and such a man, we will say, promised him a pair of boots if he would vote for the hon. member for Guysborough, and the case results in the dismissal of the officer making the canvass. Immediately after, whether on the advice of the hon. member for Guysborough I will not assume the responsibility of saying, but in one case at least a charge of perjury is brought against the witness who testifies as to what he knows and was promised, namely this pair of boots for voting for the hon. member for Guysborough. The charge of perjury is brought in an attempt to intimidate witnesses, to look them up and put them in jail in order to keep them from testifying in investigations. That actually liap-pened in Guysborough. When the case was submitted to the jury, the jury very promptly acquitted the man of perjury, and it was established beyond peradven-ture that not only was he offered the boots, but that he went to the neighbour's house and got the boots and got a drink besides. It reminds me of the fellow in the prayer service who was promised a pair of boots if he would keep from saying ' amen.' He got so worked up, like the hon. member for Richmond this afternoon, that he said: ' Boots or no boots, I will say amen.'
Where is the wit in it?

I cannot find wit, humour and brains too for the honorable mem-

ber for Temiscouata. I might go on and point out a great many cases in which the evidence was overwhelmingly in favour of the reports that have been made by Mr. Duchemin. In this particular instance the hon. member for Richmond said that he preferred to believe the ex parte statement of Mr. O'Brien as against the report of a commissioner of Mr. Duchemin's standing and, without casting any serious reflections, let me say that the standing of Mr. Duchemin at' the bar of Nova Scotia is every bit as good as the standing of the hon. member for Richmond at the bar of Nova Scotia. That question is not debatable at all. I think the hon. member will agree in that himself and when, under the privilege of this House, he casts insinuations and slurs and denunciations and says that this man is unworthy of the respect of people, I will venture this remark that he would not dare say that to Mr. Duchemin outside of this House. You may search the records of Nova Scotia, but I do not think that you will find that Mr. Duchemin was ever haled before a Supreme Court and judgment given against him disfranchising him for seven years as has been alleged in the case of the hon. gentleman from Richmond. I do not think you will find Mr. Duchemin in that position. Yet we have the hon. member foT Richmond denouncing him in the strongest terms and taking the affidavit of a man who when notified that the court was to be held at a certain place does not appear to give evidence in his own behalf, but gets hold of the hon. member for Richmond, who is his father confessor in every particular with regard to politics and says: Here, I will give you my affidavit-and as far as we on this side of the House are concerned we do not know whether the affidavit was ever sworn to before a commissioner or not. We presume it was because the hon. member has read it in the House and we are bound to take his statement, but the fact remains that the House has to judge between a reputable man at the bar who has given his testimony which is on fide here as against an ex iparte statement of an interested party, Mr. O'Brien, who is, from the evidence submitted, at least a partisan in the estimation of this House.

I thought there might have been some doubt and some hesitancy on both sides of the House as to the real facts, commonsense and law on this question before the hon. member for Kings (Mr. Foster) spoke, but I knew when I saw him get on his feet that a Daniel had come to judgment and that the whole thing would be cleared up and that we would know all about it. I invite hon. gentlemen from both sides of the House to notice the striking searchlight that he has brought to Mr. FOSTER (Kings, N.S.)
bear on this question. You could pick up pins on the street, on the floor, anywhere from the light that emanated from this thing that he calls brain. When he talks about brain he reminds me of the little boy who was asked to make a picture - of a horse on a slate. He made the picture and brought it back to the teacher and wrote the word ' horse ' under it. Of course were it not for the word ' horse ' under the picture on the slate it would never have suggested to anybody that it was a horse. In the same way about the brains of my hon. friend, he must be telling us that it is brains or we would forget that it is the product of that most useful commodity. I invite the hon. member for Kings te devote himself to a night school or somewhere where they might give him some instruction as to brains and not be misleading himself into the idea that he is talking the product of brains when he might as well be talking about the shelling of lobsters or something else. He has an idea, wherever on earth he got an idea, that talking around, beating about the bush and never coming to the point, if he is capable of conceiving a point, is clever. Let him talk as much as possible, let him keep away from the subject, let him say nothing but take up the time and play the cuttlefish, that is the idea my friend from Kings has of playing the -smart man and answering an argument. The serious question before you, Mr. Chairman, is whether O'Brien was properly tried or not. I cannot hope to retain or hold the attention of the minister but I hope that possibly somebody in the country may take notice of this O'Brien case. For that reason I propose to inquire into it a little closely. The Minister of Marine is a minister of the Crown and I am not going to read a lecture to him or to any other minister, but I submit to this Parliament that the man who occupies that position of minister of the Crown represents the Crown to subjects in this country and that it is not a light matter, in dealing with the rights of the individual, for a minister of the Crown to act carelessly and ruthlessly and indifferently. I submit to the minister and to you that this election on the 21st of September, 1911, according to the present Prime Minister, was not a party victory. What did he say at the great civic reception which was given to him in the city of Ottawa? He spoke with his laurels fresh from victory and he thanked the hundreds of thousands of Liberals of Canada who had come to his rescue and to the rescue of the country. He said that this was not a party victory but a national victory. That is the position he took on that occasion, the Liberals were to rejoice with him as well as

the Conservatives on this national victory. A few weeks afterwards he was banquetted at Halifax. The Minister of Marine was present at the banquet. The Prime Minister repeated the sentiments he had expressed at Ottawa. I would think that the results of a national victory would be treated as a national question, in keeping with the conduct we would expect, from a man who had won a national victory. In view of that position I would draw the attention of the minister to the fact that the treatment of this man O'Brien has been simply scandalous if we are_ to believe the facts as pre* sented, and I submit that I must believe O'Brien's statement where there is nothing to the contrary. The Minister of Marine has been Attorney General for many years of the province of New Brunswick and he knows "the law. He knows that this Commissioner Duchemin derived his authority from and must act in accordance with the statute passed by this House, a statute passed not by the late Government but by the present Government. It is well-known that in any court of justice the court does not become seized of jurisdiction over an individual until it is proven to the court that the notice was properly served. The first thing that the minister should look for when he gets a report from a commissioner is to see if the commissioner became seized of jurisdiction and if the notice was served. The last chapter of this statute says:
No report shall be made against any person, until reasonable notice shall have been given to him of the charge of misconduct alleged against him and he shall have been allowed! full opportunity to be heard in person or by counsel.	I
Where is the proof that O'Brien was served with notice? There is not any. Where is the proof that the charge was served upon him? There is not any, and we have the oath of Mr. O'Brien that not only was he not served but he was served at a false date and put upon a false scent. He was served with notice after the inquiry, and for a day, not the day on which the investigation was to be held at all. He received the notice two days after the investigation was held.

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext:
Where is the proof of
that?

The notice itself is here. If my friend from Kings can put this and that together, if he is capable of adding two and two together, and I take .it for granted that he is, we have the notice of Mr. Duchemin with his signature attached to it, naming a day on which the investigation was to take place at Port Malcolm. We have the report of Mr. Duchemin over his own signature saying that he held the investigation on a different day altogether and in a different place.
Surely it is clear even to the intellect of my hon. friend that there was no notice at all for the day on which the investigation was held, and no notice for the place in which it was held. That being the case, I think my hon. friend, while be would possibly have dismissed this man in any case, in view of the statute which he passed himself and which is binding on himself and his officials, will see that it is up to him to put this man O'Brien back in the lighthouse and dismiss the man who was put falsely in that position. Let him begin this thing over again for the credit of the King whom he represents, for the credit of the department over which he presides, for the credit of the people of this country and of the investigations which are being held under the statute. Begin over again and i'f Mr. O'Brien is found to deserve dismissal after having been properly dealt with and the law complied with, dismiss him. Do not let us have this disgrace upon the King. Do not let us have a commissioner of the King throwing men and their children on the street without giving the slightest semblance of defence. I ask_ the Prime Minister, or any other lawyer, if this had been a proceeding in which Mr. Duchemin was a court, and he had given a decision, as he gave here, which would infringe upon the liberties of this man O'Brien, and the man had been arrested and put in jail by virtue of this trial, what would have happened if habeas corpus or certiorari proceedings had been taken? The moment it was shown that there had been no service, away would go the decision, and the incarceration would cease, and there would be an action in the civil courts for false imprisonment. The Minister of Marine and Fisheries, the Minister of Justice, and everyone concerned in this matter are sheltering themselves behind a proceeding taken in the name of the King and under the King's commission, and in every step the commissioner has falsified the authority and power given to him to deal with the matter. I submit that there is no defence for the action of the commissioner. If the facts, as set forth by Mr. Duchemin himself in his report are correct, there is nothing left, if we are to be decent and respectable and are to maintain the dignity of this Government and of this Parliament, but to begin de novo, and have the matter sifted to the bottom. If Mr. O'Brien is guilty of partisanship let him be dismissed, but when the name of the King is introduced into the proceedings, let us see that the subject gets fair-play and justice, and let us have no mock investigations.

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext:
I would like to say a word or two with regard to what my hon. friend from North Cape Breton (Mr. McKenzie) has said in reference to myself. He referred in a slighting manner

to my lack of brains. As a matter of fact, I never laid very great stress upon the brains I may possess, and I have never endeavoured to advertise the claim that I had abnormal qualifications in that respect. But this House has been treated on more than one occasion to what the hon. member for North Cape Breton and Victoria would be pleased to call the product of the brains in that wonderful dome of thought of his, and when a remark that does not seem to suit him is addressed to him across the floor of this House by any hon. gentleman on this side, he comes across the floor and begs that the remark be not placed on ' Hansard' in order that the people may not know of it.
I rise to a question of privilege.
Take your medicine.

I am quite willing to
take anything that is coming to me properly; I do not make statements behind covers. I ask my hon. friend to name the occasion when I. asked for any favours in matters of that kind, and the party from whom I asked them.

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: I am delighted to respond to the hon. gentleman's request. On the occasion of a debate in this House between the hon. member for North Cape Breton and Victoria (Mr. McKenzie) and the hon. member for Cumberland (Mr. Rhodes), my hon. friend (Mr. McKenzie) asked by what kind of reckoning the hon. member for Cumberland with the brains he had, had arrived at the conclusion he was submitting to the House. The hon. member for Cumberland replied and used words I have quoted with regard to the hon. gentleman's polished dome of thought, and forthwith my hon. friend begged the hon. member for Cumberland not to have the remark inserted in ' Hansard.

I did nothing of the kind. I notice that the hon. member for Cumberland is not here; I should be very glad to leave him to tell the House what took place. I can assure my hon. friend that he would not be backed up by the hon. member for Cumberland in the reflections he is trying to make. The occasion referred to when there was a somewhat heated discussion in which the hon. member for Cumberland and the hon. member for Shelburne and Queens (Mr. McCurdy) and myself took part. The hon. member for Cumberland is a friend of mine, and I did not think it was creditable to either of us that the remarks should appear, and we quietly agreed that they should not appear on the record. That is all there was to it. My hon. friend's statement shows the measure of the man.
Mr. FOOTER (Kings, NjS.)

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: I am afraid the discussion is drifting on to personal matters.

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: I am perfectly willing to come back to the item, but I take notice that the hon. member does not deny what I said. I am perfectly willing to leave it to the hon. member for Cumberland or to the hon. member for Shelburne and Queens who will substantiate what I have said.

Let us hear about
Duchemin.

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: If my hon. friend would like to hear from Mr. Duchemin, we might arrange a meeting with my hon. friend. My hon. friend from North Cape Breton accused me of wandering around the subject, and yet for ten minutes he talked of a national victory in the last election. I would like to know what that has to do with the item under discussion. He went round that point for four or five minutes and finally came to the question of the statute. I have already pointed out that on every occasion when the hon. gentleman addresses this House, he proceeds to divulge the little he learned when he was a county court judge in the province of Nova Scotia. He must always rise and interpret what is plain to the ordinary layman, and what are fundamental principles of law. My hon. friend has a wonderful capacity. When he was upon the bench he was noted for his fairness, for the consideration he gave to lawyers and clients on both sides, but in the eastern part of the province of Nova Scotia it was almost impossible to get a case for a Conservative lawyer when the hon. gentleman was upon the bench. Perhaps the hon. member will deny that.
Absolutely.

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: That is the feeling that prevails in the eastern part of the province of Nova Scotia with regard to the hon. gentleman, and more than one lawyer could substantiate what I have said. He assumes an attitude of fairness in this House, but when he gets where the people cannot see him, he can say the meanest and most despicable things.
Order, order.

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: I am pleased to withdraw the remark.

Let him chew his
potatoes.

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: With regard to chewing potatoes, the hon. member for Carleton (Mr. Carvell) and the hon. member for North Cape Breton can chew, not only potatoes, but buckwheat.
What about the estimates?

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: Hon. gentleman have not been so very anxious about getting the estimates through when they have spent three or four hours this afternoon in discussing dismissals. But when an hon. member on this side of the House tries to say something which is not what they want to hear, they become very eager to have the estimates go through. I am perfectly willing to stay here all summer if necessary.

The hon. gentleman
has nothing else to do, but some of us have.

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext:
More evidence of the
smartness of my hon. friend.
Oh, oh.

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: He has something to do; he has to go down home and pay that two hundred dollar bill which his partner incurred for rum at the last election., I have no doubt it will take him some little time to earn money enough to pay the election bills that he ran last time. If the hon. gentleman wants to prolong-

That was paid for
long ago.

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: Of course, but he denied it the other day.

No, he says that it is
paid for.

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext:
No, he does not deny it
and it worries him a little. He is a man of the style of Dr. Rhindress and Mr. N.
A.	McMillan, both pure-minded men, men who are not partisans'! He has no partisans in hiis riding, every person is perfectly righteous and fair-minded and I suppose that all belong to the same church as he does.

I desire to make an observation or two inasmuch as the hon. member for Kings said something that was probably intended to have reference to myself. The hon. gentleman speaks of the high standing of Mr. Duchemin at the Bar of Nova Scotia. As the hon. gentleman is not a member of the professional Bar, I presume he had reference to the other bar, and before his judgment in that regard I bow without the slightest hesitation.

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I rise to
a question of privilege. The hon. gentleman insinuates something with reference to my judgment and experience concerning a bar other than the professional Bar. Of course, I know exactly what he is driving at, and I will tell him that, in regard to any other bar other than the legal Bar, I am not in the habit of frequenting places of that sort, and therefore, the hon. gentleman is absolutely wrong. When he insinuates anything with regard to a bar, not meaning the legal Bar, I wish to tell
him that I have no interest in, and am not in the habit of frequenting a bar, saloon, or anything of that sort.

If any misunderstanding
has arisen the hon. gentleman must concede that he is entirely to blame for it, because he 'is not a member of the professional Bar and therefore not in a position to pass judgment upon the standing of a gentleman occupying a position in tihat very distinguished and honourable profession. The hon. gentleman endeavoured to make some comparison between Mr. Duchemin and myself as regards our relative standing at the professional Bar. I am not like the hon. member for Kings who does not appear to suffer from any undue depreciation of his own talents. Therefore, I hesitate before expressing any opinion as to the standing I enjoy in the profession in the province of Nova Scotia. Suffice it to say that I am well content with the success that has come to me in the practice of my profession in Nova Scotia, and I hope that the hon. member for Kings will have similar satisfaction when he is as old as I am.
There is one other matter that I wish to refer to, and it is a personal reflection which the hon. member for Kings made I am not like the hon. member for Kings referred to the fact that some person was disqualified in Nova Scotia and deprived of the right of voting. If the hon. gentleman referred to me I think it is only right to myself and to hon. members that I should place the facts before the committee. Away back in 1894, nearly twenty years, ago, the Conservative party in my county was particularly active, as it has always been within my recollection. I was then a young man just starting out to enjoy the advantages of my profession. As I was attached to the Liberal party, the Conservatives in the county did me the honour of paying some attention to me. They thought I was a young man that they ought to watch, and if there was any way by which my character could be besmirched so that I would become less useful to the Liberal party, they were willing to resort to any means to bring that about. As base and diabolical a conspiracy as was ever conceived in the corrupted and perverted mind of man was hatched by the Conservative party to that end. The provincial elections took place in 1894, and after the elections were over prosecutions were instituted against several prominent Liberals in the county for violations of the election law, and I was singled out for their attention. A prosecution was instituted against me, different forms of corrupt acts were charged, but when the matter came to a trial every charge was dismissed by the judge. There was one

case, however, in which another species oi infraction of the law was involved. There is a canal in iny county upon which there are employed several men. In 1874 the provincial legislature passed a law which disfranchised all employees of the Department of Railways and Canals and prevented them from voting in provincial elections. In the local election of 1894 I was the agent for the Liberal candidate at the poll when one of these men presented himself and asked for a ballot. I pointed out that employees of the Department of Railways were not entitled to vote in provincial elections and that, inasmuch as canals was a branch of the Department of Railways, employees on these canals were not entitled to vote. The argument I addressed to the presiding officer resulted in the employee of the canal refusing to take the ballot and he did not vote. That matter came up in the court. The judge held that, inasmuch as at the time the provincial statute was passed in 1874 there was no subdepartment of canals, the statute could not have applied to the men employed upon this canal and that I had committed a technical offense in having addressed an argument to the presiding officer which resulted in the employee not taking the ballot and not exercising his franchise, and in that respect I had been guilty of intimidation. That was in 1894. nearly twenty years ago. If the hon. member for Kings were a member of the profession, of which he speaks and of which he professes to be a judge, he would have known that there is a statute of limitations which ought to prevent him making any reference to a matter that occurred so long ago. But in 1895 the Legislature of Nova Scotia elected me to a responsible position in that body. I was elected to the responsible position of clerk assistant of the Legislature of Nova Scotia by the unanimous vote of both parties. One would think that if the offence that I am alleged to have committed was any reflection upon my character or standing as a man and a citizen, the Conservative "Opposition in the Legislature would have protested against my appointment. But, almost immediately after the trial, with all ihe facts known to both political parties, they elected me to the responsible position of assistant clerk of the legislature, and in that election I received the support of every Conservative in the House. I was re-appointed in 1898, re-appointed again in 1901, and in 1903 I was elected to the position of chief clerk of the legislature, a .responsible and dignified position, -which I enjoyed up to the time I resigned for the purpose of becoming a candidate for the House of Mr. KYTE.
Commons in the county of Richmond, on which occasion I was elected.
Needless to say, I offered myself to the electors of the county of Richmond in the election of 1911, and I was re-elected.
In order further to show to the House the manner in which this particular matter referred to by the hon. member for Kings, (Mr. Foster)-, has been regarded in the county of Richmond, I shall refer to one more circumstance. There was a newspaper owned by the Conservative party, published in my town in 1897. On one occasion, a Conservative enthusiast, who had about the same breadth of view that the hon. member for Kings possesses, thought the time was opportune to make a charge against my character in respect of that election. As soon as the charge was made, I notified the owners of the paper that, unless they withdrew the charge and apologized to me, an action would be brought against them for damages. This is the result. In a copy of that paper dated July 7, 1897, there is the following editorial reference.

What- is the name of
the paper?

The Bras d'Or Gazette,
now the Sydney Post. It is headed:
We would do justice to Mr. Kyte
The article is as follows:
In the December, February and May issues of the Bras d'Or Gazette, there appeared several articles that reflected on Mr. G. W. Kyte, barrister, of this town, as regards his character boibh as a professional man, as well as a private citizen. That these unprovoked and unjustifiable attacks, should have been made upon Mr. Kyte, we deeply regret. We know him to be an upright, honourable and progressive citizen, and in the practice of Iris profession, he has earned for himself a reputation for honesty and industry that any young man would do well to emulate. In making this apology, we do so in order to do justice to this gentleman, as well as to assure the public that we deprecate the spirit and tone of the articles above referred to; and -we desire to give the further assurance that these articles are not attributable in any manner to those whose money and enterprise started this paper.
That was the apology made to me in respect to the same insinuations on January 7, 1897. From that hour to this, not a single suggestion has ever been made by any Conservative, be he prominent or not in the county of Richmond, or in the province of Nova Scotia, so far as I am aware, having reference to the particular matter to which my hon. friend from Kings refers. If he wants to dive into the private history of men connected with infractions of the election law, I would

ask him to look around him, and, usually occupying a seat not far removed from the hon. member for Kings, he can find a member of the Conservative party of the province of Ontario, who not only committed a criminal act, in respect of the election law, but was convicted of it and for which he served a sentence. I know it is not regarded as being to his discredit, because I understand at this moment he is designated by his leader for high judicial honours. I trust the committee will pardon me for having made this reference to a personal matter.
Make him withdraw.
Mr. Chairman,-

Give the hon. member
for Kings a chance to apologize.

Mr. Chairman, I am very reluctant to prolong this debate. I am deeply devoted to my constituents, and I am anxious to get home. Sometimes I think that the other side stands in terror of their constituents, and resort to these tactics in order to delay the time when they have to meet them, and that they are deliberately occupying the time of the House in order to postpone the time when they will have to go back to their constituents and give an account of the most remarkable conduct of which they have been guilty during this session of parliament.
It is not agreeable to me to go into the personal conduct of members of this House. I must admit that I hardly approved of the reference which the hon. member for Kings made to the hon. member for North Cape Breton (Mr. McKenzie), for I know how sensitive the hon. member for North Cape Breton is in reference to his personal appearance. I know that the hon. gentleman at election time, when he wants to represent himself to his constituents, does not use a photograph of recent times, but brings into commission an old photograph taken "when he wore the locks of an Absalom. I thought under the circumstances the hon. gentleman's remarks were a trifle unkind.
Where would my hon. friend go for a good-looking picture?

I hope my hon. friend did not think I intended to state that the picture of himself which appeared was a good-looking one. If the House has got that impression, I wish to set hon. members right in that regard.
The hon. member for Richmond (Mr. Kyte) referred to a matter in his own history, where the courts of his native province decreed him guilty of a certain offence. He seemed to take it amiss that the hon. member for Kings should have
brought this matter up after twenty years. He reminded the hon. member for Kings that the offence of which he was guilty at that time was beyond the statutes, and therefore that technically he should not be blamed. Perhaps we might be inclined to look upon it in that way if the hon. gentleman showed any indication of having repented of the sins of his former days. It seems to me, from the speech which the hon. gentleman has made this evening, that he does not appreciate the enormity of his offence. It is perhaps only right that this House should be advised as to the facts in this particular case. I would not have brought this matter up except that the hon. member himself saw fit to bring these facts before the House, and to make it appear that his record in the past was absolutely clean and straight, and that he was in a perfectly suitable position to criticise such gentlemen as Mr. Duche-min. Inasmuch as he has done this, perhaps I may read certain extracts from the decision of the trial judge on that occasion. The trial judge, who handed out that decision, was one who has a reputation in the province of Nova Scotia for very great leniency. A few weeks ago, the hon. member (Mr. Kyte), in diseusssing the case of one of his constituents who had been convicted of an offence, dwelt on the fact that the judge, who had convicted him was one who was particularly charitable in his judgments, who was very lenient, and who probably had a reputation for greater leniency than any other judge of the province of Nova Scotia. The fact is that it was the same 'judge that found the hon. gentleman guilty. There were four distinct charges against the hon. gentleman on this occasion-three of having deliberately bought the electors of Richmond county, and one of having intimidated an elector of that county. In three cases there did not appear to be any corroboration. Witnesses swore positively that the hon. gentleman had given them money for their votes. Unfortunately for the prosecution, in each case there was only one witness and this gvidence was not corroborated in any one of these cases. The hon. gentleman'went on the stand and gave his denial in each case, and Mr. Justice Graham, being a very lenient and moderate judge, acquitted the hon. gentleman on that evidence. But, in respect of the charge of intimidation, the judge, in his ruling, after going elaborately into the facts, used these words:
I cannot believe that the defendant has a bona fide belief that perjury would be committed if the man took the' oath. It seems to me no argument can be made about the matter.
The defendant is not only a barrister but says he studied three years in a college, and
he could not help knowing thait his contention which I have already quoted had not even

the appearence of an argument. I cannot give him credit for good faith the moment he states what his contention was.
Now this gentleman to whom the very lenient judge in the province of Nova Scotia could not attribute good faith is the hon. gentleman who comes into tnis .House to-night and upon his bare statement wishes us to condemn a very reputable member of the Bar of Nova Scotia The hon. gentleman contends that he has been acquitted of these crimes because the legislature of Nova Scotia appointed him to an important position. I would point out to the House and to the non. member that the reason for giving up this office, which I understand is not a very important or very remunerative one, was on account of the services he had rendered to his party by just such acts as that for which his lordship Justice Graham had taken away his right to vote. Eor five years in Nova Scotia, the hon. member for Bichmond did not -enjoy the privileges of a British citizen.
That is untrue.
