speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
I understand that
the item under discussion is, lighthouses, salaries and allowances of lightkeepers. I am afraid that both sides have wandered from the subject of discussion. It is hard for me to restrain hon. members from wandering when a discussion has been opened. But, I hope that hon. members will agree that the discussion has continued long enough.
The hon. member for Annapolis does not seem to have any terminal facilities at all.

The hon. member for Cape Breton North has a very polished terminal. In the few further remarks I have to make, I will apply myself absolutely to the question under discussion. I understand that the conduct of Mr. Du-chemin as commissioner is the matter under discussion by the committee. I wish to show the kind of commissioner Mr. Du-chemin is, and, for that purpose, to read a few words from the report he has made which bears upon what I said a few minutes ago:
I now want to refer ;to an experience that I had with Mr. G. W. Kyte, the opposition member for Richmond county. On the 26th of September, I took two investigations at) St. Peters; the accused parties were two postmasters, Chas. J. Lafford, Grand Greve, and Ewan P. McLeod, Louis Cove Road. Mr. Kyte presented himself with the accused the morning of the hearing, and stated that he was going to act as counsel for them. I advised him that in view of the fact that there was: no counsel on the other side, I would manage the investigation without the assistance of counsel. He then declared: 'Oh, but you must admit counsel.' To which I replied as before-That I would not admit counsel, but would conduct the investigation without any such asnistance. Mr. Kyte then became ex-J tremely offensive, and turbulent, interrupting! the investigation at different stages. I was obliged to tell him that unless he would maintain order, he would have to leave. He replied that I was not able to put him out, &c., &c. When he became extremely objectionable, I asked Mr. Lafford, the accused, if he was responsible for Mr. Kyte's presence at the investigation, and he replied that he was not. I accordingly went on with the investigation, and ignored Mr. Kyte.
Considering the fact that Dr. Bissett, a very reputable gentleman, a member of the local legislature and of the party to which my hon. friend belongs, spoke in this way; and the fact that the hon. member for Cape Breton North, when I appealed to him some weeks ago for an opinion on the character of Mr. Duchemin, was not prepared to state that he was in any way
biased or unfair, this committee must realize that the charges which have been made here to-night in a violent and irresponsible manner are very unsubstantial indeed. In 1896, when the Liberal Government sent a commissioner to the part of Nova Scotia in which I live to investigate these charges, it was a very exceptional matter when that commissioner found an accused person innocent, hut I am aware that Mr. Duchemin on very many occasions has found Liberal office holders who were accused of offensive conduct not guilty and they have been allowed to retain their positions by reason of his decision. I think that, considering these facts, it ill becomes gentlemen who do not occupy positions at the Bar comparable at all with that of Mr. Duchemin to come here, twelve hundred miles away from Mr. Duchemin, and make these absolutely groundless charges and aspersions against his character.

There is not much that requires an answer from me in the speech of the hon. member for Annapolis (Mr. Davidson), but I would say to him that when his own political friends pay him as high a compliment as my political opponents paid me in the apology which I have ijust read from their own newspaper, he may then consider himself worthy to associate with an assembly of gentlemen. With , regard to the statement made in respect to Dr. Bissett, it happens that I am beginning to know my hon. friend, so I am usually prepared for him. I have here an affidavit from Dr. Bissett in which he refers to the circumstances dealt with in the statement of Mr. Duchemin. That affidavit is as follows:
I,	Charles P. Bissett, of St. Peter's in the county of Richmond, medical doctor, do solemnly declare that I was not present at the investigation held by H. P. Duchemin, commissioner into charges of political partizan-ship against Ewan McLeod, postmaster at Lewis Cove Road, in the county of Richmond, held at St. Peter's in the month of September last, except for a few moments; nor was I present at the investigation of the charges against Charles J. Lafford, postmaster at Grand Greve, before Mr. Duchemin at the same place and on the same date, except for a short time.
I entered the room where the investigations were being held, shortly before they were closed, but the evidence had practically been all taken. I stated to Mr. Duchemin .that so far as I saw I was satisfied with the fairness with which he conducted the investigation. At the time I made this statement to Mr. Duchemin I was not aware that at the beginning of the investigation Mr. G. W. Kyte, M.P., had asked Mr. Duchemin for the privilege of representing Mr. McLeod at the investigation. I had not been informed of the insolent and offensive language used by Mr. Duchemin towards Mr. Kyte and his refusal



to permit Mr. Kyte to examine the witnesses and his threat to remove Mr. Kyte from the room.
I learned these facte afterwards, and the next day I met Mr. Duchemin and I told him wlhait 1 thought of his conduct. 1 make this solemn declaration conscientiously believing the same ho be true and knowing it to he of the same effect as if taken under oath and by virtue of the Canada Evidence Act.
C. P. Bissett,
Nova Scotia.
Taken and declared at St. Peters in the county of Richmond, N.S., this 14th day of December, A.D. 1912. Before me.
Angus J. iMaoCuish,

It goes to show how necessary it is to be fortified for the- hon. member for Annapolis who reads the reckless statement placed in his hand by Mr. Duchemin. This proves how reckless a character Mr. Duchemin is and I think there has been evidence adduced to-day to show how unreliable is any ex parte statement from that quarter. The hon. member for Annapolis in December and again about a month ago in this House, stated over and over that Mr. Duchemin never refused counsel at his investigations.

Excuse me, I never
made any such' statement.
The hon. gentleman's statements are on record.

I desire to state in the most emphatic way that the hon. gentleman is absolutely in error.
Mr._CHAIRMAN: The hon. member must accept the statement.
The hon. member for Cumberland made reference to the same thing.
I ask a ruling.

If the hon. member states
that he did not say so, I accept his statement, and refer hon. gentlemen to the report of the debates.
I am not satisfied with that retraction. I did not make any such statement, and I ask the hon. gentleman to take it back unequivocally.
I accept the denial and refer hon. members to the report of debates.
That is absolutely satisfactory.

Here is a statement of Mr. Duchemin in which in at least two instances he admits he did not permit counsel. He says inasmuch as the prosecution had no counsel, he would not permit me to represent the accused. Therefore, all the furore raised about the Mr. KYTE.
fairness of Mr. Duchemin and his conforming to the provisions of the Act falls to the ground and we have from his own mouth, as re-echoed by the hon. member for Annapolis, that the charges are true, that he has violated the Inquiries Act and has not permitted counsel to be heard. There is one statement which I have to make further, that as that the (hon. member for Annapolis seems to have special interest in the county of Richmond and to represent to this House certain matters relating to that county. speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: Go on, if you want to sit all night, go on.

I would like to bring up the dismissal of the port physician at Yarmouth. This is a matter which will reflect no credit on the minister. The dismissal of Dr. 0. A. Webster will certainly not add lustre to the minister, but place him before the committee and the people

in a most unenviable position. I put two questions on the Older Paper some little time ago in reference to this dismissal.
Mr. Webster had been acting in the position of port physician for a number of years to the entire satisfaction of the department, and of the mariners who were confined in the marine hospital in Yarmouth, and gave every satisfaction to all parties concerned. He was going away to take a post graduate course in London. Dr. Webster wrote to the Minister of Marine, and Fisheries on the 22nd of January and asked him for three months' leave of absence to go to London, in order to take a post graduate course. I have before me a letter from the Department of Marine and Fisheries, dated January 30, 1912, as follows:
30th January, 1912.
Sir,-I have to acknowledge receipt of your letter of the 22nd instant, applying for three months' leave of absence in order to attend a post-graduate course in England.
In reply, I have to inform you that the desired leave has been granted.
Please report when you return to duty.
I am, Sir, your obedient servant,
(Sgd.) C. Stanton, Assistant Deputy Minister. Dr. C. A. Webster,
Medical Superintendent Marine Hospital, Yarmouth, N.S.
On receipt of this document, Dr. Webster proceeded to London to take his post graduate course, taking it for granted that when the Minister of Marine and Fisheries or the officials of his department gave him leave of absence for three months he could depend upon their word. But what do we find? On March 9 a letter was sent to Dr. Webster which he did not receive until sometime after his arrival in London, and you will note that March 9 was only ten days after the Department of Marine and Fisheries had given him leave of absence. Mr. Stanton, the assistant deputy minister, wrote to Dr. Webster at Yarmouth this letter:
Sir, I have to inform you that as it is your intention to be absent from Yarmouth for some time.
And I wish to draw attention to the way that letter is worded.
As it is your intention to he absent from Yarmouth for somje time, the department has decided to discontinue your services as Port Physician at that port to attend to sick seamen entitled to relief undeT the provisions of the Canada Shipping Act, and to appoint in your room and stead Dr. S. W. Williamson. The Collector of Customs at Yarmouth has been so advised, and directed to send all sick seamen to Dr. Williamson entitled to the relief above mentioned.
I am, Sir,
Your obedient servant,
(iSgd.) C. Stanton.
Dr. C. A. Webster,
Yarmouth, N.S.,
341}
I asked some questions in the House on February 24, which were answered as follows:
Monday, February, 21, 1913.
Mr. Law:-
No. 14.
1.	Why was Dr. C. A. Webster dismissed from the position of Port Physician at Yarmouth, N.S.?
2.	Where any requests made for his dismissal? If so, by whom?
3.	If any requests were made, were they verbal or in wrting?
4.	If any charges were made against Dr. Webster, were said charges investigated? If not why not?
Mr. Hazen:-
1.	The services of Dr. Webster were discontinued in the interest of the public service.
2.	Yes, by persons enjoying the confidence of the minister.
3.	Verbal.
4.	The facts were sufficiently established not to warrant the expense of an investigation.
I criticize the action of the minister in connection with the discharge of Dr. Webster as one of the meanest and most contemptible acts that was ever performed by any minister occupying a seat in this House. Dr. Webster went away with the distinct understanding, with a letter from the Department of Marine, giving him three months' leave of absence; but ten days after he left to go to London the department coolly dismissed him and the minister cannot say he had nothing to do with it because on the 9th of February, only eighteen days' after Dr. Webster had asked for leave of absence, and only ten days after he had been granted leave this letter was sent to Mr. Knowles E. Crosby:
February 9, 1912. My Dear Sir,-	-
With reference to the matter of appointing a Port Physician at Yarmouth, will yon please forward to me a recommendation for this position, such recommendation to be signed by yourself and three members of the committee.
Your early attention to this matter will oblige.
Yours very truly,
(Sgd.) J. D. Hazen. Knowles E. Crosby, K.C.
Hebron, N.S.
In the documents which were presented to the House in answer to the motion which I made, there is not one single word of complaint against Dr. Webster. In fact I am confident that no word of complaint could be made against him. He is one of the most successful and most respected physicians in the town of Yarmouth, a man who is absolutely non-partisan. In order to prove that assertion I will state that during the last summer a gentleman who has been doing business in the near vicinity of Dr. Webster's office asked me whether Dr. Webster was a Liberal or a Conservative. I do not think a man could have any better

1080D
recommendation as to his non-partisan feelings than this statement. I understand, of course, that the gentleman who now occupies the position was given it on account of having run in the election in Yarmouth in 1908. Of course he was defeated, and I suppose that the Minister of Marine and Fisheries felt very kindly towards him for allowing himself to be made a sacrifice for the party and desired to give him some important position, for this position is worth $400 per year. I wish to refer to a letter which Mr. Crosby sent to the Minister of Marine and Fisheries:
Hebron, N.S., February 13th, 1912. Hon J. D. Hazen, K.C., M.P.,
Minister of Marine and Fisheries.
Ottawa.
Dear Sir.-
X have the honour to acknowledge the receipt of your favour of the 9th inst regarding the appointment of Port Physician at Yarmouth, and that I forward you *at once a recommendation for this office.
In compliance with your request and with the wish of the conservative party in this county, I beg to place before you the name of S. W. Williamson, M.D., who will fill the duties of that office to Itihe entire satisfaction of your department.
I am, Sir,
Your obedient servant,
(Sgd.) Knowles E. Crosby.
But there seems to have been some little hitch in connection with the matter. The Minister of Marine and Fisheries did not seem to be inclined to take the word of Knowles E. Crosby, and he was asked to send another letter signed by the whole patronage committee in the town of Yarmouth. That letter is dated February 26th, 1912:
Hebron, N.,S., Feb. 26, 1912. Hon. J. D. Hazen, K.C., M.P.,
Minister of Marine and Fisheries,
Ottawa.
Dear Sir,-Owing to the fact that my request that S. W. Williamson, M.D., receive the appointment to the position of port physician for Yarmouth, went forward without the signatures of my advisory committee, through error, several days since, and as we here are very anxious that this appointment should be made at once, I am inclosing herewith another request, signed by said committee.
I trust you will be able to accede to our request and fill this apointment as soon as possible.
I am, yours most respectfully,
(Sgd.) Knowles E. Crosby,
Howard W. Corning, M.L.A., Robert Binguy,
R. S. Bakins.
I just wish to say that when Dr. Webster left Yarmouth for London, he recommended Dr. Perrin for the position, a gentleman respected in the town of Yarmouth who occupies a high position in his profession, and who has been a strong tory all his life. I do not think he was ever guilty of giving a liberal vote. However, he is none Mr. LAW.
the worse for that; I respect him for it. Dr. Perrin was appointed, and if rumours are true, and I think I am not far astray, a couple of conservative doctors met in some office in the Department of Marine and Fisheries in Ottawa, and almost came to blows. However, Dr. Williamson was _ a lucky man to get the plunder. I desire to say again that the position in which the Minister of Marine and Fisheries has placed himself before the House and the country in connection with this matter is a very poor one. When an hon. gentleman occupying the position that he does gives his word to an official of his department that he is entitled to three months' leave of absence, and in an underhand way appoints another man to the position within ten days of leave of absence being granted, the hon. minister is entitled in my .mind to the censure of this committee and of the House. Dr. Webster was a valuable man in the position which he occupied, and if there ever was a man who "could be said to be non-partisan, he is that man. I desire to place upon record my entire disapproval of the whole proceeding. If Dr. Webster had been a partisan and had attended political meetings, if he had ever spoken at a political meeting, or had acted as agent at any ipolling place for any Liberal candidate, even then I would have expected that he would be granted an investigation. I have no regard for the man who, without any provocation whatever, endeavours to rob another man of the position, which he has filled to the satisfaction of the department and of the public. I say it is a mean and contemptible action.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
My hon. friend says that
this does not meet with his approval. I am afraid it would be rather difficult to say or do anything on this side of the House that would not meet with his disapproval. I am not at all astonished at the violent and extraordinary language which the hon. gentleman has used. Let me point out the facts in regard to this matter. I think Dr. Webster is the last man in the world who has any right to find fault because he has been removed from office. My hon. friend speaks of the contempt he has for the man who seeks to deprive another man of his position. Let us see whether he will lhave the same contempt for" the man who took office from another man who had been removed without the slightest justification. What are the facts? The facts are that Dr. Perrin was appointed port physician in 1879. The appointment is not a permanent one, it is not made by Order in Council, it is of a temporary character, and is made by departmental letter. On the 13th of December, 1896, seventeen years after Dr. Perrin had been appointed, and shortly after the elcetions of 1896 when the liberal

party came into power, Dr. Perrin wrote to the department stating that he had heard he was to be removed from office and asking to be given a fair hearing. On the 22nd of January, 1897, not more than three weeks afterwards, the then minister in a letter to Mr. Flint, the member for Yarmouth, stated that he deemed it advisable in the public interest to dispense with the office of port physician at Yarmouth, and asked for the name of a suitable, doctor to attend sick seamen when required. He dismissed the port physician and got the name of another doctor to attend to sick seamen when required, the other physician to be paid for the work he did. That was a very easy way of getting rid of Dr. Perrin, against whom no charge was made, and of appointing Dr. Webster to the position. That is how it was done. They did not dismiss Dr. Perrin. They said they did not need his services, and they dispensed with his services and appointed Dr. Charles A. Webster to do exactly the same work. Not a single charge of partisanship or of anything else is on record against Dr. Perrin. He was advised in January, 1897, that his services were no longer required.
. The collector of customs was instructed to employ Dr. Webster, and in about a year and a half, in November, 1899, the department which had said there was no need for a port physician, appointed by departmental letter Dr. Webster at a salary of $260 and on the 1st of July, 1898, they increased that amount to $400. When my hon. friend has such a contempt for the man who will take another's position, what does he think of Dr. Webster taking that position away from Dr. Perrin, when there was not a single charge against Dr. Perrin, and when the department had to resort to the subterfuge of pretending that they were going to abolish the office. These are the facts. Dr. Webster has no ground of complaint. The appointment is not permanent, it is not made by Order in Council, and in the circumstances the Government were justified in making the appointment of Dr. Williamson.

What has the hon. minister to
say as to the granting of leave of absence to Dr. Webster.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: What has that got to do with it? What difference would it have made if leave of absence had not been granted. It does not affect the merits of the case one way or the other. If hon. members have a contempt for Dr. Williamson, what do they think of the man who took the position in the circumstances under which Dr. Webster took it from Dr. Perrin in 1897?		!
The two cases are not anala-gous. Dr. Perrin is a strong conservative and I respect him for it.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
And so you got rid of
him.

I had nothing to do with it. Dr. Perrin was a strong partisan, a strong worker for his party while he held that office, and when the change of government took place he deserved to be dismissed for his connection with the elections that had just taken place. Dr. Perrin was not disappointed in that connection. On the other hand, I do not believe that Dr. Webster ever attended a political meeting in his life, and I doubt whether nine-tenths of the people of Yarmouth know which side of politics Dr. Webster is on. The minister may shirk the'proposition as much as he likes, but when he pledges the word of his department that he should have three months' leave of absence, and, within ten days, writes to the tory patronage committee asking them to name his successor- if he can defend an action like that, then any criminal can defend his action if he breaks into a man's henyard and steals hia. bans.
Agencies, rents and contingencies, $125,000.
There is an increase.

speechtext:

We have agencies at Halifax, St. John, Prince Edward Island, Quebec, Montreal, Parry Sound, Victoria, British Columbia, and Prince Rupert and sub-agencies at Sydney and Pictou. I would like to say a word with reference to ice-breaking in the harbour of Sydney. I understand from parties there, who are interested in having

that harbour opened up early in the spring, that requisitions were made last year for ice-breakers. Those requisitions could not be granted owing to the shortage in the icebreaking boats. It is just as important to have the ice broken early in Sydney harbour as it is to keep the river St. Lawrence open, because perhaps there are no other two points where there is so much coal carrying trade as between Sydney and Montreal. Last spring the Stanley was in Sydney and did very good work there in the way of ice-breaking between the mouth of the harbour and the shipping pier of the Dominion Coal Company. It is true she became disabled there, but she became disabled at other points also. I have it from the Dominion Coal Company's engineers that it is quite practicable to have the harbour of Sydney open very early in the month of March. It is proved that it is possible to keep the harbour open practically all winter between the shipping pier of the Dominion Coal Company and the mouth of the harbour. I am only too glad to give my support to the passing of this item, provided that other places besides the S,t. Lawrence river, and Thunder bay are given some consideration. I maintain that it is just as important to the whole of Canada to have Sydney harbour open early in the year as any other point; for, if a shortage of coal takes place in Montreal in the spring, it is quite practicable to ship coal from Sydney harbour to Montreal in March, provided proper attention is given to icebreaking in Sydney harbour. Many imagine that Sydney harbour is frozen over for seven months in the year. As a matter of fact, there are some winter seasons when it is open all through. It is open all year round between the mouth of the harbour and North Sydney, and it is only a matter, I should say, of a little ice breaking to have navigation open all the year round to the Atlantic, and so to the Atlantic ports. I take it that it is important to Canada that the great centres, Montreal and Quebec, should have coal. I would like to impress on the minister that next spring he should have icebreaking apparatus in Sydney harbour.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
We had a little discussion on this subject this afternoon, when it was referred to by the hon. member for North Cape Breton. We have done all we could do with the equipment at our command, and will do what we can in the future. In the spring of 1912, we were able to do a great deal more than we did this year, when the Stanley met with an accident and was laid up for repairs. We have no icebreakers down there except the Stanley and the boats that run across the Northumberland straits. In about a Mr. CARROLL.
year and a half we shall have icebreakers available, as we are going to have new icebreakers in the St. Lawrence, which will free the Montcalm for work along the gulf; and when the car ferry is put on between Prince Edward Island and New Brunswick, there will be no further use on that route for the Earl Grey and the Minto, both icebreakers. There are demands from other places, such as Dalhousie and Gaspe.	No doubt icebreakers will open the harbours earlier, and so will help the Dominion generally.
How long were the Government able to keep the harbour open at Thunder Bay ?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
Until the 10th of January, and this year we got it open earlier than usual. The result was to prevent the congestion of grain on the railway in the Northwest. The grain people tell us that it was of the greatest possible advantage. Probably from 13,000,000 to 14,000,000 bushels of grain were taken off the railway and put into ships, and the congestion of the winter before last did not exist last winter.
To provide for the administration of pilotage and the maintenance and repair of the steamer Eureka, $36,000.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
At Father Point. She

Has the minister any control over pilotage commissions such as we have in Cape Breton ?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: There is a pilotage commission who have direct control; they are appointed by Order in Council. If the pilots do not discharge their duty satisfactorily they can be removed by Order in Council.

Old and reliable pilots have been dismissed from the service at Sydney harbour and others have been suspended. They tell me it was for political reasons. As to that, I do not know. I know the minister or the department is not responsible for that, but the commission is responsible. One of the most reliable pilots we have on the coast of Sydney harbour, resident at Low Point, was dismissed a year and a half ago, and his place was filled with an inexperienced man. Many of the mariners who come there have complained to the Pilotage Commission of the appointment of an inexperineced man. It may be that these gentlemen do not see eye to eye with the commission in the matter of politics. But if there is one thing more than another in which a man's politics should not interfere with his job, it is pilotage. A pilot must be an experienced man. He does not get his position, nor his

pay from the Government; his pay comes out of the fees the pilots themselves earn. It seems to me unfair to dismiss a man from such a position even for partisanship. I am not finding fault with the minister, because I know he has no control over that. But I suggest that he point out to the commission that it is more important to have reliable and experienced men to look after the ships coming into our harbours than to have men belonging to one particular party. I know that political friends of the minister of Marine and Fisheries have regretted the dismissal of these men without his knowledge and authority. Steps should be taken so that men who have been engaged in the pilotage business for years should not be disturbed.

I brought this matter
to the notice of the commission before, but there is a little history about it that the minister should know. I have known Sydney harbour intimately for thirty years. For the first ten years of that time there was no such thing as the board of commissioners, and a man went piloting as he went fishing. If he got a steamer to bring in, he got his fee. There was very often a battle royal as to who should reach the vessel first. So the men got together and organized-grit and tory. There was no talk of politics; they were simply a body of men engaged in business. Everybody joined the organization, and, so far as I know, no politics entered into it until this Government came into power. In the fifteen years of liberal rule only one was suspended, and that was on 'the ground that he sold liquor while a pilot, and the board themselves agreed to his dismissal. But twenty-five per cent, perhaps thirty per cent of the pilots have been dismissed since this Government came into power. A man is given to understand that if he is not a tory he is not needed in the pilot business. That is high-handed, it may have been a miner or fisherman who gave up all his time to pilotage twenty-five years ago.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: Do they want apprentices there?

Yes, and everyone of
the apprentices have been dismissed as well as the pilots and the authorities had to go out to the ordinary rank and file to get men to put in their places. Five years of apprenticeship is supposed to qualify a man to be a pilot. They had to go out to the farmers and miners and people along the shore and pick up pilots and put them 'in charge of ships of enormous value to bring them into that harbour. That is not business and there is no justification for it.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
We have no knowledge of the matter in the department; I shall make inquiry about it. Speaking without having
the facts all before me it seems to me a most unwise thing to dismiss the apprentices who would be pilots in the future. Of course, it may be that there are men acting as pilots who from infirmity of hearing or 'eyesight are no longer fit for the position.
In Quebec they have to undergo an examination in this respect every year and usually a certain number have to drop out.
Pensions of $300 each to pilots, $6,300.

I should like to know
if the department intends to act on the report of the Pilotage Commission?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
We are already acting on it so far as the recommendations for the Montreal district are concerned. We are practically able ,to act on the recommendations without legislation. In the Montreal district, one of the recommendations is to give larger remuneration to the pilots. We are doing that. Another is that the Montreal office in Quebec should be placed in a different position. There are some regulations about the employment of pilots for special lines. If a man is employed for a special line of ships his name is taken off the tour de role. It was recommended that' a pilot would not have to be taken off the tour de role if a line had a vessel coming up only once a month. There is a provision that two lines having two ships coming once a month will get the services ~ of the same pilot. There are a number of regulations of that sort. The pilotage service of the Montreal district seems to the commission to be very satisfactory and the changes are not drastic or important. With regard to the Quebec district, the changes recommended are more important and it may be that we shall have to have some legislation at another session with regard to that. While the Minister of Marine. has nominally authority over the pilotage, as a matter of fact, he has little authority over the Quebec pilots, what is called the corporation of pilots has power to appoint pilots and arrange everything. The recommendation is that that corporation shall be abolished and the control placed directly in the minister. Then there is a recommendation that the present system of pooling the earnings of all the pilots shall be abolished.
It is thought that this system discourages individual effort on the part of the pilots. They also recommend a change with regard to the system at Father Point by which pilots are placed upon the ships. In the old days the pilots had sailing boats that used to sail up and down the river and they made their farthest point down the river west of Father Point. By arrangement with the Marine Department they agreed to give up the sailing boats and the Department of Marine and Fisheries provided a steamer that would always be

at Father Point to take a pilot out to the vessel. This steamer is the Eureka. The pilots go down	and lives in
boarding houses and wait until the ship comes, and they are taken on the Eureka to the ship. They say\ that it is a bad system, that these men are loafing about boarding houses for hours at a time, and they practically put it that there is a danger of their drinking, and that a pilot in this condition is not fit to pilot a ship. They recommend that a steamer be purchased that will be large enough to afford accommodation for the pilots so that they can go down and remain on the ship, under the supervision of an official of the department who will preserve order, and stay on the boat until their services are required.

I thank the minister for his clear explanation. Too much care cannot be taken in connection with the organization on a sound basis of the pilotage system. My hon. friend knows that the St. Lawrence, especially last year, has been most unfortunate in view of the numerous accidents that have taken place. We speak very often about the high insurance rates. The rates have gone up of late years on account of such accidents and certainly any action of my right hon. friend to place matters in a proper position is to be highly commended. The Shipping Federation in Montreal and the business community are waiting with anxiety the outcome of this pilotage question which has been a vexeLT question for many years.

speechtext:

years ago it was closed and an arrangement was made with the commissioners of the public hospital to take all sailors. that something be done in regard to the matter. I regard it as very important, j

What is

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
Oyster culture to-day,
under the agreement that we have made, is largely being carried on by the provinces. In Prince Edward Island the Government have gone to work on a most extensive and progressive scale. They have granted leases for 5,000 acres of barren oyster beds, the people who have leased the beds are planting them with new oysters and it is expected that the oyster industry in a few years in Prince Edward Island will be restored to what it was before it was depleted, and will be a valuable asset to the province. I understand that a similar course is being adopted in New Brunswick and Nova Scotia. I do not think that in New Brunswick they have .gone ahead as fast as they have in Prince Edward Island. In Nova Scotia we have also entered into the same arrangement with the provincial government which practically gives them the control. Following the amendment of

the Fisheries Act of last session enabling agreements to be entered into with the provincial governments whereby they would take up the leasing of areas on which to carry on artificial culture and cultivation of oysters, agreements ere entered into with the Maritime provinces and British Columbia. The work carried on by the federal government will be limited. An experimental oyster bed was, two years ago, laid out in Richmond bay, Prince Edward Island, and the following year in Caribou harbour, Pictou county. Last year an experimental bed was started in Bay du Vin, but was not finished. It will be completed during the coming year and the oyster expert will therefore devote his time to the cleaning and improving of the public beds.

speechtext:

Mr. HAZEN. '
To provide for an exhibit of fresh and cured food fish at the Toronto annual exhibition, $10,000,
I would like to ask the minister on what terms the dog fish plant at Shippegan is to be operated this year?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: I regret to say that we have been unable to make a lease there. We thought we had one made but the gentleman with whom we were dealing backed out.

This seems to be a new item in regard to the exhibit of fresh fish at Toronto. I suggest to the minister that they establish a fish kitchen at the exhibition, have some fresh fish cooked in a nice w'ay, sold cheaply and served to the people of Ontario so that they will get a taste of the good fish we have on the Atlantic coast. I am quite sure that if you once give them a taste of it they will not eat any more lake fish but will want our fish all the time. I think if that is carried out it will be a very good idea.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
I am glad to hear my hon. friend say that because that is exactly what the department is arranging to do in addition to making the exhibit. We were approached over a year ago by the -directors of the exhibition. They wanted us to make an exhibit at the fair last year. We felt that we could not, in the time at our disposal, make an exhibit that would be a credit to the department, so declined to undertake it. After talking it over we came to the conclusion that it would be good for the exhibition and a good advertisement of our good fish as well if we had at the Toronto exhibition, which is the largest annual exhibition held on the continent of North America, a first-class exhibition of the food fishes of the country arranged in an attractive manner. It would also introduce Atlantic food fishes into the West. The officials of the department who are working out the plan have made a recommendation along the line- which has been suggested by my hon. friend from Guysborough.
Salaries, building and maintenance of fishbreeding establishments, $400,000.

There is a large amount of money expended on this particular work, not too large, I admit, and I would like to ask if careful attention is paid to the appointment of officers in charge of these establishments. I have in mind a particular hatchery in Nova Scotia where the department appointed a man as superintendent two years ago. I cannot conceive of this man being a proper person for the position inasmuch as he is seventy years old. I would expect a man filling a position of such importance to have at least reasonable youth to his credit.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: My officials tell me they pay as careful attention as they can, but no doubt mistakes are made at times. A trouble does exist, I think, with regard to fish hatcheries in the fact that we have not in Canada enough men trained in that branch of science. Within the last few months the departmental officers have arranged-and I have approved of a schedule that has been prepared, arranging for the officers in the different fish hatcheries, what pay they shall receive when appointed, what the increases, and what the maximum shall be. We are trying to work out a system under which we can get better-trained officials than we have at the present time. The work has gone on very rapidly in the past two years, almost too rapidly. There have been splendid results from the salmon hatcheries, but it is doubtful if there have been any results at all from the lobster hatcheries. There are white-fish, pickerel, and salmon hatcheries which have given good results. The demand for these hatcheries is becoming greater all the time in places where streams and lakes are getting less full of fish. On Lake Erie, where there are hatcheries, there is no doubt that the supply of white-fish has been pretty well kept up; whereas in some of the other great lakes where there are no hatcheries the supply of whiteflsh has very largely decreased.
The salmon hatchery at Gaspe is quite a success.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: The salmon fishers around that coast tell me there are more salmon there than there were ten or fifteen years ago. They attribute it to that hatchery. Some of it may be due to the protection being better than it was twenty or twenty-five years ago. The number of shad was becoming less, and last year we established shad hatcheries. A shad hatchery cannot be made like other hatcheries in a fixed place; it has to be removed from place to place because the shad is such a delicate fish. You cannot take it out like a salmon, and strip it; you have to get it oyer the spawning bed when it is quite ripe. If you do not do that, you loose the shads and spawn and everything else. At the first hatchery of the kind in the Dominion last year, they got about 5,000,000 eggs that were deposited. This year they expect to do very much better. As to what the result will be, we cannot tell for perhaps three or four years. I have great hopes that it will increase the number of shads.
Is the hon. ministei going to ask for tenders for a boat on Lake Winnipeg?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: We asked for tenders. It is to take the place of a boat called the Lady of the Lake, which has been the Marine and Fisheries boat there. Not a single firm tendered. They considered that Lake Winnipeg was an out-of-the-way place, and they would have to build the boat largely here and set it up when they got it to the lake. Therefore we decided to build the boat ourselves in the Government yards at Sorel.

Whilst I was reading the Star to-night I found what I wanted to quote this afternoon about ship construction in Canada. It is as follows:
Collingwood, Out., May 23.-The steel freighter, James Carruthers, claimed to he the largest of its kind ever constructed in the British Empire, was successfully launched yesterday at the yards of the Collingwood Ship-building Company.
The new vessel was christened by Miss Lillian A. Wright, daughter of Mr. A. A. Wright, general manager of the St. Lawrence and Chicago Navigation Company, under whose colours the James Carruthers will ply on the upper lakes.
The vessel is 550 feet long, 38 feet beam, and 30 feet deep, and has a carrying capacity of 375,000 bushels of wheat, or 600,000 bushels of oats, and about 11,000 tons of coal.
I submit that to my hon. friend for his consideration.

How is the
Advisory Fishery Board getting on?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: We have it organized this year. There are three divisions, an eastern division, a Pacific division and a prairie division, the prairie division being the (provinces of Manitoba, Saskatchewan and Alberta where conditions are different. There have been two meetings of the Atlantic division here, and one meeting of the Pacific division. I think there is to be a meeting of the prairie division in June. The officials of the department believe it will be a great help.

My hon. friend suggests that lobster hatcheries are not doing good work. There is evidence to the contrary in some places. The hatchery that was established in Pictou a number of years ago has increased the crop of lobsters in that vicinity. The same thing prevails at Canso, but the Canso hatchery has not been operated so long as the one at Pictou. After his experts have been experimenting for some ten or fifteen years it is humiliating that the minister has to come before the committee and say he does not know. If his experts on this question were as they ought to be, they would follow up the spawn they put in the isea and be able to tell the minister whether any of them thrive or not.
Are any new lobster ponds to Mr. MACLEAN (Halifax): Have the lob-to be bought this year?	sters'been placed in the pond in Digby?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: No.

There is a natural lobster
pond at West Pubnico, Yarmouth county. An official of the department has inspected that pond three times, and I understand he had made a favourable report. The pond can be got for a very reasonable price. There is an increase in this vote of $77,700. That pond, I imagine could be bought for $1,000. I see that last year the minister purchased a lot in Digby for $10,000, which has been assessed for the last three or four years for $300 to $350. If the money is as plentiful as that with the Marine and Fisheries Department it is only fair they should purchase this pond at West Pubnico which will be of benefit to the fisherman of that county as well as of Shelbourne. It is a natural pond and the water flows into it and out of it as the tide moves, and no fresh water goes into it.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
The hon. gentleman
knows that the value of a property cannot be determined by the assessment. I am prepared to justify the purchase of that property and amount paid. It was reported upon by the officers of the department and every precaution taken. The matter of Pubnico has been before the department and I believe that the officers think it a good site, but we have decided not to extend the lobster ponds this year.
What did the minister get in this purchase?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
The area is nineteen acres. A dam has been built and a pond constructed. To go back to the other matter, what strikes me as a non-expert is that more information ought to be had along the line referred to by the hon. member for Guysboro. We do not know whether the lobsters which are hatched out and put in the ocean are devoured by the other fish or what becomes of them. I do not think anything is known to prove that the lobster hatchery has been productive of very good results. I am glad to heaT what the hon. gentleman says about Pictou and Canso. But should not we keep the lobsters after they are hatched out in the pond, place them in favourable locations where they could not be preyed upon, and so make sure that a fair proportion of them reach maturity. I think the investigation should take place, and the proper body to make it would be the biological board. This is without casting reflections on the officers of the department who are capable and zealous men. But we have not at this time such information as I speak of.	.
